text:
8.14 Glossary







Term
Definition




Anticlockwise moment
Turning effect that tends to rotate an object anticlockwise about a pivot


Centre of gravity
The point through which the entire weight of an object may be considered to act


Clockwise moment
Turning effect that tends to rotate an object clockwise about a pivot


Equilibrium
State where resultant force = 0 and resultant moment = 0; object is at rest or moving with constant velocity without rotation


Moment of a force
Turning effect of a force about a pivot: \(M = F \times d_{\perp}\) (unit: N m)


Neutral equilibrium
When displaced, an object stays in its new position (CG remains at same height)


Perpendicular distance
Shortest distance from pivot to the line of action of a force; used in moment calculations


Pivot
Fixed point about which an object can rotate


Principle of moments
For an object in rotational equilibrium, sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments


Stable equilibrium
When displaced, an object returns to its original position (CG rises)


Unstable equilibrium
When displaced, an object moves further from its original position (CG falls)

title: 9  Momentum
text:
9.1 Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
Core Content:

title: 9  Momentum
text:
Define momentum as mass × velocity; recall and use the equation \(p = mv\)
Define impulse as force × time for which force acts; recall and use the equation \(\text{impulse} = F\Delta t = \Delta(mv)\)

title: 9  Momentum
text:
9.2 What Is Momentum?

9.2.1 Definition and Formula
Momentum is a measure of the quantity of motion possessed by a moving object. It is defined as the product of mass and velocity:
\[p = mv\]
Where: - \(p\) = momentum (kg m/s) - \(m\) = mass (kg) - \(v\) = velocity (m/s)






Note



Key Concept: Momentum is a vector quantity—it has both magnitude and direction. The direction of momentum is the same as the direction of velocity.




9.2.2 Understanding Momentum Through Examples







Situation
Explanation




Fast-moving arrow vs. slow-moving arrow (same mass)
The faster arrow has greater momentum and causes more impact on the target


Elephant vs. dog (same velocity)
The elephant has greater momentum due to its larger mass


Two trains moving in opposite directions
They have different momenta because momentum includes direction (one positive, one negative)





9.2.3 Calculating Momentum: Worked Examples

9.2.3.1 Example 1: Basic Momentum Calculation
Question: Calculate the momentum of: (a) a runner of mass 50 kg running at 4 m/s (b) a soccer ball of mass 400 g moving at 25 m/s (c) a car of total mass 1000 kg travelling at 18 km/h
Solution:
(a) Runner: \[p = mv = 50 \times 4 = \boxed{200 \text{ kg m/s}}\]
(b) Soccer ball: First convert mass: \(400 \text{ g} = 0.4 \text{ kg}\) \[p = mv = 0.4 \times 25 = \boxed{10 \text{ kg m/s}}\]
(c) Car: First convert speed: \(18 \text{ km/h} = \frac{18 \times 1000}{3600} = 5 \text{ m/s}\) \[p = mv = 1000 \times 5 = \boxed{5000 \text{ kg m/s}}\]



9.2.3.2 Example 2: Finding Mass or Velocity from Momentum
Question: (a) What is the speed of a bus with mass 8000 kg and momentum of 88 000 kg m/s? (b) A car travelling at 12 m/s has a momentum of 14 400 kg m/s. Calculate its mass.
Solution:
(a) Speed of bus: \[p = mv \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = \frac{p}{m} = \frac{88000}{8000} = \boxed{11 \text{ m/s}}\]
(b) Mass of car: \[p = mv \quad \Rightarrow \quad m = \frac{p}{v} = \frac{14400}{12} = \boxed{1200 \text{ kg}}\]






Warning



Important: To calculate momentum in SI units (kg m/s), mass must be in kilograms and velocity in metres per second. Always check and convert units before calculating.

title: 9  Momentum
text:
9.3 Impulse and Change in Momentum

9.3.1 What Is Impulse?
When a force acts on an object for a period of time, it causes a change in the object’s momentum. This product of force and time is called impulse.
Definition: \[\text{Impulse} = F \times \Delta t\]
Where: - \(F\) = average resultant force (N) - \(\Delta t\) = time interval for which the force acts (s) - Unit: newton-second (N s)


9.3.2 The Impulse–Momentum Theorem
The impulse of a resultant force equals the change in momentum of the object:
\[F\Delta t = \Delta(mv) = \Delta p\]
Where: - \(\Delta p\) = change in momentum = \(p_{\text{final}} - p_{\text{initial}}\) (kg m/s or N s)






Note



Key Insight: The SI unit for impulse (N s) is equivalent to the SI unit for momentum (kg m/s). This confirms that impulse and change in momentum represent the same physical quantity.




9.3.3 Calculating Impulse: Worked Examples

9.3.3.1 Example 3: Impulse on a Kicked Ball
Question: A boy kicks a stationary ball of mass 0.4 kg with an average force of 100 N. The ball moves at 5 m/s immediately afterwards. Calculate: (a) the impulse of the force exerted on the ball (b) the time of contact between his boot and the ball
Solution:
(a) Impulse = change in momentum: \[\Delta p = mv_{\text{final}} - mv_{\text{initial}} = (0.4 \times 5) - (0.4 \times 0) = 2 \text{ kg m/s} = \boxed{2 \text{ N s}}\]
(b) Time of contact: \[F\Delta t = \Delta p \quad \Rightarrow \quad \Delta t = \frac{\Delta p}{F} = \frac{2}{100} = \boxed{0.02 \text{ s}}\]



9.3.3.2 Example 4: Impulse with Direction Change (Extended)
Question: A ball of mass 0.625 kg hits the ground at 4 m/s. It bounces back from the ground at 3.8 m/s. Calculate the impulse on the ball.
Solution:
Step 1: Assign directions (upwards = positive) - Initial velocity (downwards): \(u = -4.0 \text{ m/s}\) - Final velocity (upwards): \(v = +3.8 \text{ m/s}\)
Step 2: Calculate change in momentum: \[\Delta p = mv - mu = m(v - u)\] \[\Delta p = 0.625 \times [3.8 - (-4.0)] = 0.625 \times 7.8 = \boxed{4.88 \text{ N s (upwards)}}\]






Warning



Common Error: Forgetting that velocity is a vector. When an object reverses direction, the change in velocity is \(v - (-u) = v + u\), not \(v - u\).

title: 9  Momentum
section: 9.4 Resultant Force and Rate of Change of Momentum
text:
9.4 Resultant Force and Rate of Change of Momentum

9.4.1 Newton’s Second Law in Momentum Form
From the impulse–momentum theorem: \[F\Delta t = \Delta p\]
Rearranging gives the definition of resultant force:
\[F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\]
Resultant force on an object is the change in momentum per unit time.


9.4.2 Connection to \(F = ma\)
For an object of constant mass: \[F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{\Delta(mv)}{\Delta t} = m\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = ma\]
Thus, \(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\) is the more general form of Newton’s Second Law, applicable even when mass changes (e.g., rockets expelling fuel).


9.4.3 Application: Crumple Zones and Safety
Worked Example 5: Force in a Car Crash
Question: A car of mass 1250 kg crashes into a concrete wall. The speed of the car is 7.2 m/s just before impact. Calculate the average force on the car if it takes: (a) 0.1 s to come to a complete stop (b) 0.4 s to come to a complete stop
Solution:
Step 1: Calculate initial momentum (forward = positive): \[p_{\text{initial}} = mv = 1250 \times 7.2 = 9000 \text{ kg m/s}\] \[p_{\text{final}} = 0 \text{ kg m/s (car stops)}\] \[\Delta p = 0 - 9000 = -9000 \text{ N s}\]
(a) Force for \(\Delta t = 0.1 \text{ s}\): \[F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{-9000}{0.1} = \boxed{-90000 \text{ N}}\]
(b) Force for \(\Delta t = 0.4 \text{ s}\): \[F = \frac{-9000}{0.4} = \boxed{-22500 \text{ N}}\]
Interpretation: The negative sign indicates the force acts backwards (opposing motion). Increasing the stopping time by a factor of 4 reduces the force by a factor of 4.






Note



Safety Application: Crumple zones, seat belts, and airbags increase the time over which momentum changes during a collision, thereby reducing the force on passengers and minimising injury.

title: 9  Momentum
section: 9.5 The Principle of Conservation of Momentum
text:
9.5 The Principle of Conservation of Momentum

9.5.1 Statement of the Principle

When two or more objects interact in the absence of external forces, the total momentum of the system before the interaction equals the total momentum after the interaction.

\[\sum p_{\text{before}} = \sum p_{\text{after}}\]


9.5.2 Conditions for Conservation







Condition
Explanation




Closed system
No external forces act on the system (or external forces are negligible during the interaction)


One-dimensional problems
For IGCSE, we consider collisions and explosions along a straight line


Vector addition
Assign one direction as positive; opposite direction is negative





9.5.3 Types of Interactions








Type
Description
Example




Collision (objects stick together)
Objects move together after impact
Two trolleys coupling; car crash


Collision (objects separate)
Objects rebound after impact
Billiard balls; Newton’s cradle


Explosion (objects separate from rest)
Stationary system breaks apart
Firework; recoil of a gun






9.5.4 Applying Conservation of Momentum: Worked Examples

9.5.4.1 Example 6: Collision with Objects Sticking Together
Question: Trolley A of mass 2 kg travelling at 2 m/s collides with a stationary trolley B of mass 3 kg. The two trolleys stick together after the collision. Calculate: (a) the velocity of the combined trolleys immediately after collision (b) the impulse experienced by trolley B
Solution:
(a) Velocity after collision:
Step 1: Total momentum before collision: \[p_{\text{before}} = m_A v_A + m_B v_B = (2 \times 2) + (3 \times 0) = 4 \text{ kg m/s}\]
Step 2: Total momentum after collision (combined mass = 5 kg): \[p_{\text{after}} = (m_A + m_B)v = 5v\]
Step 3: Apply conservation: \[5v = 4 \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = \frac{4}{5} = \boxed{0.8 \text{ m/s (forward)}}\]
(b) Impulse on trolley B: \[\text{Impulse} = \Delta p_B = m_B v_{\text{final}} - m_B v_{\text{initial}} = (3 \times 0.8) - (3 \times 0) = \boxed{2.4 \text{ N s (forward)}}\]



9.5.4.2 Example 7: Collision with Objects Separating
Question: Ball A of mass 0.12 kg is moving forward at 0.40 m/s. It collides with a stationary ball B of mass 0.09 kg. After collision, ball B moves forward at 0.40 m/s. What is the velocity of ball A after the collision?
Solution:
Step 1: Total momentum before collision: \[p_{\text{before}} = (0.12 \times 0.40) + (0.09 \times 0) = 0.048 \text{ kg m/s}\]
Step 2: Total momentum after collision (let \(v\) = velocity of A after): \[p_{\text{after}} = (0.12 \times v) + (0.09 \times 0.40) = 0.12v + 0.036\]
Step 3: Apply conservation: \[0.12v + 0.036 = 0.048\] \[0.12v = 0.012\] \[v = \frac{0.012}{0.12} = \boxed{0.10 \text{ m/s (forward)}}\]



9.5.4.3 Example 8: Explosion from Rest (Extended)
Question: Two ice skaters, A (mass 80 kg) and B (mass 50 kg), are initially stationary on a frictionless rink. They push each other apart. Skater A moves off with velocity 0.5 m/s. Calculate: (a) the momentum of skater A (b) the momentum of skater B (c) the velocity of skater B
Solution:
(a) Momentum of A: \[p_A = m_A v_A = 80 \times 0.5 = \boxed{40 \text{ kg m/s}}\]
(b) Momentum of B: Total momentum before = 0 (both stationary) By conservation: \(p_A + p_B = 0\) \[p_B = -p_A = \boxed{-40 \text{ kg m/s}}\]
(c) Velocity of B: \[v_B = \frac{p_B}{m_B} = \frac{-40}{50} = \boxed{-0.8 \text{ m/s}}\]
Interpretation: Skater B moves at 0.8 m/s in the opposite direction to skater A.






Warning



Important: In explosion problems, the total initial momentum is zero. Therefore, the momenta of the separating objects must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

title: 9  Momentum
text:
9.6 Key Concepts Summary

9.6.1 Core Concepts

Momentum: \(p = mv\); vector quantity (kg m/s); direction same as velocity
Impulse: \(F\Delta t = \Delta p\); equals change in momentum; unit N s ≡ kg m/s
Resultant force: \(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\); rate of change of momentum (general form of \(F = ma\))
Conservation of momentum: \(\sum p_{\text{before}} = \sum p_{\text{after}}\) for closed systems with no external forces
Vector handling: Assign one direction as positive; opposite direction is negative; add algebraically



9.6.2 Extended Concepts

Direction changes: When an object reverses direction, \(\Delta v = v - (-u) = v + u\)
Safety applications: Increasing collision time reduces force (\(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\))
Explosions: Initial momentum = 0 → final momenta are equal and opposite

title: 9  Momentum
text:
9.7 Common Misconceptions

9.7.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Momentum is the same as force”
Incorrect: “A fast-moving object has a large force”
Correct: - Momentum (\(p = mv\)) is a property of a moving object - Force (\(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\)) is what changes momentum - An object can have large momentum with zero resultant force (moving at constant velocity)



9.7.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Momentum is conserved in all collisions”
Incorrect: “Total momentum is always conserved, even with friction”
Correct: - Momentum is conserved only in closed systems with no external forces - In real collisions, friction or air resistance may act as external forces - For IGCSE problems, we assume external forces are negligible during the brief collision



9.7.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Heavier objects always have more momentum”
Incorrect: “A truck always has more momentum than a car”
Correct: - Momentum depends on both mass and velocity: \(p = mv\) - A light object moving very fast can have more momentum than a heavy slow object - Example: A 0.01 kg bullet at 500 m/s (\(p = 5\) kg m/s) vs. a 1000 kg car at 0.001 m/s (\(p = 1\) kg m/s)



9.7.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Impulse and momentum are different physical quantities”
Incorrect: “Impulse (N s) and momentum (kg m/s) cannot be compared”
Correct: - The units are equivalent: \(1 \text{ N s} = 1 \text{ kg m/s}\) - Impulse equals change in momentum: \(F\Delta t = \Delta p\) - They represent the same physical dimension, just different contexts



9.7.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “In a collision, both objects experience the same change in velocity”
Incorrect: “When two objects collide, they change speed by the same amount”
Correct: - Both objects experience equal and opposite impulses (Newton’s Third Law) - But \(\Delta v = \frac{\text{impulse}}{m}\), so the lighter object experiences a larger change in velocity - Example: A tennis ball hitting a wall rebounds with large \(\Delta v\); the wall’s \(\Delta v\) is negligible



9.7.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “If momentum is conserved, kinetic energy is also conserved”
Incorrect: “Conservation of momentum means no energy is lost”
Correct: - Momentum is always conserved in closed systems - Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions - Most real collisions are inelastic: momentum conserved, but kinetic energy is converted to heat, sound, or deformation

title: 9  Momentum
text:
9.8 Worked Examples

9.8.1 Example 9: Multi-Step Conservation Problem
Question: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 8.0 m/s collides with a lorry of mass 2800 kg travelling at 2.0 m/s in the same direction. After the collision, the two vehicles stick together. Calculate their speed immediately after the collision.
Solution:
Step 1: Assign direction (forward = positive)
Step 2: Total momentum before collision: \[p_{\text{before}} = (1200 \times 8.0) + (2800 \times 2.0) = 9600 + 5600 = 15200 \text{ kg m/s}\]
Step 3: Total momentum after collision (combined mass = 4000 kg): \[p_{\text{after}} = 4000v\]
Step 4: Apply conservation: \[4000v = 15200\] \[v = \frac{15200}{4000} = \boxed{3.8 \text{ m/s (forward)}}\]



9.8.2 Example 10: Force from Momentum Change (Extended)
Question: A basketball player bounces a ball on the ground. The ball hits the ground 10 times in 20 seconds. The average change in momentum for each collision is 15 kg m/s. What is the average force that the ground exerts on the ball?
Solution:
Step 1: Total change in momentum over 20 s: \[\Delta p_{\text{total}} = 10 \times 15 = 150 \text{ kg m/s}\]
Step 2: Average force: \[F_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta p_{\text{total}}}{\Delta t} = \frac{150}{20} = \boxed{7.5 \text{ N}}\]






Note



Interpretation: This is the average force over the 20-second interval. The actual force during each brief impact is much larger, but acts for a very short time.

title: 9  Momentum
text:
9.9 Practice Questions

9.9.1 Core Level
1. Define momentum. State its SI unit.
2. Calculate the momentum of a cyclist of mass 70 kg riding at 6 m/s.
3. A force of 200 N acts on an object for 0.5 s. Calculate the impulse delivered.
4. A 0.5 kg ball is moving at 4 m/s. A force acts on it for 0.2 s, changing its velocity to 10 m/s in the same direction. Calculate:


the change in momentum


the average force


5. State the principle of conservation of momentum.
6. Two trolleys, A (mass 1.5 kg, velocity 2 m/s) and B (mass 2.5 kg, stationary), collide and stick together. Calculate their common velocity after collision.
7. Explain why crumple zones in cars reduce the force on passengers during a collision.
8. A stationary firework explodes into two pieces. Piece X (mass 0.2 kg) moves left at 15 m/s. Piece Y has mass 0.3 kg. Calculate the velocity of piece Y.


9.9.2 Extended Level
9. A ball of mass 0.2 kg strikes a wall at 8 m/s and rebounds at 6 m/s. Calculate:


the change in momentum of the ball


the impulse exerted by the wall on the ball


If the contact time is 0.05 s, calculate the average force on the ball


10. A car of mass 1500 kg travelling at 20 m/s collides head-on with a van of mass 2500 kg travelling at 10 m/s in the opposite direction. After the collision, they stick together. Calculate:


their common velocity after collision


the change in momentum of the car


the impulse experienced by the van


11. A rocket of mass 5000 kg (including fuel) is stationary in space. It ejects 100 kg of fuel backwards at 2000 m/s. Calculate the velocity of the rocket after ejection.
12. Explain, using the equation \(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\), why:


catching a fast ball with ‘soft hands’ (moving hands backwards) reduces the force on your hands


airbags reduce injury in car crashes


13. Two ice skaters push off each other. Skater P (mass 60 kg) moves at 1.2 m/s. Skater Q moves at 0.9 m/s in the opposite direction. Calculate the mass of skater Q.

title: 9  Momentum
text:
9.10 Laboratory Investigation

9.10.1 Experiment 6.1: Verifying Conservation of Momentum
Objective: To investigate the conservation of momentum in a one-dimensional collision using trolleys on a friction-compensated runway.
Apparatus: - Two dynamics trolleys with Velcro attachments (for sticking collisions)

Friction-compensated runway
Light gates or ticker-timer with tape
Electronic balance
Metre rule
Data logger (optional)

Variables: - Independent: Masses of trolleys; initial velocity of moving trolley

Dependent: Final velocity of combined trolleys (or both trolleys if separating)
Controlled: Runway angle (friction compensation); same collision mechanism

Procedure (Collision with Sticking):

Measure and record masses \(m_A\) and \(m_B\) of the two trolleys.
Set up the runway with a slight incline to compensate for friction (trolleys move at constant speed when given a gentle push).
Place trolley B stationary at the centre of the runway.
Give trolley A a gentle push so it collides with B; the Velcro causes them to stick together.
Use light gates or ticker-tape to measure:

Velocity of A before collision (\(v_A\))
Velocity of combined trolleys after collision (\(v_{\text{combined}}\))

Repeat three times for reliability.
Calculate:

Total momentum before: \(p_{\text{before}} = m_A v_A\)
Total momentum after: \(p_{\text{after}} = (m_A + m_B) v_{\text{combined}}\)

Compare \(p_{\text{before}}\) and \(p_{\text{after}}\); calculate percentage difference.

Data Table:













Trial
\(m_A\) (kg)
\(m_B\) (kg)
\(v_A\) (m/s)
\(v_{\text{combined}}\) (m/s)
\(p_{\text{before}}\) (kg m/s)
\(p_{\text{after}}\) (kg m/s)
% Difference




1









2









3










Analysis:

For each trial, calculate percentage difference: \[\% \text{ diff} = \frac{|p_{\text{before}} - p_{\text{after}}|}{(p_{\text{before}} + p_{\text{after}})/2} \times 100\%\]
If all differences are within ±10% (typical experimental accuracy), conservation of momentum is verified.
Identify sources of error: residual friction, air resistance, timing inaccuracies.

Precautions: - ✓ Ensure runway is properly friction-compensated before starting

✓ Use light gates or ticker-timer for accurate velocity measurement
✓ Ensure trolleys collide centrally to avoid rotational motion
✓ Repeat measurements to obtain reliable averages

Conclusion Template: “The experiment verified the principle of conservation of momentum: within experimental error (±___%), the total momentum before collision equalled the total momentum after collision. This confirms that in the absence of significant external forces, momentum is conserved in one-dimensional collisions.”
Extension (Supplement): - Investigate elastic collisions (using magnetic repulsion instead of Velcro)

Measure kinetic energy before and after to distinguish elastic vs. inelastic collisions

title: 9  Momentum
text:
9.14 Glossary







Term
Definition




Closed system
A system on which no external forces act; required for momentum conservation


Conservation of momentum
Principle that total momentum of a closed system remains constant during interactions


Impulse
Product of force and time for which it acts; equals change in momentum (\(F\Delta t = \Delta p\))


Inelastic collision
Collision in which kinetic energy is not conserved (converted to heat, sound, deformation); momentum is conserved


Momentum (\(p\))
Product of mass and velocity (\(p = mv\)); vector quantity; SI unit: kg m/s


Resultant force
Single force equivalent to all forces acting on an object; \(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\)


Vector quantity
Physical quantity with both magnitude and direction (e.g., momentum, velocity, force)

text:

title: 10  Energy Stores
text:
10.2 What Is Energy?

10.2.1 Definition
In physics:

Energy is the capacity to do work.


The SI unit of energy is the joule (J)
Work usually means making a body or an object move to achieve a purpose
In order to do work, energy is transferred between objects or converted from one form to another







Note



Key Concept: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one store to another or converted from one form to another. The total amount of energy remains constant.

title: 10  Energy Stores
text:
10.3 Different Forms of Energy Stores
Energy may be stored in different forms. Each form represents a different way that energy can be held within a system.

10.3.1 Potential Energy Stores
Potential energy is the stored energy in a system due to its state, shape, or position.








Type of Potential Energy
Description
Example




Chemical potential energy
Energy stored in a substance due to the position of atoms or electrons
Food, fossil fuels, batteries


Elastic (strain) energy
Energy stored in a body due to its elastic deformation
Stretched spring, compressed rubber band


Gravitational potential energy
Energy stored in a body due to its height from the ground
Book on a shelf, water behind a dam


Electrostatic potential energy
Energy stored in the electric fields of static charges
Charged capacitor in a camera flash


Nuclear energy
Energy stored in the nuclei of atoms
Uranium fuel in nuclear power plants





10.3.2 Kinetic Energy Store
Kinetic energy is the energy of a body due to its motion.

Wind has kinetic energy
Sea waves, a spinning frisbee, and a rolling soccer ball all possess kinetic energy
Kinetic energy can be used to do work (e.g., wind turning turbines to generate electricity)



10.3.3 Internal (Thermal) Energy Store
Internal (thermal) energy is the energy stored in a body due to its temperature.

The particles of a hotter body possess more internal energy than those of a colder body
Internal energy is transferred from the hotter body to the colder body



10.3.4 Other Energy Forms








Form
Description
Example




Electrical energy
Energy of an electric charge due to its motion and position
Lightning, mains electricity


Light (electromagnetic) energy
Energy carried by electromagnetic waves
Sunlight, LED lamps


Sound energy
Energy carried by mechanical waves through a medium
Music from a speaker, human voice

title: 10  Energy Stores
text:
10.4 Calculating Energy Stores (Extended)

10.4.1 Kinetic Energy
The kinetic energy (\(E_k\)) of a moving object depends on its mass and speed:
\[E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\]
Where:

\(E_k\) = kinetic energy (J)
\(m\) = mass of the body (kg)
\(v\) = speed of the body (m/s)







Warning



Important: Speed must be in metres per second (m/s) and mass in kilograms (kg) for the answer to be in joules (J).



10.4.1.1 Worked Example 1: Calculating Kinetic Energy
Question:
A bullet of mass 0.02 kg travels at a speed of 1200 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
Solution:
\[E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.02)(1200)^2\]
\[E_k = 0.01 \times 1\,440\,000 = \boxed{14\,400 \text{ J}}\]




10.4.2 Gravitational Potential Energy
The change in gravitational potential energy (\(\Delta E_p\)) depends on the mass, gravitational field strength, and change in height:
\[\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h\]
Where:

\(\Delta E_p\) = change in gravitational potential energy (J)
\(m\) = mass of the body (kg)
\(g\) = gravitational field strength (N/kg); on Earth, \(g \approx 10 \text{ N/kg}\)
\(\Delta h\) = change in height (m)


10.4.2.1 Worked Example 2: Calculating Gravitational Potential Energy
Question:
A package of 5 kg is lifted vertically through a distance of 10 m at a constant speed. Taking \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\), calculate the gravitational potential energy gained by the package.
Solution:
\[\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h = (5)(10)(10) = \boxed{500 \text{ J}}\]



10.4.2.2 Worked Example 3: Energy Conversion in a Pendulum (Extended)
Question:
Figure 7.1 shows a pendulum of mass 0.4 kg oscillating in a vacuum. If P is the lowest position of the pendulum where its maximum speed is 1.5 m/s, calculate:

the maximum kinetic energy of the pendulum
the maximum gravitational potential energy of the pendulum as it rises to its greatest height at Q
the greatest height, \(h\)

(Take \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\))
Solution:
(a) Maximum kinetic energy at P:
\[E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.4)(1.5)^2 = \boxed{0.45 \text{ J}}\]
(b) Maximum gravitational potential energy at Q:
By conservation of energy:
Loss of kinetic energy at P = Gain in gravitational potential energy at Q
\[\therefore \Delta E_p = \boxed{0.45 \text{ J}}\]
(c) Greatest height \(h\):
\[\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h\]
\[0.45 = (0.4)(10)(h)\]
\[h = \frac{0.45}{4.0} = \boxed{0.113 \text{ m}}\]

title: 10  Energy Stores
text:
10.5 7.4 Energy Transfers Between Stores
Energy is transferred between stores during events and processes. The main mechanisms of energy transfer are:

10.5.1 1. Transfer by Forces (Mechanical Work Done)

When a force moves an object through a distance, energy is transferred mechanically
Example: Pushing a trolley transfers chemical energy from your muscles to kinetic energy of the trolley



10.5.2 2. Transfer by Electrical Currents (Electrical Work Done)

When charge flows through a circuit, energy is transferred electrically
Example: A battery transfers chemical energy to electrical energy, which is then transferred to light and thermal energy in a bulb



10.5.3 3. Transfer by Heating

Energy is transferred from a hotter object to a colder object
Example: A hot cup of tea transfers thermal energy to the surrounding air



10.5.4 4. Transfer by Waves

Energy is transferred by electromagnetic, sound, or other waves
Example: Sunlight (electromagnetic waves) transfers energy from the Sun to the Earth




10.5.5 Example: Energy Transfers in an Ideal Pendulum
Figure 7.2 illustrates energy conversions in an ideal pendulum swinging without air resistance:

At position A (highest point):

The pendulum bob has maximum gravitational potential energy
Kinetic energy is zero (bob is momentarily at rest)

As the bob swings down to position B (lowest point):

Gravitational potential energy is converted to kinetic energy
The bob has maximum kinetic energy at B

As the bob swings up to position C (opposite highest point):

Kinetic energy is converted back to gravitational potential energy
The bob is momentarily at rest at C


Flow diagram:
Gravitational potential energy at A
              ↓
      Kinetic energy at B
              ↓
Gravitational potential energy at C






Note



Key Insight: Since energy cannot be created or destroyed, the kinetic energy gained must have been converted from the gravitational potential energy lost. In an ideal pendulum with no air resistance, the bob would swing forever.

title: 10  Energy Stores
section: 10.6 7.5 The Principle of Conservation of Energy
text:
10.6 7.5 The Principle of Conservation of Energy

10.6.1 Statement of the Principle

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can be converted from one form to another or transferred from one body to another. The total amount of energy remains constant.



10.6.2 Applying Conservation of Energy
When energy is converted from one form to another:
\[\text{Total energy before} = \text{Total energy after}\]

10.6.2.1 Worked Example 4: Conservation of Energy in Free Fall
Question:
A 2.0 kg flower pot accidentally falls from a height of 45 m towards the ground. Assuming negligible air resistance and taking \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\), calculate:

the gravitational potential energy of the flower pot before the fall
the speed of the flower pot just before it hits the ground

Solution:
(a) Gravitational potential energy before fall:
\[\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h = (2.0)(10)(45) = \boxed{900 \text{ J}}\]
(b) Speed just before impact:
By conservation of energy:
Loss of gravitational potential energy = Gain in kinetic energy
\[900 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\]
\[900 = \frac{1}{2}(2.0)v^2\]
\[v^2 = \frac{900}{1.0} = 900\]
\[v = \sqrt{900} = \boxed{30 \text{ m/s}}\]

10.7 Key Concepts Summary

10.7.1 Core Concepts

Energy is the capacity to do work; SI unit: joule (J)
Energy stores include: kinetic, gravitational potential, chemical, elastic (strain), nuclear, electrostatic, and internal (thermal)
Potential energy is stored energy due to state, shape, or position
Kinetic energy is energy due to motion: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\)
Gravitational potential energy change: \(\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h\)
Energy transfers occur by: forces (mechanical work), electrical currents, heating, and waves
Conservation of energy: Total energy before = Total energy after



10.7.2 Extended Concepts

Apply conservation of energy to complex examples involving multiple stages
Interpret simple flow diagrams and Sankey diagrams showing energy transfers

title: 10  Energy Stores
text:
10.8 Common Misconceptions

10.8.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Energy can be used up or destroyed”
Incorrect: “When a battery runs out, the energy is gone”
Correct:

Energy cannot be created or destroyed (conservation of energy)
When a battery “runs out”, its chemical energy store has been transferred to other stores (e.g., light, thermal, sound)
The energy is dissipated (spread out) into the surroundings, often as thermal energy




10.8.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “An object at rest has no energy”
Incorrect: “A book on a shelf has zero energy”
Correct:

A stationary object may have gravitational potential energy due to its height
It may also have chemical energy (if it is food or fuel) or internal (thermal) energy due to its temperature
Energy is a property of the system, not just motion




10.8.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Heavier objects always have more kinetic energy”
Incorrect: “A truck always has more kinetic energy than a car”
Correct:

Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\)
Speed is squared in the equation, so it has a greater effect than mass
Example: A 0.01 kg bullet at 500 m/s (\(E_k = 1250 \text{ J}\)) has more kinetic energy than a 1000 kg car at 1 m/s (\(E_k = 500 \text{ J}\))




10.8.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Gravitational potential energy depends only on height”
Incorrect: “Two objects at the same height have the same gravitational potential energy”
Correct:

Gravitational potential energy depends on mass, gravitational field strength, and height: \(\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h\)
Two objects at the same height but with different masses have different gravitational potential energies
The same object has different gravitational potential energy on Earth (\(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\)) and on the Moon (\(g = 1.6 \text{ N/kg}\))




10.8.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Energy transfers are 100% efficient”
Incorrect: “All the electrical energy in a bulb becomes light energy”
Correct:

In real processes, some energy is always dissipated (usually as thermal energy)
A filament lamp converts only about 10% of electrical energy to light; the rest becomes thermal energy
Efficiency = \(\frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}} \times 100\%\)




10.8.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “Potential energy is only gravitational”
Incorrect: “Potential energy means energy due to height”
Correct:

Potential energy is a general term for stored energy due to state, shape, or position
Types include: gravitational, chemical, elastic (strain), electrostatic, nuclear, and magnetic potential energy
Each type has a different physical origin and conversion mechanism

10.10.1 Experiment 7.1: Investigating Energy Transfers in a Pendulum
Objective:
To investigate the conversion between gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy in a swinging pendulum.

10.14 Glossary







Term
Definition




Chemical potential energy
Energy stored in a substance due to the position of atoms or electrons


Conservation of energy
Principle that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or converted; total energy remains constant


Dissipated energy
Energy that is spread out into the surroundings, usually as thermal energy, and is no longer available to do useful work

Process by which energy moves from one store to another via forces, electrical currents, heating, or waves

Energy of a body due to its motion; \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\)


Nuclear energy
Energy stored in the nuclei of atoms, released during nuclear reactions


Potential energy
Stored energy in a system due to its state, shape, or position

Diagram showing energy inputs, useful outputs, and wasted outputs; width of arrows represents energy magnitude

title: 11  Work and Power
text:
11.2 What Is Work?

11.2.1 Definition of Work in Physics
In everyday language, we use the word “work” to describe any activity that requires effort. However, in physics, work has a precise scientific meaning.

Work is done when a force causes an object to move in the direction of the force.

The amount of work done depends on two factors:

The magnitude of the force applied (in newtons, N)
The distance moved by the object in the direction of the force (in metres, m)



11.2.2 The Work–Energy Relationship
A fundamental principle in physics states:

Mechanical or electrical work done is equal to the energy transferred.

\[W = \Delta E\]
Where: - \(W\) = work done (J) - \(\Delta E\) = energy transferred (J)
This means that when work is done on an object, energy is transferred to that object. Conversely, when an object does work, it transfers energy to something else.


11.2.3 Calculating Work Done
The work done by a constant force is calculated using:
\[W = F \times d\]
Where: - \(W\) = work done (J) - \(F\) = constant force in the direction of motion (N) - \(d\) = distance moved in the direction of the force (m)






Note



Key Concept: One joule (1 J) is defined as the work done when a force of one newton moves an object through a distance of one metre in the direction of the force:
\[1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N} \times 1 \text{ m}\]




11.2.4 When Is Work NOT Done?
Work is not done in the following situations:







Situation
Explanation




Force applied but no movement
Pushing against a wall that does not move: \(d = 0\), so \(W = 0\)


Movement perpendicular to force
Carrying a bag horizontally: the upward force is perpendicular to horizontal motion, so no work is done by that force


Object moving at constant velocity with balanced forces
The net work done by the resultant force is zero (though individual forces may do work)









Warning



Common Error: Confusing “effort” with “work”. Holding a heavy object stationary requires effort but does no work in the physics sense because there is no displacement.

title: 11  Work and Power
text:
11.3 Worked Examples: Calculating Work

11.3.1 Example 1: Basic Work Calculation
Question: A librarian pushes a trolley of books with a horizontal force of 8 N. The trolley moves a distance of 5 m in the direction of the force. Calculate: (a) the work done on the trolley (b) the energy transferred to the trolley
Solution:
(a) Work done: \[W = F \times d = 8 \times 5 = \boxed{40 \text{ J}}\]
(b) Energy transferred: By the work–energy relationship: \[\Delta E = W = \boxed{40 \text{ J}}\]
Interpretation: The 40 J of mechanical work done by the librarian is transferred into kinetic energy of the trolley (and some thermal energy due to friction).



11.3.2 Example 2: Work Against Gravity
Question: A 50 N package is lifted vertically through a height of 10 m at constant speed. Calculate: (a) the work done by the lifting force (b) the gravitational potential energy gained by the package
Solution:
(a) Work done: The lifting force must equal the weight (50 N) to move at constant speed. \[W = F \times d = 50 \times 10 = \boxed{500 \text{ J}}\]
(b) Gravitational potential energy gained: By conservation of energy (neglecting losses): \[\Delta E_p = W = \boxed{500 \text{ J}}\]



11.3.3 Example 3: Work on an Incline
Question: A trolley of mass 80 kg is pushed up a gentle incline. The librarian exerts a force of 40 N parallel to the incline, moving the trolley a distance of 10 m along the slope. The vertical height gained is 0.5 m. Taking \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\): (a) Calculate the work done by the 40 N force (b) Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy of the trolley (c) Explain any difference between your answers to (a) and (b)
Solution:
(a) Work done by applied force: \[W = F \times d = 40 \times 10 = \boxed{400 \text{ J}}\]
(b) Gain in gravitational potential energy: \[\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h = 80 \times 10 \times 0.5 = \boxed{400 \text{ J}}\]
(c) Explanation: In this idealised example (neglecting friction and air resistance), the work done by the applied force equals the gain in gravitational potential energy. In reality, some work would be dissipated as thermal energy due to friction, so the gain in \(E_p\) would be slightly less than the work input.

title: 11  Work and Power
text:
11.4 What Is Power?

11.4.1 Definition of Power
While work measures the total amount of energy transferred, power measures the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.

Power is defined as work done per unit time, or equivalently, energy transferred per unit time.



11.4.2 Equations for Power
\[P = \frac{W}{t} \quad \text{or} \quad P = \frac{\Delta E}{t}\]
Where: - \(P\) = power (W) - \(W\) = work done (J) - \(\Delta E\) = energy transferred (J) - \(t\) = time taken (s)






Note



Key Concept: One watt (1 W) is defined as the power when one joule of work is done (or energy transferred) per second:
\[1 \text{ W} = 1 \text{ J/s}\]




11.4.3 Understanding Power Through Examples







Scenario
Explanation




Two boys climbing stairs (same mass, same height)
The boy who climbs faster has greater power because he does the same work in less time


Two kettles boiling water (same amount of water)
The 1000 W kettle boils water faster than the 500 W kettle because it transfers energy at a higher rate


Lifting bricks with a machine
A machine that lifts 200 kg of bricks 30 m in 50 s has power \(P = \frac{mgh}{t} = \frac{200 \times 10 \times 30}{50} = 1200 \text{ W} = 1.2 \text{ kW}\)

title: 11  Work and Power
text:
11.5 8.4 Worked Examples: Calculating Power

11.5.1 Example 4: Power of a Person
Question: Eugene, who weighs 450 N, runs up ten steps. Each step is 0.20 m high. Calculate Eugene’s power if he takes 5.0 seconds to run up the steps at constant speed.
Solution:
Step 1: Calculate total vertical height: \[h = 10 \times 0.20 = 2.0 \text{ m}\]
Step 2: Calculate work done (against gravity): \[W = F \times d = 450 \times 2.0 = 900 \text{ J}\]
Step 3: Calculate power: \[P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{900}{5.0} = \boxed{180 \text{ W}}\]



11.5.2 Example 5: Power of an Electrical Device
Question: A filament lamp rated at 40 W converts 10% of its electrical energy supply to light energy. Calculate: (a) the total electrical energy used by the lamp in 5 minutes (b) the quantity of light energy given off in this time
Solution:
(a) Total electrical energy used: \[t = 5 \times 60 = 300 \text{ s}\] \[E_{\text{total}} = P \times t = 40 \times 300 = 1.2 \times 10^4 \text{ J} = \boxed{12 \text{ kJ}}\]
(b) Light energy output: \[E_{\text{light}} = 10\% \times E_{\text{total}} = 0.10 \times 12000 = \boxed{1.2 \text{ kJ}}\]
Interpretation: The remaining 10.8 kJ is dissipated as thermal energy, which is why the lamp becomes hot during operation.



11.5.3 Example 6: Comparing Power of Machines
Question: Machine A lifts a 500 N load through 4 m in 10 s. Machine B lifts the same load through the same height in 5 s. Calculate: (a) the work done by each machine (b) the power of each machine (c) State which machine is more powerful and explain why
Solution:
(a) Work done (same for both): \[W = F \times d = 500 \times 4 = \boxed{2000 \text{ J}}\]
(b) Power of each machine:

Machine A: \(P_A = \frac{2000}{10} = \boxed{200 \text{ W}}\)
Machine B: \(P_B = \frac{2000}{5} = \boxed{400 \text{ W}}\)

(c) Comparison: Machine B is more powerful because it transfers the same amount of energy in half the time. Power depends on both the amount of work done and the time taken.

title: 11  Work and Power
text:
11.6 Key Concepts Summary

11.6.1 Core Concepts

Work is done when a force causes displacement in its direction: \(W = Fd\)
Work–energy relationship: Work done = energy transferred (\(W = \Delta E\))
Unit of work and energy: joule (J); \(1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N} \times 1 \text{ m}\)
Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy: \(P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{\Delta E}{t}\)
Unit of power: watt (W); \(1 \text{ W} = 1 \text{ J/s}\)
Work is not done when: (a) force causes no displacement, or (b) displacement is perpendicular to force



11.6.2 Extended Insights

When work is done against gravity: \(W = mg\Delta h = \Delta E_p\)
In real systems, not all work input appears as useful energy output due to dissipation (friction, heating)
Higher power means the same work can be done in less time, or more work can be done in the same time

title: 11  Work and Power
text:
11.7 Common Misconceptions

11.7.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Holding a heavy object requires work”
Incorrect: “I am doing work holding this 20 kg box”
Correct:

In physics, work requires displacement: \(W = Fd\)
If the box is held stationary, \(d = 0\), so \(W = 0\)
Your muscles expend chemical energy to maintain the force, but no mechanical work is done on the box




11.7.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Work and power are the same thing”
Incorrect: “A 100 W bulb does more work than a 60 W bulb”
Correct:

Work measures total energy transferred (J)
Power measures the rate of energy transfer (W = J/s)
A 100 W bulb transfers energy faster than a 60 W bulb, but the total work depends on how long each bulb operates




11.7.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Any force applied does work”
Incorrect: “Pushing a wall does work because I apply force”
Correct:

Work requires both force and displacement in the direction of the force
If the wall does not move (\(d = 0\)), then \(W = F \times 0 = 0\)
Effort ≠ work in the physics sense




11.7.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Power depends only on force”
Incorrect: “A larger force always means more power”
Correct:

Power depends on work done per unit time: \(P = \frac{Fd}{t}\)
A small force acting over a large distance quickly can produce more power than a large force acting slowly over a short distance
Example: A cyclist pedalling lightly but rapidly may have higher power output than one pushing hard but slowly




11.7.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Work done always equals useful energy output”
Incorrect: “If I do 100 J of work lifting a box, the box gains 100 J of potential energy”
Correct:

In ideal conditions (no friction), \(W = \Delta E_p\)
In real situations, some work is dissipated as thermal energy due to friction or air resistance
Useful energy output < total work input; efficiency = \(\frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}} \times 100\%\)

Precautions: - ✓ Ensure the stairs are clear of obstacles and dry to prevent slipping - ✓ Start the stopwatch exactly when motion begins and stop exactly at the top - ✓ Climb at a steady pace; avoid sprinting or stopping midway - ✓ Use the vertical height, not the length along the slope, for work calculation
Safety Notes: - Wear appropriate footwear with good grip - Do not attempt this experiment if you have any health conditions that could be aggravated by climbing stairs - Have a partner supervise for safety
Conclusion Template: “The average power output of the person climbing stairs was determined to be ______ W. This value represents the rate at which chemical energy from the body was converted to gravitational potential energy. The actual metabolic power input is higher due to inefficiencies in muscle action and energy dissipation as heat.”
Extension: - Compare power outputs when climbing at different speeds - Investigate how carrying an additional load affects power output - Research typical human power outputs for different activities (walking, cycling, running)

11.11 Chapter Summary

11.11.1 Key Points to Remember
✓ Work is done when a force causes displacement in its direction: \(W = Fd\)
✓ Work–energy principle: Work done = energy transferred (\(W = \Delta E\))
✓ Unit of work/energy: joule (J); \(1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N} \cdot \text{m}\)

✓ Unit of power: watt (W); \(1 \text{ W} = 1 \text{ J/s}\)
✓ Work against gravity: \(W = mg\Delta h = \Delta E_p\)
✓ Real systems: Useful energy output < work input due to dissipation; efficiency < 100%

title: 12  Pressure
text:
12.2 What Is Pressure?

12.2.1 Definition of Pressure
In physics:

Pressure is defined as force per unit area.

\[p = \frac{F}{A}\]
Where:

\(p\) = pressure (Pa or N/m²)
\(F\) = force acting perpendicular to the surface (N)
\(A\) = area of contact (m²)







Note



Key Concept: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa), where \(1 \text{ Pa} = 1 \text{ N/m}^2\). For larger pressures, kilopascals (kPa) or megapascals (MPa) are used.




12.2.2 Understanding Pressure Through Everyday Examples







Situation
Explanation




Walking on eggs with sports shoes
Wide soles distribute weight over large area → low pressure → eggs do not break


Walking on eggs with high heels
Small heel area concentrates force → high pressure → eggs break easily


Tractor with wide tyres
Large contact area reduces pressure on soft ground → prevents sinking


Sharp knife cutting
Small edge area creates high pressure for same force → cuts easily


Nail with pointed tip
Small tip area produces high pressure → penetrates wood with less force









Warning



Important: Pressure depends on both force and area. Increasing force increases pressure; increasing area decreases pressure (for constant force).

title: 12  Pressure
text:
12.3 Calculating Pressure: Worked Examples

12.3.1 Example 1: Basic Pressure Calculation
Question:
A woman weighing 600 N stands on the floor. The total area of her shoes in contact with the floor is 0.03 m².

Calculate the pressure she exerts on the floor.
If she balances on one heel with area 0.0003 m², calculate the new pressure.

Solution:
(a) Pressure with both feet:
\[p = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{600}{0.03} = \boxed{20\,000 \text{ Pa} = 2.0 \times 10^4 \text{ Pa}}\]
(b) Pressure on one heel:
\[p = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{600}{0.0003} = \boxed{2\,000\,000 \text{ Pa} = 2.0 \times 10^6 \text{ Pa}}\]
Interpretation: The pressure on one heel is 100 times greater than with both feet, explaining why high heels can damage floors.



12.3.2 Example 2: Finding Force or Area from Pressure
Question:

A polystyrene cube exerts a pressure of 89 N/m² on a horizontal surface. If the cube has mass 5.0 kg, calculate the area of contact. (Take \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\))
A force of 1200 N produces a pressure of 50 000 Pa. Calculate the area over which the force acts.

Solution:
(a) Area of contact:
Weight \(F = mg = 5.0 \times 10 = 50 \text{ N}\)
\[A = \frac{F}{p} = \frac{50}{89} = \boxed{0.56 \text{ m}^2}\]
(b) Area from pressure:
\[A = \frac{F}{p} = \frac{1200}{50\,000} = \boxed{0.024 \text{ m}^2}\]



12.3.3 Example 3: Pressure from a Rectangular Block
Question:
A block of dimensions 20 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm has density 2.0 g/cm³.

Calculate the weight of the block. (Take \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\))
On which face must the block rest to exert the greatest pressure? Calculate this pressure.
On which face must the block rest to exert the least pressure? Calculate this pressure.

Solution:
(a) Weight of block:
Volume \(V = 20 \times 10 \times 5 = 1000 \text{ cm}^3\)
Mass \(m = \rho V = 2.0 \times 1000 = 2000 \text{ g} = 2.0 \text{ kg}\)
Weight \(F = mg = 2.0 \times 10 = \boxed{20 \text{ N}}\)
(b) Greatest pressure (smallest area):
Smallest face area: \(5 \text{ cm} \times 10 \text{ cm} = 50 \text{ cm}^2 = 0.005 \text{ m}^2\)
\[p_{\text{max}} = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{20}{0.005} = \boxed{4000 \text{ Pa}}\]
(c) Least pressure (largest area):
Largest face area: \(20 \text{ cm} \times 10 \text{ cm} = 200 \text{ cm}^2 = 0.02 \text{ m}^2\)
\[p_{\text{min}} = \frac{20}{0.02} = \boxed{1000 \text{ Pa}}\]

title: 12  Pressure
text:
12.4 Pressure in Liquids

12.4.1 How Depth Affects Liquid Pressure
The pressure beneath the surface of a liquid increases with depth because:

There is more liquid above pushing down
The weight of the liquid column increases with depth

Demonstration: A container with holes at different depths shows water spurting furthest from the bottom hole, indicating greatest pressure at greatest depth.


12.4.2 How Density Affects Liquid Pressure
For the same depth:

A denser liquid exerts greater pressure because it has more mass per unit volume
Example: Seawater (\(\rho \approx 1025 \text{ kg/m}^3\)) exerts more pressure than freshwater (\(\rho \approx 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3\)) at the same depth



12.4.3 Calculating Change in Liquid Pressure (Extended)
The change in pressure beneath the surface of a liquid is given by:
\[\Delta p = \rho g \Delta h\]
Where:

\(\Delta p\) = change in pressure (Pa)
\(\rho\) = density of liquid (kg/m³)
\(g\) = gravitational field strength (N/kg); on Earth, \(g \approx 10 \text{ N/kg}\)
\(\Delta h\) = change in depth (m)







Note



Key Insight: This equation shows that liquid pressure depends only on density and depth, not on the shape or total volume of the container.

title: 12  Pressure
text:
12.5 9.4 Worked Examples: Liquid Pressure

12.5.1 Example 4: Pressure Change with Depth
Question:
A submarine descends from the surface of the sea to a depth of 3000 m. The density of seawater is 1030 kg/m³ and \(g = 10 \text{ N/kg}\).

Calculate the change in pressure experienced by the submarine.
If the pressure on the submarine changes by 0.10 MPa, calculate the change in depth.

Solution:
(a) Change in pressure:
\[\Delta p = \rho g \Delta h = 1030 \times 10 \times 3000 = \boxed{3.09 \times 10^7 \text{ Pa} = 30.9 \text{ MPa}}\]
(b) Change in depth:
\[\Delta h = \frac{\Delta p}{\rho g} = \frac{0.10 \times 10^6}{1030 \times 10} = \boxed{9.7 \text{ m}}\]






Warning



Note: The actual pressure on the submarine is the sum of liquid pressure plus atmospheric pressure at the surface (~101 kPa).





12.5.2 Example 5: Comparing Pressures in Different Liquids
Question:
Two identical containers are filled with liquids X and Y to the same height. The pressure at the bottom of container Y is greater than at the bottom of container X. What can you conclude about the densities of the liquids?
Solution:
Since \(\Delta p = \rho g \Delta h\) and \(g\) and \(\Delta h\) are the same for both containers:

Greater pressure at bottom of Y → greater density of Y

\[\therefore \boxed{\rho_Y > \rho_X}\]



12.5.3 Example 6: Pressure at Different Points in Same Liquid
Question:
Figure 9.1 shows a container of water with points A, B, and C at different depths. Point A is at the surface, B is at depth \(h\), and C is at depth \(2h\).

Compare the pressures at A, B, and C.
If the pressure at B is 5000 Pa, what is the pressure at C?

Solution:
(a) Pressure comparison:

Pressure increases with depth: \(p_C > p_B > p_A\)
Since \(p \propto \Delta h\), and depth of C is twice depth of B: \(p_C \approx 2p_B\) (ignoring atmospheric pressure)

(b) Pressure at C:
If \(p_B = 5000 \text{ Pa}\) (gauge pressure), then:
\[p_C = \rho g (2h) = 2(\rho g h) = 2 \times 5000 = \boxed{10\,000 \text{ Pa}}\]

title: 12  Pressure
text:
12.6 Key Concepts Summary

12.6.1 Core Concepts

Pressure = force per unit area: \(p = \frac{F}{A}\); unit: pascal (Pa) = N/m²
Pressure varies inversely with area: For constant force, smaller area → greater pressure
Pressure varies directly with force: For constant area, greater force → greater pressure
Liquid pressure increases with depth: More liquid above → greater weight → greater pressure
Liquid pressure increases with density: Denser liquid → greater mass per volume → greater pressure at same depth



12.6.2 Extended Concepts

Change in liquid pressure: \(\Delta p = \rho g \Delta h\); depends only on density and depth change
Pressure is isotropic in liquids: At a given depth, pressure acts equally in all directions
Total pressure = atmospheric pressure + liquid pressure (for open containers)

title: 12  Pressure
text:
12.7 Common Misconceptions

12.7.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Pressure and force are the same thing”
Incorrect: “A large force always means large pressure”
Correct:

Force is a push or pull (unit: N)
Pressure is force per unit area (unit: Pa = N/m²)
A small force on a very small area can produce very high pressure (e.g., needle piercing skin)




12.7.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Liquid pressure depends on the total amount of liquid”
Incorrect: “A wide tank has more pressure at the bottom than a narrow tube at the same depth”
Correct:

Liquid pressure depends only on depth and density, not on container shape or total volume
This is why dams are thicker at the bottom (greater pressure) regardless of lake size




12.7.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Pressure acts only downwards in liquids”
Incorrect: “Water pressure only pushes down on objects”
Correct:

Pressure in a liquid acts equally in all directions at a given depth
This is why submarines experience pressure on all sides, not just the top




12.7.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Atmospheric pressure is negligible compared to liquid pressure”
Incorrect: “We can ignore air pressure when calculating underwater pressure”
Correct:

Atmospheric pressure (~101 kPa) is significant and adds to liquid pressure
Total pressure at depth = atmospheric pressure + \(\rho g \Delta h\)




12.7.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Denser objects always sink because they experience more pressure”
Incorrect: “High pressure makes objects sink”
Correct:

Whether an object floats or sinks depends on density comparison, not pressure magnitude
Pressure increases with depth for all objects, but buoyant force depends on displaced fluid weight




12.7.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “Pressure in a liquid is the same at all depths”
Incorrect: “Water pressure is constant throughout a swimming pool”
Correct:

Pressure increases linearly with depth: \(\Delta p = \rho g \Delta h\)
Divers feel increasing pressure on their ears as they descend

title: 12  Pressure
text:
12.9 Laboratory Investigation

12.9.1 Experiment 9.1: Investigating Pressure in Liquids
Objective:
To investigate how pressure in a liquid varies with depth.
Apparatus:

Tall transparent container (e.g., measuring cylinder or plastic bottle)
Water
Three small holes drilled at different heights (e.g., 5 cm, 10 cm, 15 cm from bottom)
Ruler
Tray to catch water
Marker pen

Variables:

Independent: Depth of hole below liquid surface (\(\Delta h\))
Dependent: Horizontal distance water spurts (\(d\)) as indicator of pressure
Controlled: Liquid density, hole diameter, container shape, water level maintained

Procedure:

Drill three small holes of equal diameter at different heights on one side of the container.
Place the container in a tray and fill with water to a fixed level above the highest hole.
Quickly remove tape covering the holes and observe the water jets.
Measure the horizontal distance each jet travels before hitting the tray.
Repeat three times for reliability.
Record depth of each hole below water surface and corresponding jet distance.

Data Table:











Hole
Depth below surface \(\Delta h\) (cm)
Jet distance \(d_1\) (cm)
\(d_2\) (cm)
\(d_3\) (cm)
Average \(d\) (cm)




A
5.0






B
10.0






C
15.0







Analysis:

Plot a graph of average jet distance \(d\) (y-axis) against depth \(\Delta h\) (x-axis).
Describe the relationship observed.
Explain how jet distance relates to pressure at each depth.

Precautions:

✓ Ensure holes are of equal diameter for fair comparison
✓ Maintain constant water level during observations
✓ Measure jet distance from hole exit point horizontally
✓ Perform experiment quickly to minimise water level change

Expected Results:

Jet from lowest hole (greatest depth) travels furthest horizontally
Jet distance increases with depth, indicating pressure increases with depth

Conclusion Template:
“The experiment demonstrated that pressure in a liquid increases with depth. The horizontal distance travelled by water jets increased as the depth of the hole below the surface increased, confirming that greater depth produces greater pressure.”
Extension (Supplement):

Repeat with salt water to investigate effect of density on pressure
Use a pressure sensor to obtain quantitative pressure readings at different depths

Describe the pressure and the changes in pressure of a gas in terms of the forces exerted by particles colliding with surfaces, creating a force per unit area
Know that microscopic particles may be moved by collisions with light fast-moving molecules and correctly use the terms atoms or molecules as distinct from microscopic particles
Recall and use the equation pV = constant for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, including a graphical representation of this relationship

title: 13  Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
text:
13.2 The Three States of Matter

13.2.1 Distinguishing Properties
All matter exists in three states: solid, liquid, and gas. Each state has distinct properties that arise from the arrangement and motion of its particles.









Property
Solid
Liquid
Gas




Shape
Fixed shape
No fixed shape; takes shape of container
No fixed shape; fills entire container


Volume
Fixed volume
Fixed volume
No fixed volume; expands to fill container


Density
High density
High density (slightly less than solid)
Low density


Compressibility
Incompressible
Incompressible
Compressible


Flow
Cannot flow
Can flow
Can flow









Note



Key Concept: The properties of each state depend on the arrangement, separation, and motion of particles, not on the type of substance itself.




13.2.2 Changes of State
Matter can change from one state to another when energy is added or removed. The main changes of state are:

Melting: Solid → Liquid (at melting point)
Freezing/Solidifying: Liquid → Solid (at melting point)
Boiling: Liquid → Gas (at boiling point)
Condensing: Gas → Liquid (at boiling point)







Warning



Important: During a change of state, the temperature remains constant even though energy is being supplied or removed. This energy is used to overcome or form intermolecular forces, not to increase particle kinetic energy.
crumbs: 13  Kinetic Particle Model of Matter

title: 13  Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
text:
13.3 The Kinetic Particle Model

13.3.1 What Is the Kinetic Particle Model?
The kinetic particle model of matter states that:

All matter is made up of tiny particles (atoms, molecules, or ions)
These particles are in continuous random motion
The motion and arrangement of particles determine the properties of each state



13.3.2 Particle Arrangement and Motion










State
Particle Arrangement
Particle Separation
Particle Motion
Interparticle Forces




Solid
Regular, ordered pattern (usually)
Very close together
Vibrate about fixed positions
Very strong


Liquid
Random, disordered
Slightly further apart than solids
Move freely within the liquid, sliding past each other
Moderately strong


Gas
Random, widely spaced
Far apart
Move rapidly in all directions, colliding with each other and container walls
Negligible









Note



Visual Aid: Simple particle diagrams help represent these states: - Solid: Particles in a grid, closely packed

Liquid: Particles close but randomly arranged
Gas: Particles far apart, scattered randomly





13.3.3 How Particle Motion Relates to Temperature
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance.

When temperature increases, particles move or vibrate faster (higher average kinetic energy)
When temperature decreases, particles move or vibrate slower (lower average kinetic energy)

Absolute Zero:

The lowest possible temperature is −273 °C, known as absolute zero
At absolute zero, particles have the least possible kinetic energy (they do not stop completely due to quantum effects, but this is beyond IGCSE scope)
Absolute zero is the starting point of the Kelvin temperature scale: 0 K = −273 °C

Temperature Conversion:
\[T(\text{in K}) = \theta(\text{in °C}) + 273\]
Examples:

0 °C = 0 + 273 = 273 K
25 °C = 25 + 273 = 298 K
100 °C = 100 + 273 = 373 K







Warning



Important: A change of 1 °C is equal to a change of 1 K. Only the starting points differ.
crumbs: 13  Kinetic Particle Model of Matter

title: 13  Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
section: 13.4 Gas Pressure and the Particle Model
text:
13.4 Gas Pressure and the Particle Model

13.4.1 How Do Gases Exert Pressure?
Gas pressure is caused by the constant collisions of gas particles with the walls of their container.
Explanation using the particle model:

Gas particles move rapidly in random directions
They collide with the container walls
Each collision exerts a tiny force on the wall
The sum of all these forces per unit area is the gas pressure

\[\text{Pressure} = \frac{\text{Total force from collisions}}{\text{Area of container wall}}\]


13.4.2 Factors Affecting Gas Pressure
For a fixed mass of gas:








Change
Effect on Pressure
Particle-Level Explanation




Temperature increases (constant volume)
Pressure increases
Particles move faster → more frequent and more forceful collisions with walls


Volume decreases (constant temperature)
Pressure increases
Particles have less space → more frequent collisions with walls


Volume increases (constant temperature)
Pressure decreases
Particles have more space → less frequent collisions with walls


Temperature decreases (constant volume)
Pressure decreases
Particles move slower → less frequent and less forceful collisions









Note



Key Insight: Pressure depends on the rate and force of particle collisions with the container walls.




13.4.3 Boyle’s Law (Supplement)
For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature:
\[pV = \text{constant} \quad \text{or} \quad p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2\]
Where: - \(p\) = pressure (Pa) - \(V\) = volume (m³)
Graphical Representation:

A graph of \(p\) against \(V\) is a curve (hyperbola)
A graph of \(p\) against \(\frac{1}{V}\) is a straight line through the origin, confirming inverse proportionality

section: 13.5 10.4 Brownian Motion: Evidence for the Particle Model
text:
13.5 10.4 Brownian Motion: Evidence for the Particle Model

13.5.1 What Is Brownian Motion?
Brownian motion is the random, jerky movement of microscopic particles (e.g., smoke particles, pollen grains) suspended in a fluid (liquid or gas).
Discovery: First observed by botanist Robert Brown in 1827 when studying pollen grains in water.


13.5.2 Explanation Using the Particle Model
Brownian motion occurs because:

The suspended microscopic particles are much larger than the fluid molecules
Fluid molecules (too small to see) move rapidly and randomly
These molecules collide randomly with the suspended particles from all directions
At any instant, the collisions are unbalanced, causing the suspended particle to jerk in a random direction
The continuous, random collisions produce the observed zigzag motion







Note



Key Evidence: Brownian motion provides direct observational evidence that: - Fluids are made of tiny, moving particles

These particles are in continuous random motion
The motion is random, not directed





13.5.3 Observing Brownian Motion
Experiment: Smoke Cell
Apparatus: - Glass cell containing smoke

Microscope
Light source

Method: 1. Seal a small amount of smoke in a glass cell

Illuminate the cell with a bright light
Observe through a microscope

Observation: - Smoke particles appear as bright, dancing specks

They move in a random, jerky path
Larger particles move less vigorously than smaller ones

Conclusion: The random motion of smoke particles is caused by invisible air molecules colliding with them, supporting the kinetic particle model.
crumbs: 13  Kinetic Particle Model of Matter

title: 13  Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
text:
13.6 Key Concepts Summary

13.6.1 Core Concepts

Three states of matter have distinct properties due to particle arrangement and motion
Changes of state occur at fixed temperatures (melting/boiling points) with energy transfer but no temperature change
Kinetic particle model: Matter is made of tiny particles in continuous random motion
Temperature measures average particle kinetic energy; absolute zero (−273 °C = 0 K) is the theoretical minimum
Gas pressure results from particle collisions with container walls; increases with temperature (constant volume) or decreases with volume (constant temperature)
Brownian motion provides evidence for the particle model: random motion of suspended particles due to collisions with invisible fluid molecules



13.6.2 Extended Concepts

Interparticle forces and distances determine state properties: strong forces and close spacing in solids; weak forces and large spacing in gases
Pressure as force per unit area: Gas pressure arises from the force exerted by many particle collisions per unit area of container wall
Boyle’s Law: For fixed mass at constant temperature, \(pV = \text{constant}\); pressure and volume are inversely proportional
Terminology precision: Distinguish between atoms, molecules, ions (constituents of matter) and microscopic particles (visible under microscope, e.g., smoke particles)
crumbs: 13  Kinetic Particle Model of Matter

title: 13  Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
text:
13.7 Common Misconceptions

13.7.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Particles in a solid do not move”
Incorrect: “Particles in ice are completely still”
Correct:

Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions
They do not move from place to place, but they are not stationary
Higher temperature → more vigorous vibration




13.7.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “During boiling, temperature increases because energy is added”
Incorrect: “When water boils, its temperature keeps rising”
Correct:

During a change of state (melting, boiling), temperature remains constant
Added energy is used to overcome intermolecular forces, not to increase particle kinetic energy
This is why a boiling kettle stays at 100 °C (at standard pressure) until all water has vaporised




13.7.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Gas particles are stationary until they hit the wall”
Incorrect: “Gas particles only move when they collide”
Correct:

Gas particles are in continuous, rapid, random motion at all times
Collisions change their direction and speed, but motion never stops (except theoretically at absolute zero)




13.7.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Brownian motion is the motion of the fluid molecules themselves”
Incorrect: “We see air molecules moving in Brownian motion”
Correct:

Brownian motion is the motion of microscopic suspended particles (e.g., smoke), not the fluid molecules
Fluid molecules are too small to see; their random collisions cause the visible jerky motion of larger suspended particles




13.7.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Pressure in a gas is caused by particles pushing on each other”
Incorrect: “Gas pressure comes from particles pushing against each other”
Correct:

Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the container walls, not with each other
Particle-particle collisions redistribute energy but do not directly create pressure on the container




13.7.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “Kelvin and Celsius scales have different sized degrees”
Incorrect: “1 K is a bigger change than 1 °C”
Correct:

A change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C
Only the zero points differ: 0 K = −273 °C
Conversion: \(T(\text{K}) = \theta(°C) + 273\)




13.7.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “When volume decreases, gas particles get smaller”
Incorrect: “Compressing a gas makes the particles shrink”
Correct:

Gas particles themselves do not change size when compressed
Compression reduces the space between particles, increasing collision frequency with walls → higher pressure

title: 13  Kinetic Particle Model of Matter
text:
13.8 Worked Examples

13.8.1 Example 1: Temperature Conversion
Question: Convert the following temperatures: (a) 37 °C to kelvin (b) 300 K to degrees Celsius (c) A gas is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C. What is the change in temperature in kelvin?
Solution:
(a) 37 °C to K: \[T = \theta + 273 = 37 + 273 = \boxed{310 \text{ K}}\]
(b) 300 K to °C: \[\theta = T - 273 = 300 - 273 = \boxed{27 \text{ °C}}\]
(c) Change in temperature: Initial: \(20 \text{ °C} = 293 \text{ K}\) Final: \(80 \text{ °C} = 353 \text{ K}\) Change: \(353 - 293 = \boxed{60 \text{ K}}\)
Note: The change is also \(80 - 20 = 60 \text{ °C}\), confirming that 1 °C change = 1 K change.



13.8.2 Example 2: Gas Pressure and Particle Motion
Question: A fixed mass of gas is sealed in a rigid container. Explain, in terms of particle motion, why the pressure increases when the gas is heated.
Solution:
Step 1: Heating increases the average kinetic energy of gas particles.
Step 2: Particles move faster on average.
Step 3: Faster particles collide with the container walls: - More frequently (higher collision rate)

With greater force per collision (higher momentum change)

Step 4: Pressure = total force per unit area from collisions.
Conclusion: Both increased collision frequency and increased force per collision cause the pressure to rise.



13.8.3 Example 3: Boyle’s Law Calculation (Supplement)
Question: A gas occupies 200 cm³ at a pressure of 150 kPa. If the volume is reduced to 120 cm³ at constant temperature, calculate the new pressure.
Solution:
Given: - \(p_1 = 150 \text{ kPa}\) - \(V_1 = 200 \text{ cm}^3\) - \(V_2 = 120 \text{ cm}^3\) - Temperature constant → use \(p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2\)
Calculation: \[p_2 = \frac{p_1 V_1}{V_2} = \frac{150 \times 200}{120} = \frac{30\,000}{120} = \boxed{250 \text{ kPa}}\]
Check: Volume decreased by factor \(200/120 = 1.67\), so pressure should increase by same factor: \(150 \times 1.67 = 250\) kPa ✓



13.8.4 Example 4: Brownian Motion Explanation
Question: Describe and explain what is observed when smoke particles in air are viewed under a microscope.
Solution:
Observation: - Smoke particles appear as bright specks of light

They move in a random, jerky, zigzag path
Smaller particles move more vigorously than larger ones

Explanation: 1. Smoke particles are microscopic (visible under microscope) but much larger than air molecules

Air molecules (N₂, O₂) are too small to see but move rapidly and randomly
Air molecules constantly collide with smoke particles from all directions
At any instant, collisions are unbalanced, giving a net force in a random direction
Continuous random collisions produce the observed jerky motion

Conclusion: This Brownian motion provides evidence that air is made of tiny, rapidly moving particles.

13.10 Laboratory Investigation

13.10.1 Experiment 10.1: Observing Brownian Motion
Objective: To observe and explain the random motion of smoke particles as evidence for the kinetic particle model.
Apparatus: - Glass smoke cell with cover slip

Microscope (×100 or higher magnification)
Bright light source (LED torch or microscope lamp)
Dropper with dilute smoke suspension (or incense stick for generating smoke)

Variables: - Independent: None (observational experiment)

Dependent: Motion of smoke particles (qualitative description)
Controlled: Light intensity, magnification, smoke concentration, temperature

Procedure: 1. Prepare the smoke cell: - If using a commercial cell, ensure it is sealed and contains a small amount of smoke

If making your own, gently introduce a tiny amount of smoke into a clean glass cell and seal immediately


Place the smoke cell on the microscope stage
Illuminate the cell from the side or below to make smoke particles visible as bright specks
Focus the microscope to obtain a clear view of individual smoke particles
Observe the motion of several particles for 2–3 minutes
Sketch the path of one particle over a short time interval
Compare the motion of small particles with larger ones

Observations to Record: - Describe the path of a typical smoke particle (e.g., straight, curved, zigzag)

Note whether motion is continuous or jerky
Compare vigour of motion for particles of different sizes
Note any changes when the cell is gently warmed (e.g., by holding in hands)

Analysis: 1. Explain the observed motion using the kinetic particle model: - What causes the jerky motion?

Why is the path random?
Why do smaller particles move more vigorously?


Relate observations to the existence and motion of invisible air molecules

Precautions: - ✓ Use minimal smoke to avoid obscuring the view

✓ Avoid heating the cell excessively, which could cause convection currents
✓ Handle glass cells carefully to avoid breakage
✓ Do not look directly at bright light sources

Conclusion Template: “The observed random, jerky motion of smoke particles (Brownian motion) is caused by continuous, random collisions with invisible, rapidly moving air molecules. This provides direct evidence that gases are composed of tiny particles in continuous random motion, supporting the kinetic particle model of matter.”
Extension (Supplement): - Investigate the effect of temperature: gently warm the cell and observe changes in particle motion

Compare Brownian motion in different gases (if equipment allows)
Research historical significance: How did Einstein’s explanation of Brownian motion help confirm the existence of atoms?

13.14 Glossary







Term
Definition

The lowest possible temperature (−273 °C or 0 K), where particles have minimum kinetic energy

Change of state from solid to liquid at the melting point

A particle large enough to be seen under a microscope (e.g., smoke particle, pollen grain), but much larger than atoms or molecules

Interaction where particles change direction and/or speed; gas pressure results from collisions with container walls

Measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance
