title: 14  Thermal Properties
section: 14.2 Thermal Expansion of Solids, Liquids and Gases
text:
14.2 Thermal Expansion of Solids, Liquids and Gases

14.2.1 What Happens When Materials Are Heated?
When solids, liquids and gases are heated, they increase in volume or expand. When cooled, they decrease in volume or contract.








State
Amount of Expansion
Particle-Level Explanation




Solids
Smallest expansion
Particles vibrate more vigorously about fixed positions; strong intermolecular forces limit expansion


Liquids
Greater expansion than solids
Particles move faster and further apart; weaker intermolecular forces allow more expansion


Gases
Greatest expansion
Particles move at high speeds with negligible forces between them; large increase in volume for small temperature rise









Note



Key Concept: The particles themselves do not expand when heated. Instead, the average distance between particles increases, causing the material to occupy a larger volume.




14.2.2 Everyday Applications and Consequences of Thermal Expansion







Application
Explanation




Railway tracks
Expansion gaps allow rails to expand in hot weather without buckling; modern tracks are tensioned to fit tightly on hot days


Bridges
Expansion joints or rollers at one end allow the bridge to expand and contract without damage


Liquid-in-glass thermometers
The liquid (alcohol or mercury) expands more than the glass when heated, rising up the capillary tube


Shrink fitting
A metal part is cooled to contract, fitted into another part, then warms and expands to form a tight joint


Overhead cables
Electrical wires are hung loosely in summer to allow for contraction in winter without snapping









Warning



Important: If expansion is prevented, very large forces can develop. This is why engineers must design structures to accommodate thermal expansion.

title: 14  Thermal Properties
text:
14.3 Specific Heat Capacity

14.3.1 Internal Energy and Temperature
Internal energy is the total energy of all the particles in a substance.

When the temperature of an object increases, its internal energy increases
This is because the average kinetic energy of the particles increases
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles







Note



Key Insight: Two objects of the same mass and temperature have the same average particle kinetic energy, but may have different internal energies if they contain different numbers of particles.




14.3.2 What Is Specific Heat Capacity?
When you heat different substances, you notice that:

The more mass you heat, the more energy is needed
The greater the temperature change required, the more energy is needed
Different materials require different amounts of energy for the same temperature change

Specific heat capacity (\(c\)) is defined as:

The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (or 1 K).

Formula: \[c = \frac{\Delta E}{m\Delta\theta}\]
Where: - \(c\) = specific heat capacity (J/(kg °C) or J/(kg K))

\(\Delta E\) = thermal energy supplied (J)
\(m\) = mass of substance (kg)
\(\Delta\theta\) = temperature change (°C or K)

Rearranged for energy calculations: \[\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\]






Note



Important: A temperature change of 1 °C is equal to a temperature change of 1 K. Only the zero points of the scales differ.




14.3.3 Specific Heat Capacities of Common Materials



Material
Specific Heat Capacity (J/(kg K))




Lead
130


Mercury
140


Brass
380


Copper
400


Iron
460


Glass
670


Aluminium
900


Methylated spirit
2400


Seawater
3900


Water
4200



Key observation: Water has a very high specific heat capacity. This means:

Water heats up and cools down slowly compared to most substances
This explains why coastal areas have milder climates than inland areas
Water is used as a coolant in car engines and power stations

title: 14  Thermal Properties
text:
14.4 Worked Examples: Specific Heat Capacity

14.4.1 Example 1: Calculating Energy Required
Question: Calculate the thermal energy required to raise the temperature of 2.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C. (Take \(c_{\text{water}} = 4200 \text{ J/(kg K)}\))
Solution:
Step 1: Identify values - \(m = 2.0 \text{ kg}\)

\(\Delta\theta = 80 - 20 = 60 \text{ °C}\) (or 60 K)
\(c = 4200 \text{ J/(kg K)}\)

Step 2: Apply formula \[\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta = 2.0 \times 4200 \times 60 = \boxed{504\,000 \text{ J} = 504 \text{ kJ}}\]



14.4.2 Example 2: Finding Specific Heat Capacity
Question: A 0.50 kg metal block is heated using a 60 W heater for 5.0 minutes. The temperature of the block rises from 25 °C to 85 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal. State any assumption made.
Solution:
Step 1: Calculate energy supplied by heater \[\Delta E = P \times t = 60 \text{ W} \times (5.0 \times 60) \text{ s} = 18\,000 \text{ J}\]
Step 2: Identify other values - \(m = 0.50 \text{ kg}\)

\(\Delta\theta = 85 - 25 = 60 \text{ °C}\)

Step 3: Apply formula (assuming no heat loss to surroundings) \[c = \frac{\Delta E}{m\Delta\theta} = \frac{18\,000}{0.50 \times 60} = \boxed{600 \text{ J/(kg K)}}\]
Assumption: All thermal energy from the heater is absorbed by the metal block (no heat loss to surroundings).



14.4.3 Example 3: Temperature Change Calculation
Question: A 1.2 kg aluminium block (\(c = 900 \text{ J/(kg K)}\)) absorbs 27 000 J of thermal energy. Calculate the temperature rise of the block.
Solution:
Step 1: Rearrange formula for \(\Delta\theta\) \[\Delta\theta = \frac{\Delta E}{mc}\]
Step 2: Substitute values \[\Delta\theta = \frac{27\,000}{1.2 \times 900} = \frac{27\,000}{1080} = \boxed{25 \text{ °C}}\]

14.6 11.5 Condensation and Solidification

14.6.1 Reverse Processes: Energy Release
When a substance changes from a higher-energy state to a lower-energy state, energy is released:









Process
Change of State
Energy Transfer
Particle Explanation




Condensation
Gas → Liquid

title: 14  Thermal Properties
text:
14.7 11.6 Evaporation

14.7.1 What Is Evaporation?
Evaporation is the change of state from liquid to gas that occurs at the surface of a liquid, at any temperature (not just at the boiling point).


14.7.2 How Does Evaporation Occur? (Kinetic Particle Model)

Particles in a liquid move randomly with a range of kinetic energies
At the surface, some particles have enough kinetic energy to overcome attractive forces from other particles and atmospheric pressure
These high-energy particles escape into the air as gas molecules
The remaining particles have a lower average kinetic energy
Therefore, the temperature of the liquid decreases







Note



Key Insight: Evaporation causes cooling because the most energetic particles escape, lowering the average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid.




14.7.3 Evaporation Causes Cooling: Everyday Examples







Example
Explanation




Sweating
Sweat evaporates from skin, removing thermal energy and cooling the body


Wet cloth on forehead
Evaporation of water from the cloth cools the skin


Drying clothes on a line
Water evaporates from fabric; clothes feel cool while drying


Alcohol on skin
Alcohol evaporates quickly, causing a noticeable cooling sensation

14.8 11.7 Factors Affecting the Rate of Evaporation








Factor
Effect on Evaporation Rate
Particle-Level Explanation




Temperature
Higher temperature → faster evaporation
More particles have sufficient kinetic energy to escape the liquid surface


Surface area
Larger surface area → faster evaporation
More particles are at the surface and can escape


Air movement
Moving air (wind) → faster evaporation
Escaped particles are carried away, preventing them from returning to the liquid; maintains a concentration gradient


Humidity
Lower humidity → faster evaporation
Drier air can accept more water vapour; fewer returning particles









Warning



Important: Evaporation occurs at any temperature, while boiling occurs only at the boiling point throughout the liquid.

title: 14  Thermal Properties
text:
14.10 Key Concepts Summary

14.10.1 Core Concepts

Thermal expansion: Solids, liquids and gases expand when heated; gases expand most, solids least
Applications of expansion: Railway gaps, bridge joints, thermometers, shrink fitting
Internal energy: Total energy of all particles; increases with temperature
Specific heat capacity: \(c = \frac{\Delta E}{m\Delta\theta}\); energy to raise 1 kg by 1 °C
Changes of state: Melting and boiling occur at constant temperature; energy breaks intermolecular bonds
Melting/boiling points of water: 0 °C and 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure
Condensation/solidification: Reverse processes that release energy to surroundings
Evaporation: Surface phenomenon at any temperature; causes cooling



14.10.2 Extended Concepts

Particle explanation of expansion: Increased particle motion increases average separation; weaker forces in liquids/gases allow greater expansion
Temperature and kinetic energy: Temperature measures average kinetic energy of particles
Specific heat capacity experiments: Electrical method using \(IVt = mc\Delta\theta\) (with insulation to minimise heat loss)
Boiling vs. evaporation: Differences in location, temperature dependence, rate, and bubble formation
Factors affecting evaporation: Temperature, surface area, air movement, humidity
Cooling by evaporation: High-energy particles escape, lowering average kinetic energy of remaining liquid

title: 14  Thermal Properties
text:
14.11 Common Misconceptions

14.11.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Particles expand when heated”
Incorrect: “When a metal rod is heated, the metal particles get bigger”
Correct:

Particles themselves do not change size when heated
The average distance between particles increases due to more vigorous vibration/motion
This increased separation causes the material to expand




14.11.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Temperature increases during melting or boiling”
Incorrect: “When ice melts, its temperature rises from 0 °C”
Correct:

During a change of state, temperature remains constant even though energy is supplied
Energy is used to overcome intermolecular forces, not to increase particle kinetic energy
Temperature only rises once the change of state is complete




14.11.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Evaporation and boiling are the same process”
Incorrect: “Evaporation is just slow boiling”
Correct:

Boiling: Occurs at boiling point, throughout liquid, with bubble formation
Evaporation: Occurs at any temperature, only at surface, no bubbles
Different particle mechanisms: boiling requires energy to overcome atmospheric pressure throughout; evaporation involves only surface particles with sufficient energy




14.11.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Specific heat capacity depends on the amount of substance”
Incorrect: “A larger mass of water has a higher specific heat capacity”
Correct:

Specific heat capacity is an intensive property—it depends only on the material, not the amount
1 kg and 10 kg of water both have \(c = 4200 \text{ J/(kg K)}\)
The total energy required depends on mass, but \(c\) itself does not




14.11.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Evaporation only happens on hot days”
Incorrect: “Water only evaporates when it is warm”
Correct:

Evaporation occurs at any temperature, even below 0 °C (e.g., ice sublimating)
The rate of evaporation increases with temperature, but the process itself occurs at all temperatures
Puddles dry up on cold days, just more slowly




14.11.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “Condensation is the same as evaporation, just reversed”
Incorrect: “Condensation is evaporation going backwards”
Correct:

While condensation is the reverse change of state (gas → liquid), the energy transfer is opposite
Evaporation absorbs energy from the liquid (causing cooling)
Condensation releases energy to the surroundings (causing warming)
Different particle mechanisms: evaporation involves escape of high-energy particles; condensation involves capture of particles by attractive forces




14.11.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “All materials expand by the same amount when heated”
Incorrect: “Heating any material by 10 °C causes the same expansion”
Correct:

Different materials have different coefficients of thermal expansion
For the same temperature change: gases expand most, liquids less, solids least
Even among solids, aluminium expands more than steel for the same temperature rise
Engineers must select materials with compatible expansion properties for combined structures

title: 14  Thermal Properties
text:
14.12 Worked Examples

14.12.1 Example 4: Thermal Expansion Application
Question: A steel railway rail is 30.0 m long at 10 °C. If the coefficient of linear expansion for steel is \(1.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ /°C}\), calculate the increase in length when the temperature rises to 40 °C.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify values - Original length \(L_0 = 30.0 \text{ m}\)

Temperature change \(\Delta\theta = 40 - 10 = 30 \text{ °C}\)
Coefficient \(\alpha = 1.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ /°C}\)

Step 2: Apply linear expansion formula \[\Delta L = \alpha L_0 \Delta\theta = (1.2 \times 10^{-5}) \times 30.0 \times 30 = \boxed{0.0108 \text{ m} = 1.08 \text{ cm}}\]
Interpretation: The rail expands by just over 1 cm. Without expansion gaps, this could cause buckling.



14.12.2 Example 5: Specific Heat Capacity Comparison
Question: Equal masses of aluminium (\(c = 900 \text{ J/(kg K)}\)) and copper (\(c = 400 \text{ J/(kg K)}\)) are supplied with the same amount of thermal energy. Which metal experiences the greater temperature rise? Explain.
Solution:
Step 1: Recall formula \[\Delta\theta = \frac{\Delta E}{mc}\]
Step 2: Analyse - \(\Delta E\) and \(m\) are the same for both metals

\(\Delta\theta\) is inversely proportional to \(c\)
Copper has lower \(c\) (400 < 900)

Conclusion: Copper experiences the greater temperature rise because it requires less energy per kg per degree.
Quantitative comparison: \[\frac{\Delta\theta_{\text{Cu}}}{\Delta\theta_{\text{Al}}} = \frac{c_{\text{Al}}}{c_{\text{Cu}}} = \frac{900}{400} = 2.25\]
Copper’s temperature rises 2.25 times more than aluminium’s for the same energy input.



14.12.3 Example 6: Evaporation Cooling Calculation
Question: A person sweats 0.5 kg of water during exercise. If the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is \(2.3 \times 10^6 \text{ J/kg}\), calculate the thermal energy removed from the body by evaporation.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify values - Mass of water \(m = 0.5 \text{ kg}\)

Specific latent heat \(L_v = 2.3 \times 10^6 \text{ J/kg}\)

Step 2: Calculate energy removed \[\Delta E = mL_v = 0.5 \times 2.3 \times 10^6 = \boxed{1.15 \times 10^6 \text{ J} = 1150 \text{ kJ}}\]
Interpretation: Evaporation of sweat removes over 1 MJ of thermal energy, providing significant cooling.

14.14 Laboratory Investigation

14.14.1 Experiment 11.1: Measuring the Specific Heat Capacity of a Solid
Objective: To determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block using an electrical heating method.
Apparatus: - Metal block with holes for heater and thermometer

Electrical immersion heater (known power rating)
Thermometer or temperature sensor with data logger
d.c. power supply, ammeter, voltmeter
Insulating material (felt or polystyrene)
Electronic balance
Stopwatch

Variables: - Independent: Time of heating (or energy supplied)

Dependent: Temperature change of block
Controlled: Mass of block, insulation, initial temperature, heater power

Procedure: 1. Measure and record the mass \(m\) of the metal block.

Wrap the block in insulating material to minimise heat loss.
Insert the heater and thermometer into the drilled holes.
Connect the heater to the power supply via ammeter and voltmeter.
Record the initial temperature \(\theta_1\).
Switch on the heater and start the stopwatch simultaneously.
After a measured time \(t\) (e.g., 300 s), switch off the heater.
Continue monitoring temperature and record the highest temperature \(\theta_2\) reached.
Record the ammeter reading \(I\) and voltmeter reading \(V\) during heating.

14.16 Chapter Summary

14.16.1 Key Points to Remember
✓ Thermal expansion: All materials expand when heated; gases > liquids > solids
✓ Expansion applications: Railway gaps, bridge joints, thermometers, shrink fitting
✓ Internal energy: Total energy of particles; increases with temperature
✓ Specific heat capacity: \(c = \frac{\Delta E}{m\Delta\theta}\); material property, not mass-dependent
✓ Changes of state: Melting/boiling at constant temperature; energy breaks intermolecular bonds
✓ Water phase changes: Melts at 0 °C, boils at 100 °C (standard pressure)
✓ Condensation/solidification: Release energy to surroundings
✓ Evaporation: Surface phenomenon at any temperature; causes cooling

✓ Boiling vs. evaporation: Different in location, temperature dependence, rate, bubble formation


14.16.2 Formulae Sheet

Formula
Variables




Specific heat capacity
\(c = \frac{\Delta E}{m\Delta\theta}\)

text:
15.3 12.2 Melting and Boiling: Energy Input Without Temperature Change

15.3.1 What Is Melting?
Melting is the change of state from solid to liquid at the melting point.
Particle explanation:

In a solid, particles are held in fixed positions by strong intermolecular bonds
When energy is supplied, particles vibrate more vigorously
At the melting point, particles have enough energy to break free from their fixed positions
The solid becomes a liquid; particles can now move past each other
Temperature remains constant because energy is used to break bonds, not increase kinetic energy



15.3.2 What Is Boiling?
Boiling is the change of state from liquid to gas at the boiling point, occurring throughout the liquid.
Particle explanation:

In a liquid, particles are held together by intermolecular forces
When energy is supplied, particles move faster
At the boiling point, particles have enough energy to:

Break intermolecular bonds completely
Overcome atmospheric pressure to escape into the air

Bubbles of vapour form within the liquid and rise to the surface
Temperature remains constant because energy is used to break bonds and overcome pressure







Warning



Important: Boiling occurs at a specific temperature (the boiling point) and throughout the liquid. Evaporation occurs at any temperature and only at the surface.

section: 15.6 12.5 Factors Affecting the Rate of Evaporation
text:
15.6 12.5 Factors Affecting the Rate of Evaporation








Factor
Effect on Evaporation Rate
Particle-Level Explanation




Temperature
Higher temperature → faster evaporation
More particles have sufficient kinetic energy to escape the liquid surface


Surface area
Larger surface area → faster evaporation
More particles are at the surface and can escape


Air movement
Moving air (wind) → faster evaporation
Escaped particles are carried away, preventing them from returning to the liquid; maintains a concentration gradient


Humidity
Lower humidity → faster evaporation
Drier air can accept more water vapour; fewer returning particles









Warning



Important: Evaporation occurs at any temperature, while boiling occurs only at the boiling point throughout the liquid.

title: 15  Phase Changes
text:
15.8 Key Concepts Summary

15.8.1 Core Concepts

Melting: Solid → liquid at melting point; energy breaks intermolecular bonds; temperature constant
Boiling: Liquid → gas at boiling point; energy breaks bonds and overcomes atmospheric pressure; temperature constant
Melting/boiling points of water: 0 °C and 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure
Condensation: Gas → liquid; energy released to surroundings
Solidification: Liquid → solid; energy released to surroundings
Evaporation: Surface phenomenon at any temperature; causes cooling



15.8.2 Extended Concepts

Boiling vs. evaporation: Differences in location, temperature dependence, rate, and bubble formation
Factors affecting evaporation: Temperature, surface area, air movement, humidity
Cooling by evaporation: High-energy particles escape, lowering average kinetic energy of remaining liquid

title: 15  Phase Changes
text:
15.9 Common Misconceptions

15.9.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Temperature increases during melting or boiling”
Incorrect: “When ice melts, its temperature rises from 0 °C”
Correct:

During a change of state, temperature remains constant even though energy is supplied
Energy is used to overcome intermolecular forces, not to increase particle kinetic energy
Temperature only rises once the change of state is complete




15.9.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Evaporation and boiling are the same process”
Incorrect: “Evaporation is just slow boiling”
Correct:

Boiling: Occurs at boiling point, throughout liquid, with bubble formation
Evaporation: Occurs at any temperature, only at surface, no bubbles
Different particle mechanisms: boiling requires energy to overcome atmospheric pressure throughout; evaporation involves only surface particles with sufficient energy




15.9.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Evaporation only happens on hot days”
Incorrect: “Water only evaporates when it is warm”
Correct:

Evaporation occurs at any temperature, even below 0 °C (e.g., ice sublimating)
The rate of evaporation increases with temperature, but the process itself occurs at all temperatures
Puddles dry up on cold days, just more slowly




15.9.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Condensation is the same as evaporation, just reversed”
Incorrect: “Condensation is evaporation going backwards”
Correct:

While condensation is the reverse change of state (gas → liquid), the energy transfer is opposite
Evaporation absorbs energy from the liquid (causing cooling)
Condensation releases energy to the surroundings (causing warming)
Different particle mechanisms: evaporation involves escape of high-energy particles; condensation involves capture of particles by attractive forces




15.9.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Particles expand when heated during phase changes”
Incorrect: “When water boils, the water particles get bigger”
Correct:

Particles themselves do not change size during phase changes
The average distance between particles increases due to increased kinetic energy
In boiling, particles gain enough energy to break free from intermolecular forces and escape as gas




15.9.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “All liquids boil at 100 °C”
Incorrect: “Every liquid boils at the same temperature as water”
Correct:

Different substances have different boiling points depending on intermolecular forces
Example: Ethanol boils at 78 °C; mercury boils at 357 °C
Boiling point also depends on atmospheric pressure

title: 15  Phase Changes
text:
15.10 Worked Examples

15.10.1 Example 1: Energy During Melting
Question: A 0.5 kg block of ice at 0 °C is heated until it becomes water at 0 °C. Explain why the temperature does not rise during this process, even though energy is being supplied.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify the process: melting (solid → liquid) at melting point
Step 2: Particle explanation:

Ice particles are held in fixed positions by strong intermolecular bonds
Supplied energy is used to break these bonds, allowing particles to move freely
Energy is not used to increase particle kinetic energy
Since temperature measures average kinetic energy, temperature remains constant

Conclusion: Temperature remains at 0 °C during melting because energy is used to overcome intermolecular forces, not to increase particle motion.



15.10.2 Example 2: Evaporation Cooling Calculation
Question: A person sweats 0.3 kg of water during exercise. If the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.3 × 10⁶ J/kg, calculate the thermal energy removed from the body by evaporation.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify values - Mass of water m = 0.3 kg - Specific latent heat L_v = 2.3 × 10⁶ J/kg
Step 2: Calculate energy removed \[\Delta E = mL_v = 0.3 \times 2.3 \times 10^6 = \boxed{6.9 \times 10^5 \text{ J} = 690 \text{ kJ}}\]
Interpretation: Evaporation of sweat removes nearly 700 kJ of thermal energy, providing significant cooling to the body.



15.10.3 Example 3: Factors Affecting Evaporation (Extended)
Question: Explain why a puddle of water evaporates more quickly on a warm, windy day than on a cool, still day.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify relevant factors: - Temperature: warm day → higher temperature - Air movement: windy day → moving air
Step 2: Particle-level explanation:

Higher temperature: More water molecules at the surface have sufficient kinetic energy to overcome intermolecular forces and escape into the air
Moving air: Escaped water molecules are carried away by the wind, preventing them from returning to the liquid surface; this maintains a concentration gradient that favours further evaporation

Conclusion: Both higher temperature and air movement increase the rate of evaporation, causing the puddle to dry more quickly.

text:
15.12 Laboratory Investigation

15.12.1 Experiment 12.1: Investigating Evaporation and Cooling
Objective:
To demonstrate that evaporation causes cooling and to investigate factors affecting the rate of evaporation.
Apparatus:

Laboratory thermometer (or temperature sensor with data logger)
Absorbent tissue paper
Beaker of water at room temperature
Retort stand and clamp
Adhesive tape or rubber band
Cold air fan (or hair dryer on cool setting)
Stopwatch

Variables:

Independent: Air movement (still air vs. moving air)
Dependent: Temperature change of thermometer bulb
Controlled: Initial temperature, amount of water, type of tissue, ambient temperature

Procedure:

Cover the thermometer bulb in tissue paper and attach it with adhesive tape or a rubber band.
Dip the thermometer bulb covered with tissue paper into the water.
Clamp the thermometer on a retort stand so the bulb is in front of the fan.
Note the initial temperature.
Trial 1 (Still air): Do not turn on the fan. Record the temperature every 30 seconds for 3 minutes.
Trial 2 (Moving air): Turn on the fan to blow air over the thermometer bulb. Record the temperature every 30 seconds for 3 minutes.
Repeat each trial twice for reliability.

Data Table:








Time (s)
Temperature (Still air) / °C
Temperature (Moving air) / °C




0




30




60




90




120




150




180





Analysis:

Plot a graph of temperature (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for both trials on the same axes.
Compare the rate of temperature decrease for still air vs. moving air.
Explain the difference using the kinetic particle model.

Precautions:

✓ Ensure the tissue paper is evenly wetted before starting
✓ Position the thermometer bulb consistently for both trials
✓ Avoid touching the thermometer bulb with hands to prevent heat transfer
✓ Use the same fan speed for all moving air trials

Expected Results:

Temperature decreases in both trials due to evaporation
Temperature decreases more rapidly with moving air due to increased evaporation rate

Conclusion Template:
“The experiment demonstrated that evaporation causes cooling, as shown by the decrease in temperature of the wet thermometer bulb. The rate of cooling was greater with moving air, confirming that air movement increases the rate of evaporation by removing escaped molecules and maintaining a concentration gradient.”
Extension (Supplement):

Investigate the effect of temperature by using warm water vs. cold water
Investigate the effect of surface area by using different sizes of tissue paper
Research real-world applications: cooling towers, sweat evaporation in athletes, industrial drying processes

15.14 Chapter Summary

15.14.1 Key Points to Remember
✓ Melting: Solid → liquid at melting point; energy breaks intermolecular bonds; temperature constant
✓ Boiling: Liquid → gas at boiling point; energy breaks bonds and overcomes atmospheric pressure; temperature constant
✓ Water phase changes: Melts at 0 °C, boils at 100 °C (standard pressure)
✓ Condensation: Gas → liquid; energy released to surroundings
✓ Solidification: Liquid → solid; energy released to surroundings

15.16 Glossary







Term
Definition




Boiling
Change of state from liquid to gas occurring throughout the liquid at the boiling point; bubbles of vapour form


Boiling point
The temperature at which a liquid boils at a given pressure; for pure water at standard pressure: 100 °C


Condensation
Change of state from gas to liquid; energy is released to the surroundings


Evaporation
Change of state from liquid to gas occurring only at the surface, at any temperature; causes cooling


Melting
Change of state from solid to liquid at the melting point; energy is absorbed to break bonds


Melting point
The temperature at which a solid melts at a given pressure; for pure water at standard pressure: 0 °C


Solidification (Freezing)
Change of state from liquid to solid; energy is released as particles form fixed positions


Latent heat
Energy absorbed or released during a change of state without a change in temperature

title: 16  Thermal Transfer
text:
16.2 Introduction to Thermal Energy Transfer

16.2.1 Why Does Thermal Energy Transfer Occur?
Thermal energy always flows from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature.

When you touch a hot object, thermal energy flows from the object to your hand → your hand feels hot
When you touch a cold object, thermal energy flows from your hand to the object → your hand feels cold
When two objects are at the same temperature, there is no net flow of thermal energy between them → they are in thermal equilibrium







Note



Key Concept: Thermal energy transfer continues until thermal equilibrium is reached (both objects at the same temperature).




16.2.2 Three Methods of Thermal Energy Transfer








Method
Medium Required
How Energy Is Transferred




Conduction
Solid (best), liquid, gas
Through particle vibrations and free electron movement


Convection
Fluid (liquid or gas) only
Through bulk movement of fluid due to density differences


Radiation
None (can travel through vacuum)
Through electromagnetic waves (infrared radiation)

title: 16  Thermal Transfer
text:
16.3 Conduction

16.3.1 What Is Conduction?
Conduction is the transfer of thermal energy through a substance from a hotter region to a colder region without any bulk movement of the substance itself.

Conduction occurs mainly in solids
Metals are good thermal conductors; non-metals are generally poor thermal conductors (thermal insulators)



16.3.2 Comparing Thermal Conductors: An Experiment
Apparatus:

Four rods of equal dimensions made of copper, steel, aluminium, and glass
Bunsen burner, tripod stand, stopwatch
Wax, drawing pins

Procedure:

Attach a drawing pin to one end of each rod using a small amount of wax
Heat the opposite ends of all rods simultaneously with a Bunsen burner
Record the time taken for each drawing pin to fall

Observation:

The pin on the copper rod falls first → copper conducts thermal energy fastest
The pin on the glass rod falls last (or not at all) → glass is a poor conductor

Conclusion:
Different materials conduct thermal energy at different rates. Metals conduct better than non-metals.


16.3.3 Thermal Conductivity of Common Materials

Thermal Conductivity
Classification

Best conductor

Good conductor

Good conductor

Warning



Important: Still air is an excellent thermal insulator. Many insulating materials (e.g., fibreglass, polystyrene) work by trapping air in small pockets.




16.3.4 How Conduction Works: Particle Explanation (Extended)

16.3.4.1 In Non-Metals

Particles at the hot end vibrate more vigorously about their fixed positions
These vibrating particles collide with neighbouring particles, transferring kinetic energy
The process continues along the material → thermal energy is transferred from hot to cold
No particles move from one place to another; only energy is transferred



16.3.4.2 In Metals
Metals have an additional mechanism that makes them excellent conductors:

Metals contain free (delocalised) electrons that can move freely throughout the material
At the hot end, free electrons gain kinetic energy and move rapidly towards cooler regions
These fast-moving electrons collide with atoms in cooler regions, transferring energy
Free electron diffusion transfers energy much faster than lattice vibrations alone







Note



Key Insight: This is why metals are good conductors of both thermal energy and electricity — both processes rely on free electron movement.





16.3.5 Why Are Liquids and Gases Poor Conductors?

Particles in liquids and gases are farther apart than in solids
Collisions between particles are less frequent
Transfer of kinetic energy from hot to cold regions is slower
Therefore, conduction is inefficient in fluids







Warning



Important: Although conduction is poor in fluids, thermal energy can still be transferred efficiently by convection (see Section 13.3).

title: 16  Thermal Transfer
text:
16.4 Convection

16.4.1 What Is Convection?
Convection is the transfer of thermal energy in a fluid (liquid or gas) by means of convection currents due to differences in density.

Convection cannot occur in solids because particles cannot move freely
Convection involves the bulk movement of the fluid itself



16.4.2 How Convection Currents Form
Step-by-step explanation:

Fluid at the bottom is heated → particles gain kinetic energy and move faster
Heated fluid expands → same mass occupies larger volume → density decreases
Less dense (warmer) fluid rises because it is lighter than surrounding cooler fluid
Cooler, denser fluid sinks to replace the rising warm fluid
The cycle repeats → convection current is established



16.4.3 Demonstrating Convection in Liquids
Apparatus:

Beaker of water, Bunsen burner, potassium permanganate crystals

Procedure:

Place a few potassium permanganate crystals at the bottom of a beaker of water
Gently heat the beaker from below

Observation:

Purple streams rise from the crystals, fan out at the surface, then sink down the sides
This shows the circular motion of convection currents



16.4.4 Demonstrating Convection in Gases
Apparatus:

Convection box with two chimneys, candle, incense stick

Procedure:

Light a candle under one chimney
Hold a smoking incense stick over the other chimney

Observation:

Smoke is drawn down the cool chimney, across the box, and rises above the candle
This traces the convection current in air



16.4.5 Everyday Examples of Convection







Example
Explanation




Sea breeze (daytime)
Land heats faster than sea → warm air over land rises → cool air from sea flows in


Land breeze (night-time)
Land cools faster than sea → warm air over sea rises → cool air from land flows out


Electric kettle
Heating element at bottom → warm water rises → convection currents heat water evenly


Air conditioner
Installed near ceiling → cool air sinks → warm air rises to be cooled → room cools evenly


Hot water radiator
Heats air nearby → warm air rises → cool air drawn in → convection circulates warm air









Note



Key Insight: Convection is the dominant method of thermal energy transfer in fluids because it transfers energy much faster than conduction alone.

title: 16  Thermal Transfer
text:
16.5 Radiation

16.5.1 What Is Thermal Radiation?
Thermal radiation (also called infrared radiation) is the transfer of thermal energy in the form of electromagnetic waves.

All objects emit and absorb infrared radiation
Thermal radiation does not require a medium → it can travel through a vacuum
The Earth receives thermal energy from the Sun only by radiation (space is a vacuum)



16.5.2 Detecting Infrared Radiation

Infrared radiation is invisible to the human eye
Infrared cameras can detect and visualise infrared radiation
Warmer objects appear brighter (or in warmer colours) on infrared images



16.5.3 Factors Affecting Emission and Absorption of Infrared Radiation

16.5.3.1 1. Surface Colour and Texture



Surface Type
Emission
Absorption
Reflection




Dull, black
Good emitter
Good absorber
Poor reflector


Shiny, silver
Poor emitter
Poor absorber
Good reflector



Experiment: Comparing Emission

Fill two identical tins (one dull black, one shiny silver) with hot water
Record temperature decrease over time
Result: Dull black tin cools faster → better emitter of infrared radiation

Experiment: Comparing Absorption

Place two temperature sensors (one wrapped in dull black foil, one in shiny silver foil) at equal distance from a heat source
Record temperature increase over time
Result: Dull black foil heats faster → better absorber of infrared radiation



16.5.3.2 2. Surface Temperature

The higher the temperature of an object (relative to surroundings), the higher the rate of emission of infrared radiation
As an object cools, its rate of emission decreases



16.5.3.3 3. Surface Area

For objects of the same mass and material, the object with larger surface area emits or absorbs infrared radiation at a higher rate




16.5.4 Thermal Equilibrium and Radiation
All objects continuously emit and absorb infrared radiation. The net effect determines whether the object warms, cools, or stays at constant temperature:








Situation
Absorption vs. Emission
Result




Object cooler than surroundings
Absorption > Emission
Object warms up


Object hotter than surroundings
Emission > Absorption
Object cools down


Object same temperature as surroundings
Absorption = Emission
Object stays at constant temperature (thermal equilibrium)





16.5.5 The Greenhouse Effect and Earth’s Temperature (Extended)
How the greenhouse effect works:

Solar radiation (visible light, UV) passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface
The Earth emits infrared radiation back towards space
Greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, water vapour) in the atmosphere absorb and re-emit some of this infrared radiation
Some of this re-emitted radiation returns to Earth → additional warming

Natural greenhouse effect:

Keeps Earth’s average temperature at about 15°C (instead of −18°C without it)
Essential for life as we know it

Enhanced greenhouse effect (global warming):

Human activities increase greenhouse gas concentrations
More infrared radiation is trapped → Earth’s temperature rises







Warning



Important: The greenhouse effect is a natural and necessary process. The problem is the enhancement of this effect due to human activities.

text:
16.6 Applications and Consequences of Thermal Energy Transfer

16.6.1 Applications of Conduction







Application
Explanation




Cooking utensils
Metal pans conduct heat quickly from stove to food; handles made of wood/plastic (insulators) protect hands


Soldering irons
Copper tip conducts heat rapidly to melt solder for electronic repairs


Heat sinks
Metal fins with large surface area conduct heat away from electronic components





16.6.2 Applications of Convection







Application
Explanation




Room heating/cooling
Radiators heat air → warm air rises → convection circulates warmth; air conditioners cool air → cool air sinks → convection circulates cool air


Refrigerators
Freezing compartment at top → cool air sinks → convection currents cool the entire fridge


Weather systems
Convection currents in atmosphere drive wind patterns, cloud formation, and weather





16.6.3 Applications of Radiation







Application
Explanation




Solar panels
Blackened surfaces absorb infrared radiation from Sun to heat water


Space blankets
Shiny silver surfaces reflect infrared radiation back to body → reduce heat loss


Infrared thermometers
Detect infrared radiation emitted by objects to measure temperature without contact





16.6.4 Complex Applications Involving Multiple Methods

16.6.4.1 Example 1: Cooking Over a Campfire

Conduction: Heat transfers from fire to metal pot; from pot to food
Convection: Hot air and smoke rise above fire; convection currents heat water inside pot
Radiation: Infrared radiation from flames warms hands and surroundings



16.6.4.2 Example 2: Car Radiator Cooling System

Conduction: Hot coolant transfers heat through metal tubes to fins
Convection: Air blown by fan carries heat away from fins; coolant circulates through engine
Radiation: Black-painted fins emit infrared radiation to surroundings

title: 16  Thermal Transfer
text:
16.7 Key Concepts Summary

16.7.1 Core Concepts

Thermal energy flows from higher to lower temperature until thermal equilibrium is reached
Conduction: Transfer through solids via particle vibrations and (in metals) free electron movement
Convection: Transfer in fluids via density-driven currents; warm fluid rises, cool fluid sinks
Radiation: Transfer via infrared electromagnetic waves; requires no medium; all objects emit and absorb
Surface properties: Dull black surfaces are good emitters/absorbers; shiny silver surfaces are good reflectors
Rate of radiation emission depends on surface temperature and surface area
Thermal equilibrium: Object temperature constant when absorption rate = emission rate



16.7.2 Extended Concepts

Conduction mechanisms: Lattice vibrations (all solids) + free electron diffusion (metals only)
Poor conduction in fluids: Due to large particle separation and infrequent collisions
Greenhouse effect: Natural process that warms Earth; enhanced by human activities → global warming
Complex applications: Real-world systems often involve multiple transfer methods simultaneously

title: 16  Thermal Transfer
text:
16.8 Common Misconceptions

16.8.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Heat rises”
Incorrect: “Heat always moves upwards”
Correct: - Thermal energy flows from hot to cold, regardless of direction - Warm fluids rise because they are less dense, but this is convection, not heat itself rising - In conduction and radiation, energy can flow in any direction from hot to cold



16.8.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Metals feel colder because they are at a lower temperature”
Incorrect: “A metal spoon is colder than a plastic spoon at room temperature”
Correct: - Both objects are at the same temperature (room temperature) - Metal conducts thermal energy away from your hand faster than plastic - Your hand loses heat more quickly to metal → feels colder - This is about rate of energy transfer, not actual temperature



16.8.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Convection can occur in solids”
Incorrect: “Solids can transfer heat by convection if heated enough”
Correct: - Convection requires bulk movement of fluid - Particles in solids are fixed in position and cannot flow - Solids transfer thermal energy only by conduction (and radiation from their surface)



16.8.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Black objects are always hotter”
Incorrect: “A black car is always hotter than a white car in the Sun”
Correct: - Black surfaces absorb infrared radiation better → heat up faster in sunlight - But black surfaces also emit infrared radiation better → cool down faster in shade - The final temperature depends on the balance of absorption and emission, and the environment



16.8.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Radiation only occurs at high temperatures”
Incorrect: “Only hot objects emit infrared radiation”
Correct: - All objects with temperature above absolute zero emit infrared radiation - Cooler objects emit less radiation and at longer wavelengths - Your body, a cup of tea, and even ice cubes emit infrared radiation



16.8.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “The greenhouse effect is bad”
Incorrect: “The greenhouse effect causes global warming and should be eliminated”
Correct: - The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life on Earth - Without it, Earth’s average temperature would be about −18°C - The problem is the enhanced greenhouse effect due to increased greenhouse gases from human activities



16.8.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “Still air is a good conductor”
Incorrect: “Air conducts heat well, so it’s not useful for insulation”
Correct: - Still air is actually an excellent thermal insulator (very poor conductor) - Insulating materials (fibreglass, double-glazed windows) work by trapping air in small pockets - Moving air (wind) transfers heat by convection, but still air minimises all three transfer methods

title: 16  Thermal Transfer
text:
16.9 Worked Examples

16.9.1 Example 1: Conduction Calculation (Extended)
Question: A copper rod of length 0.5 m and cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² has one end at 100°C and the other at 20°C. The thermal conductivity of copper is 400 W/(m·K). Calculate the rate of thermal energy transfer through the rod.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify the formula for rate of conduction: \[\frac{Q}{t} = kA\frac{\Delta T}{L}\]
Step 2: Substitute values: - \(k = 400 \text{ W/(m·K)}\) - \(A = 2.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2\) - \(\Delta T = 100 - 20 = 80 \text{ K}\) - \(L = 0.5 \text{ m}\)
\[\frac{Q}{t} = 400 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-4}) \times \frac{80}{0.5}\] \[\frac{Q}{t} = 400 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 160 = \boxed{12.8 \text{ W}}\]
Interpretation: Thermal energy flows through the rod at 12.8 joules per second.



16.9.2 Example 2: Convection Current Explanation
Question: Explain why an electric kettle has its heating element at the bottom, not the top.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify the transfer method: convection in water
Step 2: Explain the process: - Heating element at bottom heats water nearby - Heated water expands → density decreases → rises - Cooler, denser water sinks to replace it - Convection current circulates water → entire kettle heats evenly
Step 3: Contrast with top heating: - If element were at top, heated water would stay at top (already least dense) - No convection current would form - Water at bottom would heat only by slow conduction → inefficient heating
Conclusion: Bottom placement enables efficient heating via convection currents.



16.9.3 Example 3: Radiation and Surface Properties
Question: Two identical metal cans, one painted dull black and one shiny silver, are filled with hot water at 80°C and left in a room at 20°C. After 10 minutes, the black can is at 55°C and the silver can is at 65°C. Explain the difference.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify the dominant transfer method: radiation (and some convection) from can surface to room
Step 2: Apply surface property knowledge: - Dull black surface: good emitter of infrared radiation → loses thermal energy faster - Shiny silver surface: poor emitter (good reflector) → loses thermal energy slower
Step 3: Relate to observations: - Black can cooled more (80°C → 55°C = 25°C drop) - Silver can cooled less (80°C → 65°C = 15°C drop) - Difference due to different emission rates
Conclusion: Surface colour and texture significantly affect the rate of thermal energy loss by radiation.



16.9.4 Example 4: Thermal Equilibrium (Extended)
Question: A cup of coffee at 70°C is left in a room at 20°C. Describe what happens to the rate of cooling over time.
Solution:
Step 1: Initial state: - Coffee much hotter than room → large temperature difference - High rate of emission of infrared radiation - High rate of convection from coffee surface to air - Coffee cools rapidly at first
Step 2: As coffee cools: - Temperature difference decreases - Rate of emission decreases (emission ∝ temperature difference) - Rate of convection decreases - Coffee cools more slowly as it approaches room temperature
Step 3: Final state: - Coffee reaches 20°C (same as room) - Absorption rate = emission rate - No net thermal energy transfer - Coffee stays at constant temperature (thermal equilibrium)
Conclusion: Rate of cooling decreases over time as temperature difference decreases.

16.13 Chapter Summary

16.13.1 Key Points to Remember
✓ Thermal energy flows from higher to lower temperature until thermal equilibrium
✓ Conduction: Transfer through solids via particle vibrations + free electrons (metals)

title: 16  Thermal Transfer
text:
16.15 Glossary







Term
Definition




Conduction
Transfer of thermal energy through a substance from hot to cold without bulk movement of the substance


Convection
Transfer of thermal energy in a fluid by means of convection currents due to density differences


Convection current
Circular movement of fluid caused by heating from below: warm fluid rises, cool fluid sinks


Emission
Process by which an object gives out infrared radiation


Free electron
Electron in a metal that is not bound to a specific atom and can move freely through the material


Greenhouse effect
Natural process where greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, warming the Earth


Infrared radiation
Electromagnetic radiation emitted by all objects with temperature above absolute zero; carries thermal energy


Lattice vibration
Vibration of atoms or molecules about fixed positions in a solid; mechanism of conduction in non-metals


Radiation
Transfer of thermal energy by electromagnetic waves (infrared); requires no medium


Thermal conductor
Material that transfers thermal energy easily (e.g., metals)


Thermal equilibrium
State where two objects at the same temperature have no net flow of thermal energy between them


Thermal insulator
Material that transfers thermal energy poorly (e.g., wood, plastic, air)


Thermal radiation
Another term for infrared radiation; transfer of thermal energy by electromagnetic waves




End of Chapter 13

title: 17  General Properties of Waves
text:
17.2 14.1 What Is Wave Motion?

17.2.1 Energy Transfer Without Matter Transfer
In physics, a wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium or space, transferring energy from one point to another without transferring matter.
Key Concept: When a wave passes through a medium, the particles of the medium oscillate (vibrate) about fixed positions, but they do not travel with the wave. Only the energy and the waveform progress forward.


17.2.2 The Source of Waves
All waves originate from an oscillation or vibration.

A vibrating guitar string produces sound waves
A vibrating dipper in water produces water waves
Oscillating electric and magnetic fields produce electromagnetic waves

title: 17  General Properties of Waves
text:
17.3 14.2 Types of Waves
Waves are classified into two main types based on the direction of particle vibration relative to the direction of wave propagation.

17.3.1 Transverse Waves
In a transverse wave, the direction of vibration is perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of wave propagation.
Examples:

Water waves (surface ripples)
Electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays)
Seismic S-waves (secondary waves)
Waves on a rope or string

Visual Representation: - Particles move up and down - Wave moves left to right - Features include crests (highest points) and troughs (lowest points)


17.3.2 Longitudinal Waves
In a longitudinal wave, the direction of vibration is parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
Examples:

Sound waves in air
Seismic P-waves (primary waves)
Waves in a compressed spring (Slinky pushed and pulled)

Visual Representation: - Particles move back and forth along the same line as the wave - Creates regions of compression (particles close together) and rarefaction (particles spread apart)






Warning



Important: Do not confuse the motion of the medium with the motion of the wave. In longitudinal waves, particles oscillate parallel to energy transfer; in transverse waves, they oscillate perpendicular to it.

title: 17  General Properties of Waves
text:
17.4 14.3 Properties of Waves
To describe waves quantitatively, we use specific terminology and measurements.

17.4.1 Key Wave Features








Feature
Definition
SI Unit




Crest
Highest point of a transverse wave
—


Trough
Lowest point of a transverse wave
—


Wavelength (\(\lambda\))
Shortest distance between two consecutive points in phase (e.g., crest to crest, or trough to trough)
metre (m)


Amplitude (\(A\))
Maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position
metre (m)


Period (\(T\))
Time taken for one complete wave to pass a point
second (s)


Frequency (\(f\))
Number of complete waves produced per second
hertz (Hz)


Wave speed (\(v\))
Distance travelled by the wave per second
metre per second (m/s)


Wavefront
Imaginary line joining adjacent points that are in phase
—





17.4.2 Relationship Between Frequency and Period
\[f = \frac{1}{T} \quad \text{and} \quad T = \frac{1}{f}\]
Example: If a wave has a period of 0.02 s, its frequency is: \[f = \frac{1}{0.02} = 50 \text{ Hz}\]


17.4.3 Displacement–Distance vs Displacement–Time Graphs








Graph Type
What It Shows
What Can Be Read




Displacement–distance
Shape of the wave at one instant in time
Wavelength (\(\lambda\)), amplitude (\(A\))


Displacement–time
Motion of a single particle over time
Period (\(T\)), amplitude (\(A\)), frequency (\(f\))

title: 17  General Properties of Waves
text:
17.5 14.4 The Wave Equation
The speed of a wave is determined by how frequently waves are produced and how long each wave is.
\[v = f\lambda\]
Where: - \(v\) = wave speed (m/s) - \(f\) = frequency (Hz) - \(\lambda\) = wavelength (m)
Derivation Insight: - In one period (\(T\)), a wave travels one wavelength (\(\lambda\)) - Speed = distance/time = \(\lambda / T\) - Since \(f = 1/T\), then \(v = f\lambda\)






Note



Key Concept: For a wave travelling through a given medium, the speed is usually constant. If frequency increases, wavelength must decrease proportionally, and vice versa.

title: 17  General Properties of Waves
text:
17.6 14.5 Wave Behaviour: Reflection, Refraction, Diffraction
Waves exhibit three fundamental behaviours when they encounter boundaries, changes in medium, or obstacles.

17.6.1 1. Reflection
When waves strike a plane barrier, they bounce back.
Law of Reflection: - Angle of incidence (\(i\)) = Angle of reflection (\(r\)) - Wavelength, frequency, and speed remain unchanged - Direction changes according to the surface geometry
Example: Water waves reflecting off a straight barrier in a ripple tank.


17.6.2 2. Refraction
Refraction occurs when waves pass from one medium to another, causing a change in speed and often a change in direction.
For Water Waves: - Deep water → faster speed, longer wavelength - Shallow water → slower speed, shorter wavelength - If waves enter at an angle, they bend towards the normal when slowing down (deep → shallow) - Frequency remains constant during refraction


17.6.3 3. Diffraction
Diffraction is the spreading out of waves when they pass through a gap or around an edge.
Key Observations: - Diffraction is most noticeable when the gap size is similar to the wavelength - If gap size \(\gg\) wavelength: waves pass through with minimal spreading - If gap size \(\approx\) wavelength: waves spread out significantly in a semi-circular pattern - Wavelength and frequency remain unchanged after diffraction






Warning



Important: Diffraction does not change the speed, frequency, or wavelength of the wave. It only changes the direction of propagation at the edges.

title: 17  General Properties of Waves
text:
17.7 Key Concepts Summary

17.7.1 Core Concepts

Waves transfer energy, not matter; particles oscillate about fixed positions
Transverse waves: vibration ⊥ propagation (e.g., light, water waves, S-waves)
Longitudinal waves: vibration ∥ propagation (e.g., sound, P-waves)
Wave features: wavelength (\(\lambda\)), frequency (\(f\)), period (\(T\)), amplitude (\(A\)), wavefront
Wave equation: \(v = f\lambda\)
Reflection: \(i = r\); speed and wavelength unchanged
Refraction: change in speed causes bending; frequency constant
Diffraction: spreading through gaps/around edges; most pronounced when gap \(\approx \lambda\)



17.7.2 Extended Concepts

Gap size vs wavelength: smaller gaps relative to \(\lambda\) produce greater diffraction
Edge diffraction: longer wavelengths diffract more around barriers than shorter wavelengths

title: 17  General Properties of Waves
text:
17.8 Common Misconceptions

17.8.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Waves carry matter along with them”
Incorrect: “Water waves push water forward across the ocean”
Correct:

Waves transfer energy, not matter
Water particles move in circular or elliptical orbits but return to their original positions
Only the wave pattern and energy progress forward




17.8.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Longitudinal waves have crests and troughs”
Incorrect: “Sound waves have crests and troughs like water waves”
Correct:

Longitudinal waves consist of compressions and rarefactions, not crests and troughs
Crests/troughs are exclusive to transverse waves
Both types still have wavelength, frequency, and amplitude




17.8.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Changing frequency changes wave speed”
Incorrect: “If I increase the frequency of a wave, it travels faster”
Correct:

Wave speed is determined by the medium, not the frequency
In a given medium, \(v\) is constant
Increasing \(f\) causes \(\lambda\) to decrease proportionally (\(v = f\lambda\))




17.8.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Refraction changes the frequency of a wave”
Incorrect: “When light enters glass, its frequency decreases”
Correct:

Frequency remains constant during refraction
Speed and wavelength change, but the source vibration rate (\(f\)) does not
Energy is conserved per photon/wave cycle




17.8.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Diffraction only happens with light”
Incorrect: “Diffraction is exclusive to electromagnetic waves”
Correct:

Diffraction occurs with all types of waves (water, sound, seismic, electromagnetic)
The degree of spreading depends on the ratio of wavelength to obstacle/gap size
Sound waves diffract around doorways because their wavelength is comparable to the door width




17.8.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “A narrower gap always increases wave speed”
Incorrect: “Waves speed up when squeezed through a small opening”
Correct:

Gap size does not affect wave speed
Speed depends only on medium properties (depth, density, tension, etc.)
Narrower gaps increase spreading (diffraction), not speed

title: 17  General Properties of Waves
text:
17.9 Worked Examples

17.9.1 Example 1: Wave Speed Calculation
Question: A wave has a frequency of 12 Hz and a wavelength of 0.25 m. Calculate its speed.
Solution: \[v = f\lambda = 12 \times 0.25 = \boxed{3.0 \text{ m/s}}\]



17.9.2 Example 2: Frequency from Period
Question: A floating buoy bobs up and down once every 2.5 seconds. Calculate the frequency of the water waves.
Solution: \[f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{2.5} = \boxed{0.40 \text{ Hz}}\]



17.9.3 Example 3: Wavelength in Different Depths
Question: Water waves travel at 1.8 m/s in deep water with a frequency of 0.60 Hz. They enter shallow water where their speed reduces to 1.2 m/s. Calculate the wavelength in both regions.
Solution: Frequency remains constant: \(f = 0.60 \text{ Hz}\)
Deep water: \[\lambda_{\text{deep}} = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{1.8}{0.60} = \boxed{3.0 \text{ m}}\]
Shallow water: \[\lambda_{\text{shallow}} = \frac{1.2}{0.60} = \boxed{2.0 \text{ m}}\]
Note: Wavelength decreases in shallow water because speed decreases while frequency remains constant.



17.9.4 Example 4: Diffraction Condition
Question: Explain why radio waves can be received behind hills, but visible light cannot.
Solution: - Radio waves have long wavelengths (metres to kilometres) - Visible light has very short wavelengths (400–700 nm) - Hills are comparable in size to radio wavelengths, causing significant diffraction around the obstacle - Hills are vastly larger than light wavelengths, so light travels in straight lines with negligible diffraction - Therefore, radio signals bend around hills, but light does not

17.11 Laboratory Investigation

17.11.1 Experiment 14.1: Investigating Diffraction in a Ripple Tank
Objective: To investigate how gap size and wavelength affect the diffraction of water waves.
Apparatus: - Ripple tank with transparent base - Light source and projection screen - Straight wave generator (dipper or motor-driven bar) - Adjustable barriers (two flat plates) - Ruler - Stroboscope or video camera (optional) - Power supply for wave generator
Variables: - Independent: Gap width; wavelength (adjusted via frequency) - Dependent: Degree of wave spreading (qualitative observation and measurement of diffraction angle) - Controlled: Water depth, wave generator amplitude, projection distance
Procedure: 1. Set up the ripple tank with uniform water depth (~5 mm).

Adjust the wave generator to produce plane waves at a low frequency (~5 Hz).
Measure and record the wavelength \(\lambda\) from the projected pattern.
Place two barriers to form a gap. Set the gap width to approximately \(2\lambda\).

Reduce the gap width to approximately \(\lambda\), then to \(0.5\lambda\). Observe and sketch changes.
Increase the frequency to double the wavelength (keeping depth constant). Repeat steps 4–6.

title: 18  Light: Reflection and Refraction
text:
18.2 Introduction to Light

18.2.1 What Is Light?
Light is a form of electromagnetic radiation that is visible to the human eye. It travels in straight lines and can be reflected, refracted, and dispersed.
Key properties of light:

Light travels at approximately \(3.0 \times 10^8\) m/s in a vacuum
Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation)
Light can be reflected, refracted, absorbed, or transmitted
Light exhibits both wave and particle properties (beyond IGCSE scope)







Note



Key Concept: We see objects because light from them enters our eyes. Luminous objects (e.g., the Sun, a lamp) emit their own light. Non-luminous objects (e.g., a book, a wall) are visible because they reflect light from a luminous source into our eyes.




18.2.2 Representing Light: Rays and Beams
In physics, we use light rays to represent the path of light:








Term
Definition
Diagram Representation




Ray
A straight line with an arrow indicating the direction of light travel
Single line with arrow


Beam
A bundle of parallel, convergent, or divergent rays
Multiple parallel/convergent/divergent lines


Parallel beam
Rays that are parallel to each other
Parallel lines with arrows


Convergent beam
Rays that meet at a point
Lines converging to a point


Divergent beam
Rays that spread out from a point
Lines spreading from a point

title: 18  Light: Reflection and Refraction
text:
18.3 Reflection of Light

18.3.1 The Law of Reflection
When light strikes a smooth, polished surface (e.g., a plane mirror), it is reflected in a predictable manner.
Key terms for reflection:

Incident ray: The ray of light that strikes the reflecting surface
Reflected ray: The ray of light that bounces off the reflecting surface
Point of incidence: The point where the incident ray strikes the surface
Normal: An imaginary line perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence
Angle of incidence (\(i\)): The angle between the incident ray and the normal
Angle of reflection (\(r\)): The angle between the reflected ray and the normal

The Law of Reflection states:

The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection: \(i = r\)
The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane







Warning



Important: Angles are always measured from the normal, not from the surface itself.




18.3.2 Images Formed by Plane Mirrors
When you look into a plane mirror, you see an image of yourself. This image has specific characteristics:







Characteristic
Description




Same size
The image is the same size as the object


Same distance
The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front


Virtual
The image cannot be captured on a screen; light rays do not actually meet at the image position


Upright
The image is the right way up (not inverted)


Laterally inverted
Left and right are swapped (e.g., text appears reversed)





18.3.3 Ray Diagrams for Plane Mirrors
To locate the position of an image formed by a plane mirror:
Step 1: Draw the mirror as a straight line with shading on the back (silvered side).
Step 2: Mark the object position in front of the mirror.
Step 3: Draw the image behind the mirror at the same distance as the object is in front.
Step 4: From the top of the image, draw two rays to the eye (dotted lines behind the mirror, solid lines in front).
Step 5: Draw the incident rays from the object to the mirror, ensuring \(i = r\) at each point of incidence.






Note



Key Insight: The image is virtual because the rays only appear to come from behind the mirror. In reality, the light rays reflect off the mirror and enter the eye.




18.3.4 Applications of Plane Mirrors







Application
Explanation




Periscope
Two plane mirrors at 45° allow viewing over obstacles (e.g., in submarines)


Rear-view mirrors
Drivers use plane or slightly curved mirrors to see behind vehicles


Optical instruments
Mirrors redirect light in telescopes, microscopes, and cameras


Vision testing
Mirrors extend the apparent distance of eye charts in small rooms


Blind corner mirrors
Curved mirrors help drivers see around corners in shops or on roads

title: 18  Light: Reflection and Refraction
text:
18.4 Refraction of Light

18.4.1 What Is Refraction?
Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium to another with a different optical density.
Why does refraction occur?

Light travels at different speeds in different media
When light enters a denser medium (e.g., air → glass), it slows down and bends towards the normal
When light enters a less dense medium (e.g., glass → air), it speeds up and bends away from the normal

Key terms for refraction:

Incident ray: The ray approaching the boundary between two media
Refracted ray: The ray that has passed into the second medium and changed direction
Normal: An imaginary line perpendicular to the boundary at the point of incidence
Angle of incidence (\(i\)): The angle between the incident ray and the normal
Angle of refraction (\(r\)): The angle between the refracted ray and the normal



18.4.2 Snell’s Law and Refractive Index
For light passing from air (or vacuum) into another medium:
\[n = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}\]
Where: - \(n\) = refractive index of the medium (no unit) - \(i\) = angle of incidence in air/vacuum - \(r\) = angle of refraction in the medium
Refractive index can also be defined as:
\[n = \frac{\text{speed of light in vacuum}}{\text{speed of light in medium}} = \frac{c}{v}\]

Note



Key Insight: A higher refractive index means light travels slower in that medium and bends more towards the normal when entering from air.




18.4.3 Apparent Depth and Real Depth
When viewing an object underwater, it appears shallower than it actually is due to refraction.
Relationship: \[n = \frac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}\]
Example: A coin at the bottom of a pool appears closer to the surface than it really is. Light rays from the coin refract away from the normal as they leave the water, making the coin appear at a shallower position.

title: 18  Light: Reflection and Refraction
text:
18.5 Total Internal Reflection

18.5.1 What Is the Critical Angle?
When light travels from a denser medium to a less dense medium (e.g., glass → air):

As the angle of incidence increases, the angle of refraction increases more rapidly
At a certain angle of incidence, the angle of refraction becomes 90° (the refracted ray travels along the boundary)
This specific angle of incidence is called the critical angle (\(c\))

Definition: The critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the less dense medium is 90°.


18.5.2 Total Internal Reflection
When the angle of incidence in the denser medium exceeds the critical angle:

No refraction occurs
All the light is reflected back into the denser medium
This phenomenon is called total internal reflection

Conditions for total internal reflection:

Light must travel from a denser medium to a less dense medium
The angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle



18.5.3 Calculating Critical Angle
For light travelling from a medium of refractive index \(n\) to air:
\[n = \frac{1}{\sin c} \quad \text{or} \quad \sin c = \frac{1}{n}\]
Example: For glass with \(n = 1.5\): \[\sin c = \frac{1}{1.5} = 0.667 \quad \Rightarrow \quad c = \sin^{-1}(0.667) \approx 42^\circ\]


18.5.4 Applications of Total Internal Reflection







Application
Explanation




Optical fibres
Light is trapped inside a glass/plastic core by total internal reflection; used for high-speed data transmission in telecommunications


Prisms in binoculars
Right-angled prisms reflect light by total internal reflection, producing upright images without silvered surfaces


Periscopes
Prisms can replace mirrors for clearer, more durable image reflection


Endoscopes
Flexible optical fibres allow doctors to see inside the body without invasive surgery


Reflectors on bicycles
Prismatic reflectors return light to its source using total internal reflection









Warning



Important: Total internal reflection is 100% efficient (no light is lost), unlike reflection from a silvered mirror which absorbs some light.

title: 18  Light: Reflection and Refraction
text:
18.6 Key Concepts Summary

18.6.1 Core Concepts

Reflection: Light bounces off a surface; \(i = r\); incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in same plane
Plane mirror image: Same size, same distance behind mirror, virtual, upright, laterally inverted
Refraction: Light bends when passing between media of different optical density due to change in speed
Snell’s Law: \(n = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}\) for light entering from air/vacuum
Refractive index: \(n = \frac{c}{v}\); higher \(n\) means slower light speed and greater bending
Critical angle: Angle of incidence in denser medium for which refraction angle = 90°
Total internal reflection: Complete reflection when \(i > c\) and light travels denser → less dense medium



18.6.2 Extended Concepts

Apparent depth: \(n = \frac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}\); objects underwater appear shallower
Optical fibres: Use total internal reflection to transmit light/data over long distances with minimal loss
Ray diagram constructions: Using geometry and \(i = r\) to locate images and trace light paths

title: 18  Light: Reflection and Refraction
text:
18.7 Common Misconceptions

18.7.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “The angle of incidence is measured from the mirror surface”
Incorrect: “Angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the mirror”
Correct: - Angles of incidence and reflection are always measured from the normal (perpendicular to the surface)

Measuring from the surface gives the complement of the correct angle
This error leads to incorrect ray diagrams and calculations




18.7.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Virtual images can be captured on a screen”
Incorrect: “A mirror image can be projected onto a wall”
Correct: - Virtual images are formed where light rays appear to come from, but do not actually meet

Only real images (where rays actually converge) can be captured on a screen
Plane mirrors always produce virtual images




18.7.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Refraction changes the frequency of light”
Incorrect: “When light enters glass, its frequency decreases”
Correct: - Frequency remains constant during refraction

Speed and wavelength change, but frequency (determined by the source) does not
This is why the colour of light does not change when it refracts




18.7.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from air to glass”
Incorrect: “Light can undergo total internal reflection entering a denser medium”
Correct: - Total internal reflection only occurs when light travels from a denser to a less dense medium

When entering a denser medium (air → glass), light always refracts (bends towards normal)
The critical angle concept only applies for denser → less dense transitions




18.7.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “A higher refractive index means light travels faster”
Incorrect: “Diamond has a high refractive index, so light travels fast in it”
Correct: - Refractive index \(n = \frac{c}{v}\); higher \(n\) means slower light speed in the medium

Diamond (\(n = 2.42\)) slows light to about \(1.24 \times 10^8\) m/s, much slower than in air
Greater slowing causes greater bending towards the normal




18.7.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “Lateral inversion means the image is upside down”
Incorrect: “A mirror turns your image upside down”
Correct: - Lateral inversion means left and right are swapped, not top and bottom

Your right hand appears as the left hand in the mirror image
The image remains upright; only the horizontal orientation is reversed




18.7.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “Critical angle is the same for all materials”
Incorrect: “All glass has a critical angle of 42°”
Correct: - Critical angle depends on refractive index: \(\sin c = \frac{1}{n}\)

Different types of glass have different \(n\) values (1.48–1.96), so critical angles vary (~32°–43°)
Water (\(n = 1.33\)) has \(c \approx 49^\circ\); diamond (\(n = 2.42\)) has \(c \approx 24^\circ\)

title: 18  Light: Reflection and Refraction
text:
18.8 Worked Examples

18.8.1 Example 1: Law of Reflection Calculation
Question: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of 35° to the normal. (a) What is the angle of reflection? (b) What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray?
Solution:
(a) Angle of reflection: By the law of reflection: \(r = i = \boxed{35^\circ}\)
(b) Angle between incident and reflected rays: Angle = \(i + r = 35^\circ + 35^\circ = \boxed{70^\circ}\)



18.8.2 Example 2: Plane Mirror Image Distance
Question: A person stands 2.5 m in front of a plane mirror. (a) How far is the image from the mirror? (b) How far is the person from their image? (c) If the person moves 0.5 m closer to the mirror, what is the new distance between the person and their image?
Solution:
(a) Image distance from mirror: Image distance = object distance = \(\boxed{2.5 \text{ m}}\)
(b) Person-to-image distance: Distance = \(2.5 + 2.5 = \boxed{5.0 \text{ m}}\)
(c) New distance after moving closer: New object distance = \(2.5 - 0.5 = 2.0 \text{ m}\) New image distance = \(2.0 \text{ m}\) New person-to-image distance = \(2.0 + 2.0 = \boxed{4.0 \text{ m}}\)



18.8.3 Example 3: Snell’s Law Calculation
Question: Light travels from air into glass (\(n = 1.50\)) at an angle of incidence of 40°. Calculate the angle of refraction.
Solution:
Step 1: Write Snell’s Law: \[n = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}\]
Step 2: Rearrange for \(\sin r\): \[\sin r = \frac{\sin i}{n} = \frac{\sin 40^\circ}{1.50}\]
Step 3: Calculate: \[\sin r = \frac{0.643}{1.50} = 0.429\] \[r = \sin^{-1}(0.429) = \boxed{25.4^\circ}\]
Interpretation: The ray bends towards the normal as expected when entering a denser medium.



18.8.4 Example 4: Critical Angle and Total Internal Reflection
Question: The refractive index of a certain type of glass is 1.60. (a) Calculate the critical angle for this glass. (b) A ray of light inside this glass strikes the glass-air boundary at an angle of incidence of 45°. Will total internal reflection occur? Explain.
Solution:
(a) Critical angle: \[\sin c = \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1}{1.60} = 0.625\] \[c = \sin^{-1}(0.625) = \boxed{38.7^\circ}\]
(b) Will TIR occur? - Angle of incidence \(i = 45^\circ\)

Critical angle \(c = 38.7^\circ\)
Since \(i > c\) (\(45^\circ > 38.7^\circ\)) and light is travelling from denser (glass) to less dense (air) medium:
Yes, total internal reflection will occur.




18.8.5 Example 5: Apparent Depth Calculation
Question: A fish is actually 1.2 m below the surface of a pond. The refractive index of water is 1.33. Calculate the apparent depth of the fish as seen by an observer directly above.
Solution:
Step 1: Use the apparent depth formula: \[n = \frac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}\]
Step 2: Rearrange for apparent depth: \[\text{apparent depth} = \frac{\text{real depth}}{n} = \frac{1.2}{1.33} = \boxed{0.90 \text{ m}}\]
Interpretation: The fish appears to be only 0.90 m deep, not 1.2 m, due to refraction at the water-air boundary.

18.10 Laboratory Investigation

18.10.1 Experiment 15.1: Investigating Refraction Using a Rectangular Glass Block
Objective: To verify Snell’s Law and determine the refractive index of glass by measuring angles of incidence and refraction.
Apparatus: - Rectangular glass block

Ray box with single slit
White paper
Protractor

Dependent: Angle of refraction (\(r\))
Controlled: Same glass block, same wavelength of light, same experimental setup

Procedure: 1. Place the glass block on a sheet of white paper and trace its outline.

Remove the block and draw a normal line at the centre of one of the longer faces.
Draw an incident ray at an angle of incidence \(i = 30^\circ\) to the normal.
Replace the glass block exactly on its outline.

Mark the point where the ray emerges from the opposite face of the block.
Remove the block and draw the refracted ray inside the block and the emergent ray.
Measure the angle of refraction \(r\) inside the block.

Snell’s Law
\(n = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}\)
\(n\)=refractive index, \(i\)=incidence angle (in air), \(r\)=refraction angle


Refractive index (speed)
\(n = \frac{c}{v}\)
\(c\)=speed in vacuum (\(3.0 \times 10^8\) m/s), \(v\)=speed in medium


Critical angle
\(\sin c = \frac{1}{n}\)
\(c\)=critical angle, \(n\)=refractive index of denser medium


Apparent depth
\(n = \frac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}\)
For viewing objects through a plane boundary

title: 18  Light: Reflection and Refraction
text:
18.14 Glossary







Term
Definition




Angle of incidence (\(i\))
Angle between the incident ray and the normal at the point of incidence


Angle of reflection (\(r\))
Angle between the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence


Angle of refraction (\(r\))
Angle between the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence


Apparent depth
The depth at which an object appears to be when viewed through a refracting medium


Critical angle (\(c\))
The angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the less dense medium is 90°


Incident ray
The ray of light approaching a boundary or reflecting surface


Lateral inversion
The swapping of left and right in an image formed by a plane mirror


Normal
An imaginary line perpendicular to a surface or boundary at the point of incidence


Refracted ray
The ray of light that has passed into a second medium and changed direction


Refractive index (\(n\))
Ratio of speed of light in vacuum to speed in medium; or \(\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}\) for air → medium


Reflection
The rebounding of light at a surface; governed by \(i = r\)


Refraction
The bending of light as it passes from one medium to another due to a change in speed


Total internal reflection
Complete reflection of light within a denser medium when \(i > c\) at a boundary with a less dense medium


Virtual image
An image formed where light rays appear to come from but do not actually meet; cannot be captured on a screen




End of Chapter 15
