title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
Know the main regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of frequency and in order of wavelength
Know that all electromagnetic waves travel at the same high speed in a vacuum
Describe typical uses of the different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum including:

Radio waves: radio and television transmissions, astronomy, radio frequency identification (RFID)
Microwaves: satellite television, mobile phones (cell phones), microwave ovens
Infrared: electric grills, short range communications such as remote controllers for televisions, intruder alarms, thermal imaging, optical fibres
Visible light: vision, photography, illumination
Ultraviolet: security marking, detecting fake bank notes, sterilising water
X-rays: medical scanning, security scanners
Gamma rays: sterilising food and medical equipment, detection of cancer and its treatment

Describe the harmful effects on people of excessive exposure to electromagnetic radiation, including:

Microwaves: internal heating of body cells
Infrared: skin burns
Ultraviolet: damage to surface cells and eyes, leading to skin cancer and eye conditions
X-rays and gamma rays: mutation or damage to cells in the body

Know that communication with artificial satellites is mainly by microwaves:

Some satellite phones use low orbit artificial satellites
Some satellite phones and direct broadcast satellite television use geostationary satellites




Know that the speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and is approximately the same in air
Know that many important systems of communications rely on electromagnetic radiation including:

Mobile phones and wireless internet use microwaves because microwaves can penetrate some walls and only require a short aerial for transmission and reception
Bluetooth uses radio waves because radio waves pass through walls but the signal is weakened on doing so
Optical fibres (visible light or infrared) are used for cable television and high-speed broadband because glass is transparent to visible light and some infrared; visible light and short wavelength infrared can carry high rates of data

Know the difference between a digital and analogue signal
Know that a sound can be transmitted as a digital or analogue signal
Explain the benefits of digital signalling including increased rate of transmission of data and increased range due to accurate signal regeneration

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.2 16.1 What Is the Electromagnetic Spectrum?

19.2.1 Discovery of Invisible Light
In 1800, astronomer Sir Frederick William Herschel conducted an experiment using a prism to split sunlight into a spectrum. He placed thermometers in different parts of the visible spectrum and beyond.
Observation:

The thermometer placed just beyond the red light showed the highest temperature reading
This indicated the presence of invisible radiation beyond visible red light

Conclusion:

The electromagnetic spectrum contains more than just visible light
Invisible regions exist that can only be detected by instruments



19.2.2 The Electromagnetic Spectrum
The electromagnetic spectrum consists of all types of electromagnetic waves arranged in order of frequency or wavelength.
Key properties:

All electromagnetic waves are transverse waves
All electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\)
Frequency (\(f\)) and wavelength (\(\lambda\)) are related by: \(c = f\lambda\)







Note



Key Concept: Since \(c\) is constant, frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional: higher frequency means shorter wavelength, and vice versa.




19.2.3 Main Regions of the Electromagnetic Spectrum








Region
Approximate Wavelength Range
Approximate Frequency Range




Radio waves
> 10⁻¹ m
< 3 × 10⁹ Hz


Microwaves
10⁻³ m to 10⁻¹ m
3 × 10⁹ Hz to 3 × 10¹¹ Hz


Infrared
7 × 10⁻⁷ m to 10⁻³ m
3 × 10¹¹ Hz to 4 × 10¹⁴ Hz


Visible light
4 × 10⁻⁷ m to 7 × 10⁻⁷ m
4 × 10¹⁴ Hz to 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz


Ultraviolet
10⁻⁸ m to 4 × 10⁻⁷ m
7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz to 3 × 10¹⁶ Hz


X-rays
10⁻¹¹ m to 10⁻⁸ m
3 × 10¹⁶ Hz to 3 × 10¹⁹ Hz


Gamma rays
< 10⁻¹¹ m
> 3 × 10¹⁹ Hz



Order of increasing frequency (decreasing wavelength):

Radio waves → Microwaves → Infrared → Visible light → Ultraviolet → X-rays → Gamma rays

Memory aid: “Rugby Match Is Very Unusual, Xciting Games”

Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Visible → Ultraviolet → X-rays → Gamma

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.3 16.2 Uses of Electromagnetic Radiation

19.3.1 Radio Waves
Typical uses:

Radio and television transmissions: Tall broadcast towers send radio waves carrying sound and image data to receivers
Astronomy: Large radio telescopes detect radio waves from stars, galaxies, and other astronomical objects
Radio Frequency Identification (RFID): Radio waves transfer data for tracking items with RFID tags

Why radio waves are suitable:

Long wavelengths (up to 1 km) allow diffraction around obstacles like buildings and hills
Can pass through walls, enabling indoor reception
Low energy means they are generally safe for continuous exposure



19.3.2 Microwaves
Typical uses:

Satellite television: Microwaves carry image and sound data from satellites to ground-based dishes
Mobile phones (cell phones): Convert sound to microwave signals for wireless communication
Microwave ovens: Cause water molecules in food to vibrate, generating heat for cooking
Wireless internet (Wi-Fi): Transmit data between devices and routers

Why microwaves are suitable:

Can penetrate clouds and some building materials
Short wavelengths allow compact aerials for transmission and reception
High frequencies enable high data transmission rates



19.3.3 Infrared Radiation
Typical uses:

Electric grills and heaters: Convert electrical energy to infrared for heating and cooking
Remote controllers: Simple LEDs emit infrared pulses to control televisions and other devices
Intruder alarms: Infrared transmitters and detectors sense when a beam is blocked
Thermal imaging: Detectors convert infrared to electrical signals, producing thermal images showing temperature variations
Optical fibres: Some infrared wavelengths pass through glass with minimal signal loss, enabling long-distance data transmission

Why infrared is suitable:

Easily generated and detected using simple electronic components
Causes heating effects useful for cooking and warmth
Short-range communication minimises interference



19.3.4 Visible Light
Typical uses:

Vision: Human eyes detect visible light, enabling us to see our surroundings
Photography: Sensors sensitive to visible light capture images in cameras
Illumination: Light sources provide visibility for work, safety, and aesthetics
Optical fibres: Visible light undergoes total internal reflection for data transmission

Why visible light is suitable:

Detected by human eyes without special equipment
Can be focused and manipulated using lenses and mirrors
High frequencies enable high data rates in optical communication



19.3.5 Ultraviolet Radiation
Typical uses:

Security marking: Chemicals that glow under UV light create invisible markings for authentication
Detecting fake banknotes: UV lamps reveal security features invisible under normal light
Sterilising water: UV radiation damages microorganisms, making water safe to drink

Why ultraviolet is suitable:

High energy can break chemical bonds in microorganisms
Causes fluorescence in certain materials for detection purposes
Can be generated using specialised lamps



19.3.6 X-rays
Typical uses:

Medical scanning: X-rays penetrate soft tissues but are absorbed by bones, producing images for diagnosis
Security scanners: Airport baggage scanners use X-rays to detect hidden weapons or contraband

Why X-rays are suitable:

High penetrating power allows imaging of internal structures
Different materials absorb X-rays to different degrees, creating contrast in images



19.3.7 Gamma Rays
Typical uses:

Sterilising food and medical equipment: Gamma rays kill bacteria and other microorganisms without heating
Detection and treatment of cancer: Gamma rays can destroy cancer cells; radioactive tracers emitting gamma rays help locate tumours

Why gamma rays are suitable:

Extremely high penetrating power reaches deep into materials and tissues
High energy can kill cells and break chemical bonds

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.4 16.3 Harmful Effects of Electromagnetic Radiation

19.4.1 General Principle
The harmful effects of electromagnetic radiation depend on:

Frequency/energy: Higher frequency radiation carries more energy per photon
Intensity: Greater intensity means more radiation energy absorbed
Exposure time: Longer exposure increases total energy absorbed
Type of tissue: Different body tissues respond differently to radiation



19.4.2 Specific Harmful Effects







Radiation Type
Harmful Effects of Excessive Exposure




Microwaves
Internal heating of body cells; can cause tissue damage if intensity is very high


Infrared
Skin burns; excessive exposure to intense infrared sources can damage skin


Ultraviolet
Damage to surface cells and eyes; can cause skin cancer, premature skin ageing, cataracts, and macular degeneration


X-rays
Mutation or damage to cells; excessive exposure increases cancer risk; can harm developing foetuses


Gamma rays
Mutation or damage to cells; high doses can cause radiation sickness; increases long-term cancer risk









Warning



Important: Normal, controlled use of electromagnetic radiation (e.g., medical X-rays, UV sterilisation) is safe. Harm occurs only with excessive or uncontrolled exposure.




19.4.3 Safety Precautions

Microwaves: Maintain safe distance from operating microwave ovens; ensure door seals are intact
Infrared: Use protective eyewear when working with intense infrared sources; avoid prolonged exposure to heat lamps
Ultraviolet: Wear sunscreen and protective clothing outdoors; avoid staring at UV lamps; use UV-blocking sunglasses
X-rays and gamma rays: Use lead shielding; minimise exposure time; maintain distance from sources; only trained personnel should operate equipment

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.5 16.4 Electromagnetic Waves in Communication

19.5.1 Speed of Electromagnetic Waves
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum:
\[c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\]
In air, the speed is approximately the same (slightly less, but the difference is negligible for most purposes).
Worked Example: Signal Travel Time
Question: How long does it take a microwave signal to travel from Earth to a geostationary satellite 36,000 km away and back?
Solution:
Step 1: Calculate total distance \[\text{Total distance} = 36,000 \text{ km} + 36,000 \text{ km} = 72,000 \text{ km} = 7.2 \times 10^7 \text{ m}\]
Step 2: Apply speed formula \[t = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}} = \frac{7.2 \times 10^7}{3.0 \times 10^8} = \boxed{0.24 \text{ s}}\]
Interpretation: Communication via geostationary satellites has a noticeable delay of about 0.24 seconds for a round trip.


19.5.2 Satellite Communication
Types of artificial satellites:









Type
Altitude
Characteristics
Uses




Geostationary satellites
~36,000 km above equator
Orbit period = 24 hours; appear stationary relative to Earth
Direct broadcast TV, some satellite phones, weather monitoring


Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites
~500–2,000 km above Earth
Orbit period ~90 minutes; move rapidly across sky
Some satellite phones, Earth observation, internet constellations



Why microwaves for satellite communication?

Can penetrate clouds and atmosphere with minimal attenuation
Short wavelengths allow compact, directional aerials on satellites and ground stations
High frequencies support high data transmission rates for TV and internet



19.5.3 Wireless Communication Technologies

19.5.3.1 Mobile Phones and Wireless Internet

Use microwaves (typically 800 MHz to 2.6 GHz)
Microwaves can penetrate some walls, enabling indoor use
Short wavelengths allow compact aerials in mobile devices
High frequencies support voice, text, and data transmission



19.5.3.2 Bluetooth

Uses radio waves (2.4 GHz band)
Radio waves pass through walls but are weakened, limiting range to ~10 m
Suitable for short-range device-to-device communication (e.g., phone to speaker)



19.5.3.3 Optical Fibres

Use visible light or short-wavelength infrared (650–1600 nm)
Glass is transparent to these wavelengths; light undergoes total internal reflection
Very high frequencies enable extremely high data rates (terabits per second)
Minimal signal loss over long distances; ideal for cable TV and broadband internet







Note



Key Insight: The choice of electromagnetic region for a communication technology depends on wavelength, penetration ability, data capacity, and practical considerations like aerial size.

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.6 16.5 Analogue and Digital Signals

19.6.1 What Is a Signal?
A signal is a varying quantity that carries information. In communication systems, signals represent sound, images, or data.


19.6.2 Analogue Signals
Characteristics:

Have continuous values that vary smoothly over time
Information is encoded in variations of amplitude, frequency, or phase
Examples: traditional radio broadcasts, vinyl records, analogue telephone lines

Graphical representation:
Value
  ^
  |    /\/\    /\
  |   /    \  /  \
  |  /      \/    \
  +------------------> Time


19.6.3 Digital Signals
Characteristics:

Have discrete values, typically two states: ‘on’ (1) and ‘off’ (0)
Information is encoded as sequences of binary digits (bits)
Examples: digital TV, mobile phone calls, internet data, CDs

Graphical representation:
Value
  ^
1 |  ┌─┐  ┌───┐  ┌─
  |  │ │  │   │  │
0 |──┘ └──┘   └──┘──> Time


19.6.4 Transmitting Sound as Signals
Sound can be transmitted using either analogue or digital signals:
Analogue transmission:

Microphone converts sound waves to continuous electrical signals
Signals modulate a carrier wave (e.g., radio wave)
Receiver demodulates and converts back to sound

Digital transmission:

Microphone converts sound to analogue electrical signals
Analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) samples and encodes signals as binary data
Binary data modulates a carrier wave for transmission
Receiver demodulates and digital-to-analogue converter (DAC) reconstructs sound

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.7 16.6 Benefits of Digital Signalling

19.7.1 Increased Data Transmission Rate

Digital signals can be compressed using mathematical algorithms
Compression reduces the number of bits needed to represent the same information
More data can be transmitted in the same time → higher data rates
Enables high-quality video streaming, fast internet downloads



19.7.2 Accurate Signal Regeneration
Problem with analogue signals:

Noise (unwanted variations) accumulates during transmission
Amplifiers boost both signal and noise → degraded quality over long distances

Advantage of digital signals:

Only two values (1 and 0) are expected
If noise is not too large, the original signal can be regenerated accurately
Repeaters along the transmission path recover and retransmit clean digital signals
Enables high-quality communication over very long distances



19.7.3 Other Benefits

Error detection and correction: Digital systems can detect and correct transmission errors
Encryption: Digital data can be encrypted for secure communication
Multiplexing: Multiple digital signals can be combined and transmitted simultaneously
Storage and processing: Digital signals are easily stored, copied, and processed by computers

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.8 Key Concepts Summary

19.8.1 Core Concepts

Electromagnetic spectrum regions in order of increasing frequency: radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma
All electromagnetic waves travel at \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\) in vacuum; speed approximately same in air
Uses of each region: Radio (broadcasting, RFID), microwave (satellites, phones, ovens), infrared (heating, remote controls, thermal imaging), visible (vision, photography), UV (security, sterilisation), X-ray (medical imaging, security), gamma (sterilisation, cancer treatment)
Harmful effects: Microwaves (internal heating), infrared (skin burns), UV (skin/eye damage, cancer), X-rays/gamma (cell damage, mutation, cancer)
Satellite communication: Mainly uses microwaves; geostationary (~36,000 km) and LEO (~500–2,000 km) satellites serve different purposes



19.8.2 Extended Concepts

Communication technologies: Mobile phones/Wi-Fi use microwaves (penetrate walls, short aerials); Bluetooth uses radio waves (pass through walls but weaken); optical fibres use visible/short-wavelength infrared (high data rates, low loss)
Analogue vs digital signals: Analogue = continuous values; digital = discrete values (1/0); sound can be transmitted either way
Benefits of digital signalling: Higher data rates via compression; accurate regeneration over long distances; error correction; encryption; easy storage/processing

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.9 Common Misconceptions

19.9.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Different electromagnetic waves travel at different speeds”
Incorrect: “Radio waves travel slower than light”
Correct:

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum: \(3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\)
Differences in wavelength and frequency do not affect speed in vacuum
In materials (e.g., glass), different frequencies may travel at slightly different speeds (dispersion), but this is not the case in vacuum/air




19.9.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Higher frequency means more dangerous radiation”
Incorrect: “Gamma rays are always dangerous; radio waves are always safe”
Correct:

Danger depends on intensity, exposure time, and frequency, not frequency alone
Low-intensity gamma rays (e.g., medical tracers) can be safe; high-intensity radio waves can cause heating
Normal, controlled use of any electromagnetic radiation is generally safe




19.9.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Microwaves cook food by making it radioactive”
Incorrect: “Microwave ovens make food radioactive”
Correct:

Microwaves cause water molecules to vibrate, generating heat through friction
This is a non-ionising process; it does not change the chemical structure of food or make it radioactive
Food heated in a microwave is no different from food heated by other methods




19.9.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Digital signals are always better than analogue”
Incorrect: “Analogue signals are obsolete; digital is always superior”
Correct:

Digital signals have advantages for long-distance transmission, storage, and processing
Analogue signals can be simpler and adequate for short-range, low-complexity applications
Choice depends on application requirements, cost, and available technology




19.9.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Optical fibres use any type of light”
Incorrect: “Any light can travel through optical fibres”
Correct:

Optical fibres are transparent only to visible light and short-wavelength infrared
Other wavelengths (e.g., long-wavelength infrared, ultraviolet) are absorbed or scattered
The specific wavelengths used (650–1600 nm) are chosen for minimal loss in glass




19.9.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “All ultraviolet radiation comes from the Sun”
Incorrect: “UV radiation only comes from sunlight”
Correct:

The Sun is a major natural source of UV radiation
Artificial sources include UV lamps for sterilisation, tanning beds, and certain types of lighting
Some electrical equipment (e.g., welding arcs) also emits UV radiation




19.9.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “X-rays and gamma rays are the same thing”
Incorrect: “X-rays and gamma rays are identical; the names are interchangeable”
Correct:

Both are high-frequency, high-energy electromagnetic radiation
Origin differs: X-rays are produced by electron transitions; gamma rays are produced by nuclear processes
Energy ranges overlap, but gamma rays typically have higher frequencies
Applications and safety precautions may differ based on source and energy

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.10 Worked Examples

19.10.1 Example 1: Ordering Electromagnetic Waves
Question: Arrange the following electromagnetic waves in order of increasing wavelength: visible light, microwaves, gamma rays, infrared, radio waves.
Solution:
Step 1: Recall order of increasing frequency: gamma → X-ray → UV → visible → infrared → microwave → radio
Step 2: Since wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency, reverse the order for increasing wavelength:
\[\text{gamma rays} < \text{visible light} < \text{infrared} < \text{microwaves} < \text{radio waves}\]
Answer: Gamma rays, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves



19.10.2 Example 2: Calculating Wavelength
Question: A mobile phone uses microwaves with a frequency of 1.8 GHz. Calculate the wavelength of these microwaves. (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\))
Solution:
Step 1: Convert frequency to Hz \[f = 1.8 \text{ GHz} = 1.8 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz}\]
Step 2: Apply wave equation \[c = f\lambda \quad \Rightarrow \quad \lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8}{1.8 \times 10^9} = \boxed{0.17 \text{ m} = 17 \text{ cm}}\]
Interpretation: The wavelength is about 17 cm, which is why mobile phone aerials can be compact.



19.10.3 Example 3: Signal Travel Time to Satellite
Question: A geostationary satellite is 36,000 km above the Earth. Calculate the minimum time delay for a signal to travel from Earth to the satellite and back.
Solution:
Step 1: Total distance for round trip \[d = 2 \times 36,000 \text{ km} = 72,000 \text{ km} = 7.2 \times 10^7 \text{ m}\]
Step 2: Time calculation \[t = \frac{d}{c} = \frac{7.2 \times 10^7}{3.0 \times 10^8} = \boxed{0.24 \text{ s}}\]
Interpretation: This 0.24 s delay is noticeable in satellite phone conversations and live satellite TV broadcasts.



19.10.4 Example 4: Digital vs Analogue Signal Quality
Question: Explain why a digital TV signal received over a long distance via satellite maintains better quality than an analogue TV signal transmitted over the same distance.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify key difference: signal regeneration
Step 2: Analogue signal behaviour: - Noise accumulates during transmission - Amplifiers boost both signal and noise - Quality degrades progressively with distance
Step 3: Digital signal behaviour: - Only two values (1/0) are expected - Repeaters detect and regenerate clean digital signals - Noise is eliminated at each regeneration point
Conclusion: Digital signals can be accurately regenerated at repeaters, maintaining quality over long distances; analogue signals accumulate noise that cannot be removed.

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.12 Laboratory Investigation

19.12.1 Experiment 16.1: Investigating Infrared Radiation
Objective: To demonstrate the detection of infrared radiation and its heating effect.
Apparatus:

Infrared lamp or heat source
Thermometer or temperature sensor with data logger
Black and white/silver surfaces (e.g., painted metal plates)
Retort stand and clamp
Stopwatch

Variables:

Independent: Surface colour/texture (black vs. white/silver)
Dependent: Temperature change over time
Controlled: Distance from heat source, initial temperature, exposure time

Procedure:

Set up the infrared lamp at a fixed distance from the test surfaces.
Place the black surface and the white/silver surface at equal distances from the lamp.
Attach a thermometer or temperature sensor to each surface.
Record the initial temperature of each surface.
Switch on the infrared lamp and start the stopwatch.
Record the temperature of each surface every 30 seconds for 5 minutes.
Switch off the lamp and allow surfaces to cool.
Repeat the experiment with the surfaces swapped to check for consistency.

Data Table:








Time (s)
Temperature of black surface (°C)
Temperature of white/silver surface (°C)




0




30




60




90




120




150




180




210




240




270




300





Analysis:

Plot a graph of temperature (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for both surfaces on the same axes.
Compare the rates of temperature increase for the two surfaces.
Explain the difference in terms of absorption of infrared radiation.

Precautions:

✓ Keep the distance from the lamp to each surface constant
✓ Avoid touching the hot surfaces; use tongs if necessary
✓ Ensure the thermometer bulbs are in good thermal contact with the surfaces
✓ Allow surfaces to return to room temperature between trials

Expected Results:

The black surface will heat up faster than the white/silver surface
This demonstrates that dark, dull surfaces absorb infrared radiation more effectively than light, shiny surfaces

Conclusion Template:
“The experiment demonstrated that black, dull surfaces absorb infrared radiation more effectively than white, shiny surfaces, as shown by the faster temperature rise of the black surface. This supports the principle that surface colour and texture affect the absorption of infrared radiation.”
Extension (Supplement):

Investigate the emission of infrared radiation by comparing cooling rates of hot black and white surfaces
Research applications: solar water heaters (blackened surfaces), space blankets (shiny surfaces)

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.14 Chapter Summary

19.14.1 Key Points to Remember
✓ Electromagnetic spectrum order (increasing frequency): radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma
✓ All EM waves travel at \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\) in vacuum; approximately same in air
✓ Uses: Radio (broadcasting, RFID), microwave (satellites, phones, ovens), infrared (heating, remote controls, thermal imaging), visible (vision, photography), UV (security, sterilisation), X-ray (medical imaging, security), gamma (sterilisation, cancer treatment)
✓ Harmful effects: Microwaves (internal heating), infrared (skin burns), UV (skin/eye damage, cancer), X-rays/gamma (cell damage, mutation, cancer)
✓ Satellite communication: Uses microwaves; geostationary (~36,000 km) for TV/phones; LEO (~500–2,000 km) for phones/observation
✓ Wireless tech: Mobile/Wi-Fi use microwaves (penetrate walls, short aerials); Bluetooth uses radio waves (pass through walls but weaken); optical fibres use visible/short IR (high data rates, low loss)
✓ Analogue vs digital: Analogue = continuous values; digital = discrete (1/0); digital enables compression, regeneration, error correction
✓ Digital benefits: Higher data rates, accurate regeneration over distance, encryption, easy storage/processing


19.14.2 Formulae Sheet








Quantity
Formula
Variables




Wave speed
\(c = f\lambda\)
\(c\)=speed in vacuum (\(3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\)), \(f\)=frequency (Hz), \(\lambda\)=wavelength (m)


Signal travel time
\(t = \frac{d}{c}\)
\(t\)=time (s), \(d\)=distance (m), \(c\)=speed of EM waves

title: 19  Electromagnetic Spectrum
text:
19.16 Glossary







Term
Definition




Analogue signal
A signal with continuous values that vary smoothly over time; information encoded in amplitude, frequency, or phase variations


Digital signal
A signal with discrete values, typically two states (‘on’/1 and ‘off’/0); information encoded as binary data


Electromagnetic spectrum
The complete range of electromagnetic waves arranged in order of frequency or wavelength


Electromagnetic wave
A transverse wave consisting of oscillating electric and magnetic fields; can travel through vacuum at speed \(c\)


Frequency (\(f\))
Number of complete waves passing a point per second; unit: hertz (Hz)


Geostationary satellite
A satellite orbiting ~36,000 km above the equator with an orbital period of 24 hours, appearing stationary relative to Earth


Infrared radiation
Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible red light; associated with heating effects


Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite
A satellite orbiting ~500–2,000 km above Earth with an orbital period of ~90 minutes


Microwave
Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths between radio waves and infrared; used in communication and cooking


Optical fibre
A thin glass or plastic fibre that transmits light by total internal reflection; used for high-speed data transmission


Total internal reflection
The complete reflection of light within a denser medium when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle; principle behind optical fibres


Ultraviolet radiation
Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths shorter than visible violet light; can cause fluorescence and cell damage


Wavelength (\(\lambda\))
Shortest distance between two consecutive points in phase on a wave; unit: metre (m)

title: 20  Sound
section: 20.2 17.1 Production and Nature of Sound Waves
text:
20.2 17.1 Production and Nature of Sound Waves

20.2.1 How Is Sound Produced?
Sound is produced by vibrating sources placed in a medium.

When a guitar string vibrates, it pushes and pulls on the surrounding air particles
When vocal cords vibrate, they create pressure variations in the air
When a drum skin is struck, it vibrates and transfers energy to the air







Note



Key Concept: Without vibration, there is no sound. If you stop a vibrating object (e.g., by placing your hand on a ringing bell), the sound stops because the vibration stops.




20.2.2 The Longitudinal Nature of Sound Waves
Sound waves are longitudinal waves. This means:

The direction of vibration of particles is parallel to the direction of wave propagation
Sound waves propagate as a series of compressions and rarefactions









Term
Description
Particle Arrangement




Compression
Region where air pressure is higher than surrounding pressure
Particles are close together


Rarefaction
Region where air pressure is lower than surrounding pressure
Particles are spread apart



Visual representation of a sound wave:
Direction of wave propagation →

Compression    Rarefaction    Compression    Rarefaction
[|||||]        [   ]          [|||||]        [   ]
particles      particles      particles      particles
close          spread         close          spread
together       apart          together       apart






Warning



Important: Do not confuse the motion of individual particles with the motion of the wave. Particles oscillate back and forth about fixed positions; they do not travel with the wave.




20.2.3 The Audible Range of Human Hearing
The human ear can detect sound waves within a specific range of frequencies:

Lower limit: approximately 20 Hz
Upper limit: approximately 20 000 Hz (or 20 kHz)

Terminology:



Term
Frequency Range
Audible to Humans?




Infrasound
Below 20 Hz
No


Audible sound
20 Hz to 20 kHz
Yes


Ultrasound
Above 20 kHz
No



Note: The upper limit of hearing decreases with age. Many adults cannot hear sounds above 15–17 kHz.

title: 20  Sound
text:
20.3 17.2 Transmission of Sound

20.3.1 Why Is a Medium Needed?
Sound waves require a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel because:

Sound is produced by particle vibrations
These vibrations must be transferred from one particle to the next
In a vacuum, there are no particles to vibrate → sound cannot travel

Demonstration: The Bell Jar Experiment

An electric bell is suspended inside a sealed bell jar
When the bell rings with air inside, the sound is clearly heard
As air is pumped out, the sound becomes fainter
When a near-vacuum is achieved, the sound cannot be heard (though the bell is still visibly vibrating)

Conclusion: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.


20.3.2 Speed of Sound in Different Media
The speed of sound depends on the medium through which it travels:



Medium
Approximate Speed of Sound (m/s)




Air (at 20°C)
330–350


Water
≈ 1500


Steel
≈ 5000


Granite
≈ 5400



General rule: Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases.
Explanation using particle model:

In solids, particles are closely packed → vibrations transfer quickly between particles
In liquids, particles are slightly further apart → transfer is slower
In gases, particles are far apart → transfer is slowest







Note



Key Insight: The speed of sound also depends on temperature. In air, sound travels faster at higher temperatures because particles have more kinetic energy and collide more frequently.




20.3.3 Measuring the Speed of Sound in Air
Method: Distance–Time Measurement
Apparatus:

Two observers (A and B) positioned a known distance apart (e.g., 500 m)
Electronic starting pistol (produces flash and sound simultaneously)
Stopwatch
Measuring tape

Procedure:

Observer A fires the electronic starting pistol
Observer B starts the stopwatch when seeing the flash (light travels almost instantaneously)
Observer B stops the stopwatch when hearing the sound
Record the time interval \(t\)
Calculate speed: \(v = \frac{d}{t}\)

Example calculation:

Distance \(d = 500 \text{ m}\)
Time \(t = 1.5 \text{ s}\)
Speed \(v = \frac{500}{1.5} = 333 \text{ m/s}\)

Precautions:

✓ Repeat the experiment and take an average to minimise random errors
✓ Interchange positions of observers to cancel wind effects
✓ Use a large distance to reduce timing error relative to total time

title: 20  Sound
text:
20.4 17.3 Loudness and Pitch

20.4.1 What Affects Loudness?
Loudness is related to the amplitude of a sound wave.

Larger amplitude → louder sound
Smaller amplitude → softer sound

Particle explanation:

Larger amplitude means particles oscillate with greater displacement
This creates larger pressure variations (greater difference between compressions and rarefactions)
The ear detects these larger pressure variations as a louder sound



20.4.2 What Affects Pitch?
Pitch is related to the frequency of a sound wave.

Higher frequency → higher pitch
Lower frequency → lower pitch

Particle explanation:

Higher frequency means particles oscillate more times per second
The ear interprets more frequent pressure variations as a higher-pitched sound



20.4.3 Visualising Sound Waves with a C.R.O.
A cathode-ray oscilloscope (c.r.o.) connected to a microphone can display sound waveforms:







Waveform Feature
What It Represents




Height of wave (from rest position)
Amplitude → loudness


Distance between successive peaks
Wavelength → related to frequency and pitch


Number of waves per second on screen
Frequency → pitch



Example comparisons:

A loud, low-pitched sound: large amplitude, widely spaced peaks
A soft, high-pitched sound: small amplitude, closely spaced peaks

title: 20  Sound
text:
20.5 17.4 Echoes and Ultrasound

20.5.1 What Is an Echo?
An echo is the reflection of sound waves from a hard, flat surface.
How echoes form:

Sound waves travel from a source towards a surface (e.g., a wall or cliff)
The waves strike the surface and are reflected back
The reflected waves reach the listener after a time delay

Law of reflection for sound:

Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection
Both angles measured from the normal to the reflecting surface

Calculating distance using echoes:
\[d = \frac{v \times t}{2}\]
Where: - \(d\) = distance to reflecting surface (m)

\(v\) = speed of sound in the medium (m/s)
\(t\) = time for echo to return (s)
Divide by 2 because sound travels to the surface and back

Worked Example: Echo Calculation
Question: A ship sends a sound pulse downwards into the sea. An echo from the seabed is received 0.4 s later. If the speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s, calculate the depth of the sea.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify values - \(v = 1500 \text{ m/s}\)

\(t = 0.4 \text{ s}\)

Step 2: Apply formula \[d = \frac{v \times t}{2} = \frac{1500 \times 0.4}{2} = \boxed{300 \text{ m}}\]



20.5.2 What Is Ultrasound?
Ultrasound is sound with a frequency higher than 20 kHz (above the upper limit of human hearing).


20.5.3 Uses of Ultrasound

20.5.3.1 1. Non-Destructive Testing of Materials

Ultrasound is sent through materials such as metal pipes or concrete slabs
Defects (cracks, cavities) reflect or scatter the ultrasound
By analysing the reflected signals, engineers can locate and size defects without damaging the material



20.5.3.2 2. Medical Scanning of Soft Tissue

Ultrasound pulses are sent into the body via a transducer
Different tissues reflect ultrasound to different degrees
The time taken for echoes to return is used to build up an image of internal structures
Advantages over X-rays: Ultrasound is non-ionising and safer for scanning foetuses and soft tissues



20.5.3.3 3. Sonar (Sound Navigation and Ranging)

Ships use sonar to detect the depth of the seabed or the position of objects underwater
A pulse of ultrasound is sent downwards; the time for the echo to return is measured
Depth is calculated using \(d = \frac{v \times t}{2}\)

Worked Example: Sonar Calculation
Question: A submarine uses sonar to detect a shoal of fish. The ultrasound pulse returns after 0.12 s. If the speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s, calculate the distance to the shoal.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify values - \(v = 1500 \text{ m/s}\)

\(t = 0.12 \text{ s}\)

Step 2: Apply formula \[d = \frac{v \times t}{2} = \frac{1500 \times 0.12}{2} = \boxed{90 \text{ m}}\]

title: 20  Sound
text:
20.6 Key Concepts Summary

20.6.1 Core Concepts

Sound production: Sound is produced by vibrating sources in a medium
Longitudinal waves: Sound waves consist of compressions and rarefactions; particle vibration is parallel to wave propagation
Audible range: Humans can hear frequencies from approximately 20 Hz to 20 kHz
Medium required: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum; it requires a medium (solid, liquid, or gas)
Speed of sound: Approximately 330–350 m/s in air; faster in liquids and solids
Speed measurement: Use distance–time method with flash and sound from a starting pistol
Loudness and pitch: Loudness depends on amplitude; pitch depends on frequency
Echoes: Reflection of sound waves; used to calculate distances
Ultrasound: Sound with frequency > 20 kHz; used in testing, medical scanning, and sonar



20.6.2 Extended Concepts

Compression and rarefaction: Regions of high and low pressure in a longitudinal sound wave
Speed comparison: Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases
Ultrasound applications: Non-destructive testing, medical imaging, sonar depth/distance calculations

title: 20  Sound
text:
20.7 Common Misconceptions

20.7.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Sound can travel through a vacuum”
Incorrect: “Sound from explosions in space movies is realistic”
Correct: - Sound requires a medium (particles) to transfer vibrations

In a vacuum, there are no particles → sound cannot propagate
Space is a near-vacuum → no sound can travel through it




20.7.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Particles travel with the sound wave”
Incorrect: “Air molecules move from the speaker to your ear when you hear music”
Correct: - Particles oscillate back and forth about fixed positions

They transfer energy to neighbouring particles through collisions
Only the wave pattern and energy travel forward, not the particles themselves




20.7.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Loudness depends on frequency”
Incorrect: “High-pitched sounds are always louder than low-pitched sounds”
Correct: - Loudness depends on amplitude (size of pressure variations)

Pitch depends on frequency (number of vibrations per second)
A low-pitched sound can be very loud if it has large amplitude




20.7.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Ultrasound is harmful because it is ‘ultra’”
Incorrect: “Ultrasound is dangerous because it is very high frequency”
Correct: - Ultrasound is non-ionising radiation and is generally safe at diagnostic intensities

It is preferred over X-rays for scanning foetuses because it does not damage cells
Harm depends on intensity and exposure time, not just frequency




20.7.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Echoes are a different type of sound”
Incorrect: “An echo is a special kind of sound wave”
Correct: - An echo is simply a reflected sound wave

It has the same frequency, speed, and wavelength as the original sound
The only difference is the direction of propagation and the time delay




20.7.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “Sound travels at the same speed in all materials”
Incorrect: “Sound travels at 340 m/s everywhere”
Correct: - Speed of sound depends on the medium and its properties (density, elasticity, temperature)

In air: ~330–350 m/s; in water: ~1500 m/s; in steel: ~5000 m/s
Temperature also affects speed: sound travels faster in warmer air




20.7.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “Ultrasound cannot be used for distance measurement”
Incorrect: “Ultrasound is only for medical imaging”
Correct: - Ultrasound is ideal for distance measurement because: - High frequency → short wavelength → precise measurements

Can be directed in narrow beams
Reflects well from boundaries between different materials
Used in sonar, parking sensors, and industrial thickness gauging

title: 20  Sound
text:
20.8 Worked Examples

20.8.1 Example 1: Frequency and Period
Question: A tuning fork vibrates at a frequency of 440 Hz. Calculate: (a) the period of one vibration (b) the number of complete vibrations in 2.5 seconds
Solution:
(a) Period: \[T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{440} = \boxed{0.00227 \text{ s} = 2.27 \text{ ms}}\]
(b) Number of vibrations: \[\text{Number} = f \times t = 440 \times 2.5 = \boxed{1100 \text{ vibrations}}\]



20.8.2 Example 2: Speed of Sound Calculation
Question: A student stands 170 m from a large wall and claps her hands. She hears the echo 1.0 s later. Calculate the speed of sound in air.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify that sound travels to the wall and back \[\text{Total distance} = 2 \times 170 = 340 \text{ m}\]
Step 2: Apply speed formula \[v = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} = \frac{340}{1.0} = \boxed{340 \text{ m/s}}\]



20.8.3 Example 3: Ultrasound in Medical Scanning
Question: An ultrasound scanner sends a pulse into a patient’s abdomen. The pulse reflects off the foetus and returns to the scanner after 0.00012 s. If the speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1540 m/s, calculate the depth of the foetus below the scanner.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify values - \(v = 1540 \text{ m/s}\)

\(t = 0.00012 \text{ s}\)

Step 2: Apply echo formula \[d = \frac{v \times t}{2} = \frac{1540 \times 0.00012}{2} = \boxed{0.0924 \text{ m} = 9.24 \text{ cm}}\]



20.8.4 Example 4: Comparing Loudness and Pitch
Question: Two sound waves are displayed on a c.r.o. Wave A has an amplitude of 2.0 cm and a wavelength of 4.0 cm. Wave B has an amplitude of 1.0 cm and a wavelength of 2.0 cm. The time base is the same for both. Compare the loudness and pitch of the two sounds.
Solution:
Loudness comparison: - Amplitude of A (2.0 cm) > Amplitude of B (1.0 cm)

Therefore, Sound A is louder than Sound B

Pitch comparison: - Wavelength of A (4.0 cm) > Wavelength of B (2.0 cm)

Since \(v = f\lambda\) and \(v\) is constant, longer wavelength → lower frequency
Therefore, Sound A has a lower pitch than Sound B

Conclusion: Sound A is louder but lower-pitched than Sound B.

title: 20  Sound
text:
20.10 Laboratory Investigation

20.10.1 Experiment 17.1: Measuring the Speed of Sound Using Echoes
Objective: To determine the speed of sound in air by measuring the time for an echo to return from a reflecting surface.
Apparatus: - Two flat wooden boards (to create a sharp clap)

Stopwatch
Measuring tape (at least 50 m)
Large flat wall or building (reflecting surface)

Variables: - Independent: Distance to reflecting surface

Dependent: Time for echo to return
Controlled: Same clapping method, same observer timing, same environmental conditions

Procedure: 1. Measure and mark a distance \(d\) (e.g., 50 m) from a large flat wall.

Stand at the marked position facing the wall.
Clap the two boards together sharply and listen for the echo.
Practise clapping rhythmically so that each clap coincides with the echo of the previous clap.
Once a steady rhythm is achieved, have a partner time 20 claps using a stopwatch.
Record the total time \(t_{\text{total}}\) for 20 claps.
Calculate the time for one round trip: \(t = \frac{t_{\text{total}}}{20}\)
Calculate the speed of sound: \(v = \frac{2d}{t}\)
Repeat for different distances and calculate an average value.

Data Table:










Trial

Calculated speed \(v\) (m/s)

Analysis: 1. Calculate the speed of sound for each trial using \(v = \frac{2d}{t}\)

Calculate the average speed from all trials
Compare your result with the accepted value (~340 m/s) and discuss possible sources of error

Precautions: - ✓ Choose a quiet location to hear echoes clearly

✓ Ensure the reflecting surface is large and flat for a clear echo
✓ Practise the clapping rhythm before timing to reduce reaction time errors
✓ Use a distance of at least 50 m to make timing errors relatively small

Expected Results: - The calculated speed should be close to 330–350 m/s, depending on air temperature

Repeating at different distances helps identify and reduce systematic errors

Conclusion Template: “The speed of sound in air was determined to be ______ m/s. This value is [close to/different from] the accepted value of 340 m/s, which may be due to [reaction time errors/temperature variations/wind effects/etc.].”
Extension (Supplement): - Investigate how temperature affects the speed of sound by conducting the experiment at different times of day

Compare the speed of sound in different media (e.g., through a metal rod vs. through air)

✓ Sound production: Vibrating sources in a medium produce sound waves

Formula

20.14 Glossary







Term
Definition




Amplitude
Maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position; determines loudness of sound


Audible range
Range of frequencies detectable by the human ear (~20 Hz to ~20 kHz)


Compression
Region in a longitudinal sound wave where particles are close together and pressure is high


Echo
Reflection of sound waves from a hard, flat surface; used to calculate distances


Frequency (\(f\))
Number of complete waves (or vibrations) per second; unit: hertz (Hz); determines pitch


Infrasound
Sound with frequency below 20 Hz; inaudible to humans


Longitudinal wave
Wave in which particle vibration is parallel to the direction of wave propagation


Pitch
Perception of how high or low a sound is; determined by frequency


Rarefaction
Region in a longitudinal sound wave where particles are spread apart and pressure is low


Sonar
Sound Navigation and Ranging; uses ultrasound pulses to detect objects and measure distances underwater


Ultrasound
Sound with frequency higher than 20 kHz; inaudible to humans but useful in medical and industrial applications

Know that the relative strength of a magnetic field is represented by the spacing of the magnetic field lines

title: 21  Simple Phenomena of Magnetism
text:
21.2 18.1 Magnets and Magnetic Materials

21.2.1 What Is a Magnet?
A magnet is an object that exerts a magnetic force. This force causes magnets to display certain characteristic properties.
Key properties of magnets:

Magnets attract magnetic materials
The poles of magnets have the strongest magnetic force
A freely suspended magnet points to the north–south direction
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract



21.2.2 Magnetic and Non-Magnetic Materials



Magnetic Materials
Non-Magnetic Materials




Steel
Copper


Iron
Wood


Cobalt
Plastic


Nickel
Brass


Magnetite (lodestone)
Glass









Note



Key Concept: Magnetic materials are materials that can be attracted to a magnet. Non-magnetic materials cannot be attracted to a magnet.




21.2.3 Poles of a Magnet
The ends of a magnet are called poles. There are two types:

North pole (N pole): The end that points towards the Earth’s geographic North Pole when the magnet is freely suspended
South pole (S pole): The end that points towards the Earth’s geographic South Pole when the magnet is freely suspended

Law of Magnetic Poles:

Like poles repel each other (N–N or S–S)
Unlike poles attract each other (N–S)







Warning



Important: The magnetic poles of a magnet cannot be isolated. If you break a magnet in half, you get two smaller magnets, each with its own N and S pole.

title: 21  Simple Phenomena of Magnetism
text:
21.3 18.2 Induced Magnetism

21.3.1 What Is Induced Magnetism?
Induced magnetism is the process by which an unmagnetised magnetic material becomes magnetised when placed near a permanent magnet.
How induction works:

When an unmagnetised iron bar is brought near the N pole of a permanent magnet
The magnet’s magnetic field causes the magnetic domains in the iron to align
The end of the iron bar nearest to the magnet becomes an induced S pole
The far end becomes an induced N pole
The iron bar is now an induced magnet and can attract other magnetic materials







Note



Key Insight: Induced magnetism does not require physical contact. The magnetic field alone can induce magnetism in a nearby magnetic material.




21.3.2 Temporary vs Permanent Magnets








Property
Temporary Magnets (Soft Iron)
Permanent Magnets (Steel)




Ease of magnetisation
Easily magnetised
Difficult to magnetise


Strength as induced magnet
Stronger induced magnet
Weaker induced magnet


Retention of magnetism
Loses magnetism easily
Retains magnetism well


Typical uses
Electromagnets, relay cores
Compass needles, fridge magnets, loudspeakers









Warning



Important: The choice between soft iron and steel depends on the application. Use soft iron when you need a magnet that can be switched on and off; use steel when you need a magnet that stays magnetised.

title: 21  Simple Phenomena of Magnetism
text:
21.4 18.3 Magnetic Fields

21.4.1 What Is a Magnetic Field?
A magnetic field is a region of space in which a magnetic pole experiences a force.
Key characteristics:

Magnetic fields are invisible but can be visualised using field lines
The direction of the magnetic field at any point is the direction of the force on the N pole of a magnet placed at that point
Magnetic field lines always emerge from the N pole and enter the S pole



21.4.2 Drawing Magnetic Field Lines
Rules for drawing magnetic field lines:

Field lines start at the N pole and end at the S pole
Field lines never cross each other
The density of field lines indicates field strength: closer lines = stronger field
Field lines are continuous curves

Pattern around a bar magnet:
        N                           S
        |                           |
   ---->|                           |<----
  /     |                           |     \
 /      |                           |      \
|       |                           |       |
 \      |                           |      /
  \     |                           |     /
   ---->|                           |<----
        |                           |






Note



Key Concept: The magnetic field is strongest at the poles, where the field lines are most concentrated.




21.4.3 Plotting Magnetic Field Lines Experimentally
Method 1: Using a plotting compass
Apparatus:

Bar magnet
Plotting compass (small magnetic compass)
Plain paper
Pencil

Procedure:

Place the bar magnet at the centre of a sheet of paper
Mark the outline of the magnet and label its N and S poles
Place the plotting compass near the N pole
Mark the positions of both ends of the compass needle with dots
Move the compass so that its S end is at the previous N mark
Mark the new position of the N end
Repeat until you reach the S pole of the magnet
Join the dots to form a smooth curve — this is one magnetic field line
Repeat from different starting points to plot several field lines

Method 2: Using iron filings
Apparatus:

Bar magnet
Iron filings
Sheet of paper or glass plate

Procedure:

Place the magnet under a sheet of paper
Sprinkle iron filings evenly over the paper
Tap the paper gently
The iron filings align along the magnetic field lines, revealing the field pattern







Warning



Safety note: Iron filings are small and can be hazardous if inhaled. Handle with care and clean up thoroughly after the experiment.

title: 21  Simple Phenomena of Magnetism
text:
21.5 18.4 Magnetic Forces and Field Interactions

21.5.1 Why Do Magnets Exert Forces?
Extended concept: Magnetic forces arise from interactions between magnetic fields.
Explanation:

Every magnet produces a magnetic field around it
When two magnets are brought close together, their magnetic fields interact
The interaction produces a force:

If the fields reinforce each other (unlike poles), the force is attractive
If the fields oppose each other (like poles), the force is repulsive








Note



Key Insight: Magnetic forces are non-contact forces — they act at a distance through the magnetic field, without physical contact between the magnets.




21.5.2 Representing Field Strength
The relative strength of a magnetic field is represented by the spacing of the magnetic field lines:

Closer field lines → stronger magnetic field
Wider spaced field lines → weaker magnetic field

Example: Near the poles of a bar magnet, field lines are closely packed → strong field. Far from the magnet, field lines are widely spaced → weak field.

title: 21  Simple Phenomena of Magnetism
text:
21.6 18.5 Applications of Magnets

21.6.1 Uses of Permanent Magnets







Application
Explanation




Compass needles
A freely suspended magnet aligns with Earth’s magnetic field, indicating direction


Refrigerator door seals
Magnetic strips hold the door closed against the steel frame


Loudspeakers
Permanent magnets interact with electromagnets to produce sound vibrations


Electric motors
Permanent magnets provide a constant magnetic field for motor operation


Magnetic door catches
Magnets hold doors or cabinets closed without mechanical latches





21.6.2 Uses of Electromagnets
What is an electromagnet?
An electromagnet is a temporary magnet formed when electric current flows through a coil of wire. Placing a soft iron core inside the coil greatly increases the magnetic field strength.
Advantages of electromagnets:

Can be switched on and off by controlling the current
Magnetic field strength can be varied by changing the current
Polarity can be reversed by reversing the current direction








Application
Explanation




Scrapyard cranes
Electromagnets lift and release magnetic scrap metal on demand


Relays and circuit breakers
Electromagnets control switching of electrical circuits


MRI machines
Powerful electromagnets create detailed images of the human body


Maglev trains
Electromagnets levitate and propel trains with minimal friction


Electric bells
Electromagnets repeatedly attract and release a hammer to ring a bell









Note



Key Concept: Electromagnets use soft iron cores because soft iron loses its magnetism quickly when the current is switched off — essential for devices that need to be switched on and off.

title: 21  Simple Phenomena of Magnetism
text:
21.7 Key Concepts Summary

21.7.1 Core Concepts

Magnets exert magnetic forces; have N and S poles; like poles repel, unlike poles attract
Magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt) are attracted to magnets; non-magnetic materials are not
Induced magnetism: Unmagnetised magnetic materials become temporary magnets when placed in a magnetic field
Temporary magnets (soft iron): easily magnetised, lose magnetism easily; Permanent magnets (steel): hard to magnetise, retain magnetism
Magnetic field: Region where a magnetic pole experiences a force; direction = direction of force on N pole
Field lines: Emerge from N pole, enter S pole; never cross; density indicates field strength
Plotting field lines: Use plotting compass or iron filings to visualise magnetic field patterns
Applications: Permanent magnets (compasses, door seals); electromagnets (cranes, relays, MRI)



21.7.2 Extended Concepts

Magnetic forces result from interactions between magnetic fields — a non-contact force acting at a distance
Field line spacing represents relative field strength: closer lines = stronger field; wider spacing = weaker field

title: 21  Simple Phenomena of Magnetism
text:
21.8 Common Misconceptions

21.8.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Magnetic poles can be isolated”
Incorrect: “If I cut a magnet in half, I get an isolated N pole and an isolated S pole”
Correct: - Magnetic poles always occur in pairs (N and S)

Cutting a magnet produces two smaller magnets, each with its own N and S pole
Isolated magnetic monopoles have never been observed experimentally




21.8.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “All metals are magnetic”
Incorrect: “Copper, aluminium, and gold are attracted to magnets”
Correct: - Only certain metals (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt, and some alloys) are magnetic

Most metals (copper, aluminium, gold, silver, brass) are non-magnetic
Magnetism depends on the atomic structure, not just whether a material is metallic




21.8.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Induced magnetism requires physical contact”
Incorrect: “A magnet must touch an iron nail to magnetise it”
Correct: - Induced magnetism occurs through the magnetic field, not by contact

An iron nail becomes magnetised when placed near (but not touching) a permanent magnet
The strength of induced magnetism decreases with distance from the magnet




21.8.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Magnetic field lines are physical entities”
Incorrect: “Magnetic field lines are real lines that exist in space”
Correct: - Magnetic field lines are a conventional representation to visualise the direction and strength of a magnetic field

They are not physical objects but a useful model for understanding magnetic phenomena
The actual magnetic field is continuous throughout the region around a magnet




21.8.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “The Earth’s geographic North Pole is a magnetic N pole”
Incorrect: “The North Pole of a compass points to the Earth’s magnetic N pole”
Correct: - The Earth’s geographic North Pole is actually near a magnetic S pole

The N pole of a compass is attracted to the Earth’s magnetic S pole (near geographic North)
This is why compass needles point north — opposite poles attract




21.8.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “Stronger magnets have more field lines”
Incorrect: “A stronger magnet has more magnetic field lines drawn around it”
Correct: - The number of field lines drawn is arbitrary and chosen for clarity

What matters is the spacing of field lines: closer spacing indicates stronger field
Field line density (lines per unit area) represents field strength, not the total number of lines




21.8.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “Electromagnets are always stronger than permanent magnets”
Incorrect: “Electromagnets are always more powerful than permanent magnets”
Correct: - Electromagnets can be made very strong by increasing current or number of coil turns

However, small permanent magnets (e.g., neodymium magnets) can be extremely strong
The choice depends on the application: electromagnets for controllability; permanent magnets for constant field without power

title: 21  Simple Phenomena of Magnetism
text:
21.9 Worked Examples

21.9.1 Example 1: Identifying Magnetic Materials
Question: A student has four rods labelled A, B, C and D. She brings the N pole of a bar magnet close to each rod and observes: - Rod A is attracted to the magnet

Rod B is repelled by the magnet
Rod C shows no effect
Rod D is attracted weakly

Identify the likely material of each rod and explain your reasoning.
Solution:
Rod A: Magnetic material (e.g., soft iron) — attracted due to induced magnetism
Rod B: Permanent magnet with N pole facing the bar magnet’s N pole — like poles repel
Rod C: Non-magnetic material (e.g., copper, wood) — no magnetic interaction
Rod D: Weakly magnetic material or a magnet with S pole facing the bar magnet’s N pole but at a greater distance
Key reasoning: - Attraction can occur with either induced magnetism or unlike poles

Repulsion only occurs between like poles of two magnets
No effect indicates a non-magnetic material




21.9.2 Example 2: Drawing Magnetic Field Lines
Question: Sketch the magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet. Indicate: (a) the direction of the field lines

where the field is strongest
one point where the field is zero

Solution:
(a) Direction of field lines: - Field lines emerge from the N pole and curve around to enter the S pole

Arrows on field lines point from N to S outside the magnet

(b) Strongest field: - At the poles, where field lines are most closely packed
(c) Point of zero field: - At the midpoint between two identical magnets with like poles facing each other (neutral point)

Or, theoretically, at infinity where the field becomes negligible

        N                           S
        |                           |
   ---->|                           |<----
  /      \                       /      \
 /        \                     /        \
|          \                   /          |
 \          \                 /          /
  \          \               /          /
   ---->|     \             /     |<----
        |      \           /      |
        |       \         /       |
        |        \       /        |
        |         \     /         |
        |          \   /          |
        |           \ /           |
        |            X            |  ← Neutral point (field ≈ 0)



21.9.3 Example 3: Induced Magnetism Calculation (Conceptual)
Question: A soft iron nail is placed near the N pole of a bar magnet. (a) What pole is induced at the end of the nail nearest to the magnet?

Explain why the nail is attracted to the magnet.
What happens to the nail’s magnetism when the bar magnet is removed?

Solution:
(a) Induced pole: - The end nearest the magnet becomes an induced S pole (opposite to the magnet’s N pole)
(b) Reason for attraction: - Unlike poles attract: the induced S pole of the nail is attracted to the N pole of the magnet

The magnetic field of the permanent magnet aligns domains in the iron, creating a net magnetic moment

(c) After magnet removal: - Soft iron loses its induced magnetism quickly

The nail returns to an unmagnetised state because its domains randomise again




21.9.4 Example 4: Field Strength and Line Spacing (Extended)
Question: Two bar magnets are placed with their N poles facing each other, separated by a small gap. (a) Sketch the magnetic field pattern in the region between the poles.

Explain why a small iron filings placed at the midpoint between the poles experiences no net magnetic force.

Solution:
(a) Field pattern between like poles:
        N                           N
        |                           |
   <----|                           |---->
  /      \                       /      \
 /        \                     /        \
|          \                   /          |
 \          \                 /          /
  \          \               /          /
   <----|     \             /     |---->
        |      \           /      |
        |       \         /       |
        |        \       /        |
        |         \     /         |
        |          \   /          |
        |           \ /           |
        |            X            |  ← Neutral point

Field lines from each N pole repel each other
Field lines curve away from the gap region
At the midpoint, fields from both magnets are equal and opposite

(b) Zero net force at midpoint: - The magnetic field from the left magnet points to the right at the midpoint

The magnetic field from the right magnet points to the left at the midpoint
These fields are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction → net field = 0
With zero magnetic field, an iron filing experiences no net magnetic force

title: 21  Simple Phenomena of Magnetism
text:
21.11 Laboratory Investigation

21.11.1 Experiment 18.1: Plotting Magnetic Field Lines
Objective: To plot the magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet using a plotting compass and to determine the direction of the magnetic field.
Apparatus: - Bar magnet

Plotting compass (small magnetic compass)
Plain A4 paper
Pencil
Ruler
Adhesive tape

Variables: - Independent: Position around the magnet

Dependent: Orientation of compass needle (direction of field)
Controlled: Same magnet, same compass, same paper, same experimental conditions

Procedure: 1. Tape the plain paper to a flat, non-magnetic surface (e.g., wooden table)

Place the bar magnet at the centre of the paper and trace its outline; label the N and S poles
Place the plotting compass near the N pole of the magnet
Mark two dots on the paper: one at each end of the compass needle
Move the compass so that its S-end dot coincides with the previous N-end dot
Mark the new position of the N-end dot
Repeat steps 5–6 until you reach the S pole of the magnet or the edge of the paper
Remove the magnet and compass; join the dots with a smooth curve to form one magnetic field line
Add an arrow to the field line indicating the direction from N to S
Repeat steps 3–9 starting from different points near the N pole to plot at least 5 field lines
Observe the spacing of field lines near the poles and far from the magnet

Data Recording: - Sketch the completed field pattern on a separate sheet

Note the direction of arrows on all field lines
Record observations about field line spacing at different locations

Analysis: 1. Describe the overall shape of the magnetic field pattern

State where the field lines are closest together and where they are furthest apart
Explain what the spacing of field lines tells you about magnetic field strength
Confirm that field lines never cross and always run from N to S outside the magnet

Precautions: - ✓ Keep other magnetic materials (e.g., steel rulers, mobile phones) away from the experiment

✓ Ensure the plotting compass moves freely and is not stuck
✓ Mark dots precisely to ensure accurate field line plotting
✓ Work on a non-magnetic surface to avoid interference

Expected Results: - Field lines emerge from N pole, curve around, and enter S pole

Field lines are closest near the poles (strongest field) and spread out with distance (weaker field)
All field lines have arrows pointing from N to S outside the magnet

Conclusion Template: “The experiment successfully plotted the magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet. Field lines were observed to emerge from the N pole and enter the S pole, with closer spacing near the poles indicating stronger field strength. The direction of the magnetic field at any point was confirmed to be the direction of force on the N pole of the plotting compass.”
Extension (Supplement): - Investigate the field pattern when two bar magnets are placed with like poles facing each other

Compare the field patterns of a bar magnet and a horseshoe magnet
Use iron filings as an alternative method to visualise field patterns (with appropriate safety measures)

title: 21  Simple Phenomena of Magnetism
text:
21.15 Glossary







Term
Definition




Electromagnet
A temporary magnet formed when electric current flows through a coil; often includes a soft iron core to strengthen the field


Induced magnetism
The process by which an unmagnetised magnetic material becomes magnetised when placed in a magnetic field


Magnetic field
A region of space in which a magnetic pole experiences a force


Magnetic field line
An imaginary line used to represent the direction and relative strength of a magnetic field; emerges from N pole, enters S pole


Magnetic material
A material that can be attracted to a magnet (e.g., iron, steel, nickel, cobalt)


Magnetised
Having acquired magnetic properties; able to exert magnetic forces


North pole (N pole)
The end of a magnet that points towards the Earth’s geographic North Pole when freely suspended


Permanent magnet
A magnet made from magnetically hard material (e.g., steel) that retains its magnetism after being magnetised


Plotting compass
A small magnetic compass used to determine the direction of a magnetic field at a point


South pole (S pole)
The end of a magnet that points towards the Earth’s geographic South Pole when freely suspended


Temporary magnet
A magnet made from magnetically soft material (e.g., soft iron) that is easily magnetised but loses magnetism easily


Unmagnetised
Not having acquired magnetic properties; not able to exert magnetic forces

Explain that the sum of the currents into a junction is the same as the sum of the currents out of the junction
Calculate the combined resistance of two resistors in parallel
Describe the action of a variable potential divider
Recall and use the equation for two resistors used as a potential divider: R1/R2 = V1/V2

title: 22  Electric Charge and Circuits
text:
22.2 19.1 Electric Charge

22.2.1 What Is Electric Charge?
Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter. There are two types of electric charge:

Positive charge (+)
Negative charge (–)

Key properties of electric charge:

Like charges repel each other (positive–positive or negative–negative)
Unlike charges attract each other (positive–negative)
Charge is conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred







Note



Key Concept: The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C). One coulomb is the charge transported by a constant current of one ampere in one second.




22.2.2 Charging by Friction
When two different insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons may be transferred from one material to the other.
Example: Charging a plastic rod with a cloth

Rub a plastic rod with a dry cloth
Electrons are transferred from the cloth to the plastic rod
The plastic rod gains electrons → becomes negatively charged
The cloth loses electrons → becomes positively charged

Detection of electrostatic charges:

A gold-leaf electroscope can detect the presence of charge
When a charged object is brought near the electroscope, the gold leaf diverges due to repulsion of like charges







Warning



Important: Only electrons (negative charges) are transferred during charging by friction. Protons remain fixed in the atomic nucleus.




22.2.3 Conductors and Insulators








Type
Description
Examples




Electrical conductors
Materials that allow electric charge to flow easily through them
Metals (copper, aluminium), graphite, salt water


Electrical insulators
Materials that do not allow electric charge to flow easily through them
Plastic, rubber, glass, dry wood, air



Electron model explanation:

In conductors (metals): Some electrons are free to move throughout the material (free electrons). When a potential difference is applied, these free electrons drift, creating an electric current.
In insulators: Electrons are tightly bound to their atoms and cannot move freely. No significant current flows even when a potential difference is applied.

Experiment: Distinguishing conductors and insulators
Apparatus:

Battery, bulb, connecting wires, test materials

Procedure:

Set up a simple circuit with a battery and bulb
Insert the test material into the circuit
Observe whether the bulb lights up

Observation:

Bulb lights up → material is a conductor
Bulb does not light up → material is an insulator

title: 22  Electric Charge and Circuits
text:
22.3 19.2 Electric Current

22.3.1 What Is Electric Current?
Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge.
\[I = \frac{Q}{t}\]
Where: - \(I\) = electric current (A) - \(Q\) = charge flowing (C) - \(t\) = time (s)






Note



Key Concept: One ampere (1 A) is defined as one coulomb of charge passing a point per second: \(1 \text{ A} = 1 \text{ C/s}\).




22.3.2 Conventional Current vs Electron Flow








Concept
Direction
Explanation




Conventional current
Positive → Negative
Historical convention established before electrons were discovered


Electron flow
Negative → Positive
Actual movement of free electrons in metallic conductors









Warning



Important: In circuit analysis and diagrams, we use conventional current direction (positive to negative), even though electrons actually flow in the opposite direction.




22.3.3 Direct Current (d.c.) vs Alternating Current (a.c.)








Type
Description
Examples




Direct current (d.c.)
Current flows in one direction only
Batteries, solar cells, d.c. power supplies


Alternating current (a.c.)
Current reverses direction periodically
Mains electricity (50 Hz or 60 Hz), a.c. generators





22.3.4 Measuring Electric Current: Ammeters

Ammeters measure electric current in amperes (A)
Must be connected in series with the component being measured
Analogue ammeters: Use a moving coil mechanism; read from a scale
Digital ammeters: Display numerical values; often more precise

Precautions when using ammeters:

✓ Always connect in series, never in parallel
✓ Select an appropriate range to avoid damaging the meter
✓ For analogue meters, avoid parallax error by viewing the scale perpendicularly

title: 22  Electric Charge and Circuits
text:
22.4 19.3 Electromotive Force and Potential Difference

22.4.1 What Is Electromotive Force (e.m.f.)?
Electromotive force (e.m.f.) is the electrical work done by a source in moving a unit charge around a complete circuit.
\[E = \frac{W}{Q}\]
Where: - \(E\) = e.m.f. (V) - \(W\) = work done or energy transferred (J) - \(Q\) = charge (C)
Key points about e.m.f.:

Measured in volts (V)
Represents the total energy per unit charge supplied by the source
Measured across the terminals of a source when no current is flowing (open circuit)



22.4.2 What Is Potential Difference (p.d.)?
Potential difference (p.d.) is the work done by a unit charge passing through a component.
\[V = \frac{W}{Q}\]
Where: - \(V\) = potential difference (V) - \(W\) = work done or energy transferred (J) - \(Q\) = charge (C)
Key points about p.d.:

Also measured in volts (V)
Represents the energy transferred per unit charge by a component
Measured across a component when current is flowing



22.4.3 Measuring Potential Difference: Voltmeters

Voltmeters measure potential difference in volts (V)
Must be connected in parallel across the component being measured
Analogue voltmeters: Use a moving coil mechanism; read from a scale
Digital voltmeters: Display numerical values; often more precise

Precautions when using voltmeters:

✓ Always connect in parallel, never in series
✓ Select an appropriate range to avoid damaging the meter
✓ For analogue meters, avoid parallax error by viewing the scale perpendicularly

title: 22  Electric Charge and Circuits
text:
22.5 19.4 Resistance and Ohm’s Law

22.5.1 What Is Electrical Resistance?
Resistance is a measure of how much a component opposes the flow of electric current.
\[R = \frac{V}{I}\]
Where: - \(R\) = resistance (Ω) - \(V\) = potential difference across the component (V) - \(I\) = current through the component (A)






Note



Key Concept: One ohm (1 Ω) is defined as the resistance when a potential difference of one volt produces a current of one ampere: \(1 \text{ Ω} = 1 \text{ V/A}\).




22.5.2 Ohm’s Law
For a metallic conductor at constant temperature:

The current through the conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.

\[V \propto I \quad \text{or} \quad V = IR\]
Conditions for Ohm’s Law to apply:

Temperature must remain constant
The conductor must be ohmic (e.g., a fixed resistor)



22.5.3 Factors Affecting the Resistance of a Wire
For a metallic wire at constant temperature:








Factor
Effect on Resistance
Explanation




Length (\(L\))
\(R \propto L\) (directly proportional)
Longer wire → more collisions for electrons → higher resistance


Cross-sectional area (\(A\))
\(R \propto \frac{1}{A}\) (inversely proportional)
Thicker wire → more paths for electrons → lower resistance


Material
Depends on resistivity (\(\rho\))
Different materials have different numbers of free electrons


Temperature
For metals: \(R\) increases with temperature
Higher temperature → more lattice vibrations → more electron collisions





22.5.4 Current–Voltage (I–V) Characteristics








Component
I–V Graph Shape
Explanation




Fixed resistor
Straight line through origin
Ohmic conductor; constant resistance


Filament lamp
Curve with decreasing gradient
Resistance increases as filament heats up


Diode
Conducts in one direction only; very high resistance in reverse
Allows current in forward bias; blocks current in reverse bias

title: 22  Electric Charge and Circuits
text:
22.6 19.5 Electrical Energy and Power

22.6.1 Electrical Power
Electrical power is the rate at which electrical energy is transferred.
\[P = IV\]
Where: - \(P\) = power (W) - \(I\) = current (A) - \(V\) = potential difference (V)
Alternative forms (using \(V = IR\)):
\[P = I^2R \quad \text{or} \quad P = \frac{V^2}{R}\]


22.6.2 Electrical Energy
Electrical energy transferred by a component:
\[E = IVt\]
Where: - \(E\) = energy (J) - \(I\) = current (A) - \(V\) = potential difference (V) - \(t\) = time (s)


22.6.3 The Kilowatt-Hour (kW h)
The kilowatt-hour is a practical unit for measuring electrical energy used in homes.
\[1 \text{ kW h} = 1000 \text{ W} \times 3600 \text{ s} = 3.6 \times 10^6 \text{ J}\]
Calculating cost of electricity:
\[\text{Cost} = \text{Energy used (kW h)} \times \text{Cost per kW h}\]






Note



Key Insight: The kilowatt-hour is used because the joule is too small for practical household energy measurements.
