title: 22  Electric Charge and Circuits
text:
22.8 19.7 Series and Parallel Circuits

22.8.1 Series Circuits
Key properties:

Current is the same at every point: \(I_{\text{total}} = I_1 = I_2 = I_3\)
Total p.d. is the sum of individual p.d.s: \(V_{\text{total}} = V_1 + V_2 + V_3\)
Total resistance is the sum of individual resistances: \(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\)
If one component fails (e.g., a lamp blows), the entire circuit stops working



22.8.2 Parallel Circuits
Key properties:

Total current from source is the sum of branch currents: \(I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\)
p.d. across each branch is the same: \(V_{\text{total}} = V_1 = V_2 = V_3\)
Combined resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance: \(\frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}\)
If one component fails, other branches continue to work



22.8.3 Advantages of Parallel Connection for Lamps

Each lamp receives the full supply voltage → operates at rated brightness
Lamps can be switched on/off independently
If one lamp fails, others continue to work
Adding more lamps does not reduce brightness of existing lamps

title: 22  Electric Charge and Circuits
text:
22.9 19.8 Potential Dividers

22.9.1 What Is a Potential Divider?
A potential divider is a circuit that produces an output voltage that is a fraction of the input voltage.
Basic potential divider circuit:
     V_in
      │
     ┌┴┐
     │R1│
     └┬┘
      ├─── V_out
     ┌┴┐
     │R2│
     └┬┘
      │
     GND
Equation for output voltage:
\[V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\]
Alternative form:
\[\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{V_1}{V_2}\]


22.9.2 Applications of Potential Dividers







Application
Explanation




Volume control
Variable resistor adjusts output voltage to amplifier


Light sensor
LDR in potential divider; output voltage changes with light intensity


Temperature sensor
Thermistor in potential divider; output voltage changes with temperature


Reference voltage
Provides stable reference voltage for electronic circuits

title: 22  Electric Charge and Circuits
text:
22.10 Key Concepts Summary

22.10.1 Core Concepts

Electric charge: Two types (+ and –); like charges repel, unlike attract; measured in coulombs (C)
Charging by friction: Transfer of electrons only; insulators can be charged, conductors cannot (unless insulated)
Conductors vs insulators: Conductors have free electrons; insulators have bound electrons
Electric current: Rate of flow of charge; \(I = Q/t\); measured in amperes (A) with ammeters in series
d.c. vs a.c.: d.c. flows one way; a.c. reverses direction periodically
e.m.f. and p.d.: Both measured in volts; e.m.f. is energy supplied per charge by source; p.d. is energy transferred per charge by component
Resistance: Opposition to current flow; \(R = V/I\); measured in ohms (Ω)
Ohm’s Law: \(V = IR\) for ohmic conductors at constant temperature
Factors affecting resistance: \(R \propto L\), \(R \propto 1/A\), depends on material and temperature
Electrical power and energy: \(P = IV\); \(E = IVt\); kilowatt-hour (kW h) for practical energy measurement
Circuit symbols: Standard symbols for components; ammeters in series, voltmeters in parallel
Series circuits: Same current; p.d.s add; resistances add
Parallel circuits: Currents add; same p.d.; combined resistance less than smallest
Potential dividers: Produce fraction of input voltage; \(V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\)



22.10.2 Extended Concepts

Electric fields: Region where a charge experiences a force; direction = force on positive charge
Field patterns: Radial around point charge; uniform between parallel plates
I–V characteristics: Resistor (linear), filament lamp (curve), diode (one-way conduction)
Kirchhoff’s laws: Sum of currents at junction = 0; sum of p.d.s around loop = 0
Combined resistance in parallel: \(\frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}\)

title: 22  Electric Charge and Circuits
text:
22.11 Common Misconceptions

22.11.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Current is used up as it flows through a circuit”
Incorrect: “The current is smaller after passing through a lamp”
Correct: - Current is conserved in a series circuit; the same current flows through all components - What is “used up” is energy, not charge or current - The p.d. across a component represents energy transferred per charge, not current loss



22.11.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Electrons flow from positive to negative”
Incorrect: “Electrons move from the positive terminal of a battery to the negative terminal”
Correct: - Electrons (negative charges) flow from negative to positive - Conventional current is defined as flowing from positive to negative (historical convention) - In circuit analysis, we use conventional current direction



22.11.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “A voltmeter should be connected in series”
Incorrect: “To measure voltage, connect the voltmeter in the same path as the current”
Correct: - Voltmeters must be connected in parallel across the component - Connecting a voltmeter in series would break the circuit (very high resistance) - Ammeters are connected in series; voltmeters in parallel



22.11.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Resistance depends only on the material”
Incorrect: “All copper wires have the same resistance”
Correct: - Resistance depends on four factors: length, cross-sectional area, material, and temperature - For a given material at constant temperature: \(R \propto \frac{L}{A}\) - A longer or thinner wire has higher resistance



22.11.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Ohm’s Law applies to all components”
Incorrect: “All electrical components obey \(V = IR\)”
Correct: - Ohm’s Law applies only to ohmic conductors (e.g., fixed resistors) at constant temperature - Filament lamps, diodes, and thermistors are non-ohmic; their I–V graphs are not straight lines - Always check the I–V characteristic before applying Ohm’s Law



22.11.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “Adding resistors in parallel increases total resistance”
Incorrect: “More resistors in parallel means more resistance”
Correct: - Adding resistors in parallel decreases total resistance - Each new branch provides an additional path for current - Formula: \(\frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \dots\) → \(R_{\text{total}}\) is less than the smallest \(R\)



22.11.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “The kilowatt-hour is a unit of power”
Incorrect: “My electricity bill charges me per kilowatt-hour of power used”
Correct: - The kilowatt-hour (kW h) is a unit of energy, not power - Power is measured in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW) - Energy = Power × Time → kW h = kW × h

title: 22  Electric Charge and Circuits
text:
22.12 Worked Examples

22.12.1 Example 1: Charge and Current Calculation
Question: A current of 0.5 A flows through a wire for 2 minutes. Calculate: (a) the charge that passes a point in the wire (b) the number of electrons that pass that point (charge of one electron = \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C)
Solution:
(a) Charge: \[I = 0.5 \text{ A}, \quad t = 2 \times 60 = 120 \text{ s}\] \[Q = It = 0.5 \times 120 = \boxed{60 \text{ C}}\]
(b) Number of electrons: \[\text{Number} = \frac{Q}{e} = \frac{60}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = \boxed{3.75 \times 10^{20} \text{ electrons}}\]



22.12.2 Example 2: Resistance Calculation
Question: A resistor has a potential difference of 6.0 V across it when a current of 0.25 A flows through it. Calculate: (a) the resistance of the resistor (b) the power dissipated by the resistor (c) the energy transferred in 5 minutes
Solution:
(a) Resistance: \[R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{6.0}{0.25} = \boxed{24 \text{ Ω}}\]
(b) Power: \[P = IV = 0.25 \times 6.0 = \boxed{1.5 \text{ W}}\]
(c) Energy: \[t = 5 \times 60 = 300 \text{ s}\] \[E = IVt = 0.25 \times 6.0 \times 300 = \boxed{450 \text{ J}}\]



22.12.3 Example 3: Series Circuit Analysis
Question: Two resistors, \(R_1 = 10 \text{ Ω}\) and \(R_2 = 20 \text{ Ω}\), are connected in series to a 12 V battery. Calculate: (a) the total resistance (b) the current in the circuit (c) the p.d. across each resistor
Solution:
(a) Total resistance: \[R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 = 10 + 20 = \boxed{30 \text{ Ω}}\]
(b) Current: \[I = \frac{V}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{12}{30} = \boxed{0.4 \text{ A}}\]
(c) p.d. across each resistor: \[V_1 = IR_1 = 0.4 \times 10 = \boxed{4.0 \text{ V}}\] \[V_2 = IR_2 = 0.4 \times 20 = \boxed{8.0 \text{ V}}\] Check: \(V_1 + V_2 = 4.0 + 8.0 = 12.0 \text{ V}\) ✓



22.12.4 Example 4: Parallel Circuit Analysis (Extended)
Question: Two resistors, \(R_1 = 6 \text{ Ω}\) and \(R_2 = 3 \text{ Ω}\), are connected in parallel to a 12 V supply. Calculate: (a) the combined resistance (b) the current through each resistor (c) the total current from the supply
Solution:
(a) Combined resistance: \[\frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{2}{6} = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\] \[R_{\text{total}} = \boxed{2 \text{ Ω}}\]
(b) Current through each resistor: \[I_1 = \frac{V}{R_1} = \frac{12}{6} = \boxed{2.0 \text{ A}}\] \[I_2 = \frac{V}{R_2} = \frac{12}{3} = \boxed{4.0 \text{ A}}\]
(c) Total current: \[I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2 = 2.0 + 4.0 = \boxed{6.0 \text{ A}}\] Check: \(I_{\text{total}} = \frac{V}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{12}{2} = 6.0 \text{ A}\) ✓



22.12.5 Example 5: Potential Divider Calculation (Extended)
Question: A potential divider circuit has \(R_1 = 400 \text{ Ω}\) and \(R_2 = 600 \text{ Ω}\) connected to a 10 V supply. Calculate: (a) the output voltage \(V_{\text{out}}\) across \(R_2\) (b) the current through the divider
Solution:
(a) Output voltage: \[V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = 10 \times \frac{600}{400 + 600} = 10 \times \frac{600}{1000} = \boxed{6.0 \text{ V}}\]
(b) Current through divider: \[R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 = 400 + 600 = 1000 \text{ Ω}\] \[I = \frac{V_{\text{in}}}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{10}{1000} = \boxed{0.01 \text{ A} = 10 \text{ mA}}\]

text:
22.14 Laboratory Investigation

22.14.1 Experiment 19.1: Determining Resistance Using Voltmeter-Ammeter Method
Objective: To determine the resistance of a fixed resistor using the voltmeter-ammeter method and verify Ohm’s Law.
Apparatus: - Fixed resistor (unknown value)

Variable resistor (rheostat)
d.c. power supply (0–12 V)
Ammeter (0–1 A)
Voltmeter (0–15 V)
Connecting wires
Switch

Dependent: Current through resistor
Controlled: Same resistor, same temperature, same circuit configuration

Procedure: 1. Set up the circuit as shown in the diagram below: - Connect the power supply, switch, rheostat, ammeter, and fixed resistor in series - Connect the voltmeter in parallel across the fixed resistor

Open the switch between readings to minimise heating of the resistor

Use the potential divider configuration to study the effect of varying \(R_1\) or \(R_2\) on \(V_{\text{out}}\)

title: 22  Electric Charge and Circuits
text:
22.16 Chapter Summary

22.16.1 Key Points to Remember
✓ Electric charge: Two types (+ and –); like repel, unlike attract; measured in coulombs (C)
✓ Charging by friction: Transfer of electrons only; insulators can be charged
✓ Conductors vs insulators: Conductors have free electrons; insulators have bound electrons
✓ Electric current: \(I = Q/t\); measured in amperes (A) with ammeters in series
✓ d.c. vs a.c.: d.c. one direction; a.c. reverses periodically
✓ e.m.f. and p.d.: Both in volts; e.m.f. = energy supplied per charge; p.d. = energy transferred per charge
✓ Resistance: \(R = V/I\); measured in ohms (Ω); \(R \propto L\), \(R \propto 1/A\)
✓ Ohm’s Law: \(V = IR\) for ohmic conductors at constant temperature
✓ Electrical power and energy: \(P = IV\); \(E = IVt\); kW h for practical energy measurement
✓ Circuit symbols: Standard symbols; ammeters in series, voltmeters in parallel
✓ Series circuits: Same current; p.d.s add; \(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + \dots\)
✓ Parallel circuits: Currents add; same p.d.; \(\frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \dots\)
✓ Potential dividers: \(V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\)


22.16.2 Formulae Sheet








Quantity
Formula
Variables




Electric current
\(I = \frac{Q}{t}\)
\(I\)=current (A), \(Q\)=charge (C), \(t\)=time (s)


Resistance
\(R = \frac{V}{I}\)
\(R\)=resistance (Ω), \(V\)=p.d. (V), \(I\)=current (A)


Electrical power
\(P = IV = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}\)
\(P\)=power (W)


Electrical energy
\(E = IVt = Pt\)
\(E\)=energy (J)


e.m.f. / p.d.
\(E \text{ or } V = \frac{W}{Q}\)
\(W\)=work/energy (J), \(Q\)=charge (C)


Combined resistance (series)
\(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \dots\)
—


Combined resistance (parallel)
\(\frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3} + \dots\)
—


Potential divider
\(V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\)
\(R_1\), \(R_2\) = divider resistances

title: 23  Electrical Quantities
text:
23.2 20.1 Electric Charge

23.2.1 What Is Electric Charge?
Electric charge is a fundamental property of matter. There are two types of electric charge:

Positive charge (+)
Negative charge (–)

Key properties of electric charge:

Like charges repel each other (positive–positive or negative–negative)
Unlike charges attract each other (positive–negative)
Charge is conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred







Note



Key Concept: The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C). One coulomb is the charge transported by a constant current of one ampere in one second.




23.2.2 Charging by Friction
When two different insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons may be transferred from one material to the other.
Example: Charging a plastic rod with a cloth

Rub a plastic rod with a dry cloth
Electrons are transferred from the cloth to the plastic rod
The plastic rod gains electrons → becomes negatively charged
The cloth loses electrons → becomes positively charged

Detection of electrostatic charges:

A gold-leaf electroscope can detect the presence of charge
When a charged object is brought near the electroscope, the gold leaf diverges due to repulsion of like charges







Warning



Important: Only electrons (negative charges) are transferred during charging by friction. Protons remain fixed in the atomic nucleus.




23.2.3 Conductors and Insulators








Type
Description
Examples




Electrical conductors
Materials that allow electric charge to flow easily through them
Metals (copper, aluminium), graphite, salt water


Electrical insulators
Materials that do not allow electric charge to flow easily through them
Plastic, rubber, glass, dry wood, air



Electron model explanation:

In conductors (metals): Some electrons are free to move throughout the material (free electrons). When a potential difference is applied, these free electrons drift, creating an electric current.
In insulators: Electrons are tightly bound to their atoms and cannot move freely. No significant current flows even when a potential difference is applied.

Experiment: Distinguishing conductors and insulators
Apparatus:

Battery, bulb, connecting wires, test materials

Procedure:

Set up a simple circuit with a battery and bulb
Insert the test material into the circuit
Observe whether the bulb lights up

Observation:

Bulb lights up → material is a conductor
Bulb does not light up → material is an insulator

title: 23  Electrical Quantities
text:
23.3 20.2 Electric Field (Supplement)

23.3.1 What Is an Electric Field?
An electric field is a region of space in which an electric charge experiences a force.
Key characteristics:

Electric fields are invisible but can be visualised using field lines
The direction of the electric field at any point is the direction of the force on a positive charge placed at that point
Electric field lines always emerge from positive charges and enter negative charges



23.3.2 Drawing Electric Field Lines
Rules for drawing electric field lines:

Field lines start at positive charges and end at negative charges
Field lines never cross each other
The density of field lines indicates field strength: closer lines = stronger field
Field lines are continuous curves

Simple electric field patterns:







Pattern
Description




Around a point charge
Radial lines emerging from a positive charge or converging to a negative charge


Around a charged conducting sphere
Similar to a point charge at the centre; no field inside the conductor


Between parallel plates
Uniform, parallel lines from positive to negative plate









Note



Key Concept: The electric field is strongest near charges, where the field lines are most concentrated.

title: 23  Electrical Quantities
text:
23.4 20.3 Electric Current

23.4.1 What Is Electric Current?
Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge.
\[I = \frac{Q}{t}\]
Where: - \(I\) = electric current (A) - \(Q\) = charge flowing (C) - \(t\) = time (s)






Note



Key Concept: One ampere (1 A) is defined as one coulomb of charge passing a point per second: \(1 \text{ A} = 1 \text{ C/s}\).




23.4.2 Conventional Current vs Electron Flow








Concept
Direction
Explanation




Conventional current
Positive → Negative
Historical convention established before electrons were discovered


Electron flow
Negative → Positive
Actual movement of free electrons in metallic conductors









Warning



Important: In circuit analysis and diagrams, we use conventional current direction (positive to negative), even though electrons actually flow in the opposite direction.




23.4.3 Direct Current (d.c.) vs Alternating Current (a.c.)








Type
Description
Examples




Direct current (d.c.)
Current flows in one direction only
Batteries, solar cells, d.c. power supplies


Alternating current (a.c.)
Current reverses direction periodically
Mains electricity (50 Hz or 60 Hz), a.c. generators





23.4.4 Measuring Electric Current: Ammeters

Ammeters measure electric current in amperes (A)
Must be connected in series with the component being measured
Analogue ammeters: Use a moving coil mechanism; read from a scale
Digital ammeters: Display numerical values; often more precise

Precautions when using ammeters:

✓ Always connect in series, never in parallel
✓ Select an appropriate range to avoid damaging the meter
✓ For analogue meters, avoid parallax error by viewing the scale perpendicularly

title: 23  Electrical Quantities
text:
23.5 20.4 Electromotive Force and Potential Difference

23.5.1 What Is Electromotive Force (e.m.f.)?
Electromotive force (e.m.f.) is the electrical work done by a source in moving a unit charge around a complete circuit.
\[E = \frac{W}{Q}\]
Where: - \(E\) = e.m.f. (V) - \(W\) = work done or energy transferred (J) - \(Q\) = charge (C)
Key points about e.m.f.:

Measured in volts (V)
Represents the total energy per unit charge supplied by the source
Measured across the terminals of a source when no current is flowing (open circuit)



23.5.2 What Is Potential Difference (p.d.)?
Potential difference (p.d.) is the work done by a unit charge passing through a component.
\[V = \frac{W}{Q}\]
Where: - \(V\) = potential difference (V) - \(W\) = work done or energy transferred (J) - \(Q\) = charge (C)
Key points about p.d.:

Also measured in volts (V)
Represents the energy transferred per unit charge by a component
Measured across a component when current is flowing



23.5.3 Measuring Potential Difference: Voltmeters

Voltmeters measure potential difference in volts (V)
Must be connected in parallel across the component being measured
Analogue voltmeters: Use a moving coil mechanism; read from a scale
Digital voltmeters: Display numerical values; often more precise

Precautions when using voltmeters:

✓ Always connect in parallel, never in series
✓ Select an appropriate range to avoid damaging the meter
✓ For analogue meters, avoid parallax error by viewing the scale perpendicularly

title: 23  Electrical Quantities
text:
23.6 20.5 Resistance and Ohm’s Law

23.6.1 What Is Electrical Resistance?
Resistance is a measure of how much a component opposes the flow of electric current.
\[R = \frac{V}{I}\]
Where: - \(R\) = resistance (Ω) - \(V\) = potential difference across the component (V) - \(I\) = current through the component (A)






Note



Key Concept: One ohm (1 Ω) is defined as the resistance when a potential difference of one volt produces a current of one ampere: \(1 \text{ Ω} = 1 \text{ V/A}\).




23.6.2 Ohm’s Law
For a metallic conductor at constant temperature:

The current through the conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.

\[V \propto I \quad \text{or} \quad V = IR\]
Conditions for Ohm’s Law to apply:

Temperature must remain constant
The conductor must be ohmic (e.g., a fixed resistor)



23.6.3 Factors Affecting the Resistance of a Wire
For a metallic wire at constant temperature:








Factor
Effect on Resistance
Explanation




Length (\(L\))
\(R \propto L\) (directly proportional)
Longer wire → more collisions for electrons → higher resistance


Cross-sectional area (\(A\))
\(R \propto \frac{1}{A}\) (inversely proportional)
Thicker wire → more paths for electrons → lower resistance


Material
Depends on resistivity (\(\rho\))
Different materials have different numbers of free electrons


Temperature
For metals: \(R\) increases with temperature
Higher temperature → more lattice vibrations → more electron collisions





23.6.4 Current–Voltage (I–V) Characteristics








Component
I–V Graph Shape
Explanation




Fixed resistor
Straight line through origin
Ohmic conductor; constant resistance


Filament lamp
Curve with decreasing gradient
Resistance increases as filament heats up


Diode
Conducts in one direction only; very high resistance in reverse
Allows current in forward bias; blocks current in reverse bias

title: 23  Electrical Quantities
text:
23.7 20.6 Electrical Energy and Power

23.7.1 Electrical Power
Electrical power is the rate at which electrical energy is transferred.
\[P = IV\]
Where: - \(P\) = power (W) - \(I\) = current (A) - \(V\) = potential difference (V)
Alternative forms (using \(V = IR\)):
\[P = I^2R \quad \text{or} \quad P = \frac{V^2}{R}\]


23.7.2 Electrical Energy
Electrical energy transferred by a component:
\[E = IVt\]
Where: - \(E\) = energy (J) - \(I\) = current (A) - \(V\) = potential difference (V) - \(t\) = time (s)


23.7.3 The Kilowatt-Hour (kW h)
The kilowatt-hour is a practical unit for measuring electrical energy used in homes.
\[1 \text{ kW h} = 1000 \text{ W} \times 3600 \text{ s} = 3.6 \times 10^6 \text{ J}\]
Calculating cost of electricity:
\[\text{Cost} = \text{Energy used (kW h)} \times \text{Cost per kW h}\]






Note



Key Insight: The kilowatt-hour is used because the joule is too small for practical household energy measurements.

title: 23  Electrical Quantities
text:
23.8 Key Concepts Summary

23.8.1 Core Concepts

Electric charge: Two types (+ and –); like charges repel, unlike attract; measured in coulombs (C)
Charging by friction: Transfer of electrons only; insulators can be charged, conductors cannot (unless insulated)
Conductors vs insulators: Conductors have free electrons; insulators have bound electrons
Electric current: Rate of flow of charge; \(I = Q/t\); measured in amperes (A) with ammeters in series
d.c. vs a.c.: d.c. flows one way; a.c. reverses direction periodically
e.m.f. and p.d.: Both measured in volts; e.m.f. is energy supplied per charge by source; p.d. is energy transferred per charge by component
Resistance: Opposition to current flow; \(R = V/I\); measured in ohms (Ω)
Ohm’s Law: \(V = IR\) for ohmic conductors at constant temperature
Factors affecting resistance: \(R \propto L\), \(R \propto 1/A\), depends on material and temperature
Electrical power and energy: \(P = IV\); \(E = IVt\); kilowatt-hour (kW h) for practical energy measurement



23.8.2 Extended Concepts

Electric fields: Region where a charge experiences a force; direction = force on positive charge
Field patterns: Radial around point charge; uniform between parallel plates
I–V characteristics: Resistor (linear), filament lamp (curve), diode (one-way conduction)
Quantitative resistance relationships: \(R = \rho \frac{L}{A}\) for metallic conductors

title: 23  Electrical Quantities
text:
23.9 Common Misconceptions

23.9.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Current is used up as it flows through a circuit”
Incorrect: “The current is smaller after passing through a lamp”
Correct:

Current is conserved in a series circuit; the same current flows through all components
What is “used up” is energy, not charge or current
The p.d. across a component represents energy transferred per charge, not current loss




23.9.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Electrons flow from positive to negative”
Incorrect: “Electrons move from the positive terminal of a battery to the negative terminal”
Correct:

Electrons (negative charges) flow from negative to positive
Conventional current is defined as flowing from positive to negative (historical convention)
In circuit analysis, we use conventional current direction




23.9.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “A voltmeter should be connected in series”
Incorrect: “To measure voltage, connect the voltmeter in the same path as the current”
Correct:

Voltmeters must be connected in parallel across the component
Connecting a voltmeter in series would break the circuit (very high resistance)
Ammeters are connected in series; voltmeters in parallel




23.9.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Resistance depends only on the material”
Incorrect: “All copper wires have the same resistance”
Correct:

Resistance depends on four factors: length, cross-sectional area, material, and temperature
For a given material at constant temperature: \(R \propto \frac{L}{A}\)
A longer or thinner wire has higher resistance




23.9.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Ohm’s Law applies to all components”
Incorrect: “All electrical components obey \(V = IR\)”
Correct:

Ohm’s Law applies only to ohmic conductors (e.g., fixed resistors) at constant temperature
Filament lamps, diodes, and thermistors are non-ohmic; their I–V graphs are not straight lines
Always check the I–V characteristic before applying Ohm’s Law




23.9.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “The kilowatt-hour is a unit of power”
Incorrect: “My electricity bill charges me per kilowatt-hour of power used”
Correct:

The kilowatt-hour (kW h) is a unit of energy, not power
Power is measured in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW)
Energy = Power × Time → kW h = kW × h




23.9.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “Charging by friction creates new charge”
Incorrect: “Rubbing a rod with cloth creates electric charge”
Correct:

Charging by friction transfers existing electrons from one material to another
Charge is conserved; no new charge is created or destroyed
The total charge of the system remains zero (one object gains electrons, the other loses the same amount)

title: 23  Electrical Quantities
text:
23.10 Worked Examples

23.10.1 Example 1: Charge and Current Calculation
Question: A current of 0.5 A flows through a wire for 2 minutes. Calculate: (a) the charge that passes a point in the wire (b) the number of electrons that pass that point (charge of one electron = \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C)
Solution:
(a) Charge: \[I = 0.5 \text{ A}, \quad t = 2 \times 60 = 120 \text{ s}\] \[Q = It = 0.5 \times 120 = \boxed{60 \text{ C}}\]
(b) Number of electrons: \[\text{Number} = \frac{Q}{e} = \frac{60}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = \boxed{3.75 \times 10^{20} \text{ electrons}}\]



23.10.2 Example 2: Resistance Calculation
Question: A resistor has a potential difference of 6.0 V across it when a current of 0.25 A flows through it. Calculate: (a) the resistance of the resistor (b) the power dissipated by the resistor (c) the energy transferred in 5 minutes
Solution:
(a) Resistance: \[R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{6.0}{0.25} = \boxed{24 \text{ Ω}}\]
(b) Power: \[P = IV = 0.25 \times 6.0 = \boxed{1.5 \text{ W}}\]
(c) Energy: \[t = 5 \times 60 = 300 \text{ s}\] \[E = IVt = 0.25 \times 6.0 \times 300 = \boxed{450 \text{ J}}\]



23.10.3 Example 3: e.m.f. and p.d. Calculation (Supplement)
Question: A battery does 120 J of work in moving 20 C of charge around a complete circuit. A lamp in the circuit has a p.d. of 4.0 V across it. Calculate: (a) the e.m.f. of the battery (b) the charge that passes through the lamp in 10 s if the current is 0.5 A
Solution:
(a) e.m.f. of battery: \[E = \frac{W}{Q} = \frac{120}{20} = \boxed{6.0 \text{ V}}\]
(b) Charge through lamp: \[I = 0.5 \text{ A}, \quad t = 10 \text{ s}\] \[Q = It = 0.5 \times 10 = \boxed{5.0 \text{ C}}\]



23.10.4 Example 4: Electrical Energy Cost Calculation
Question: A 2.4 kW electric heater is used for 3 hours each day for a week. If electricity costs $0.25 per kW h, calculate: (a) the total energy used in kW h (b) the total cost
Solution:
(a) Energy used: \[P = 2.4 \text{ kW}, \quad t = 3 \text{ h/day} \times 7 \text{ days} = 21 \text{ h}\] \[E = Pt = 2.4 \times 21 = \boxed{50.4 \text{ kW h}}\]
(b) Total cost: \[\text{Cost} = 50.4 \times 0.25 = \boxed{\$12.60}\]



23.10.5 Example 5: Resistance and Wire Dimensions (Supplement)
Question: A copper wire of length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 0.50 mm² has a resistance of 0.068 Ω. Calculate the resistance of another copper wire of the same material with: (a) length 4.0 m and area 0.50 mm² (b) length 2.0 m and area 1.0 mm²
Solution:
(a) Double the length, same area: \[R \propto L \quad \Rightarrow \quad R_{\text{new}} = R \times \frac{L_{\text{new}}}{L} = 0.068 \times \frac{4.0}{2.0} = \boxed{0.136 \text{ Ω}}\]
(b) Same length, double the area: \[R \propto \frac{1}{A} \quad \Rightarrow \quad R_{\text{new}} = R \times \frac{A}{A_{\text{new}}} = 0.068 \times \frac{0.50}{1.0} = \boxed{0.034 \text{ Ω}}\]

title: 23  Electrical Quantities
text:
23.11 Practice Questions

23.11.1 Core Level

23.14 Chapter Summary

23.14.1 Key Points to Remember
✓ Electric charge: Two types (+ and –); like repel, unlike attract; measured in coulombs (C)
✓ Charging by friction: Transfer of electrons only; insulators can be charged
✓ Conductors vs insulators: Conductors have free electrons; insulators have bound electrons
✓ Electric current: \(I = Q/t\); measured in amperes (A) with ammeters in series
✓ d.c. vs a.c.: d.c. one direction; a.c. reverses periodically
✓ e.m.f. and p.d.: Both in volts; e.m.f. = energy supplied per charge; p.d. = energy transferred per charge
✓ Resistance: \(R = V/I\); measured in ohms (Ω); \(R \propto L\), \(R \propto 1/A\)
✓ Ohm’s Law: \(V = IR\) for ohmic conductors at constant temperature
✓ Electrical power and energy: \(P = IV\); \(E = IVt\); kW h for practical energy measurement
✓ Circuit symbols: Standard symbols; ammeters in series, voltmeters in parallel
✓ Electric field: Region where charge experiences force; direction = force on positive charge


23.14.2 Formulae Sheet








Quantity
Formula
Variables




Electric current
\(I = \frac{Q}{t}\)
\(I\)=current (A), \(Q\)=charge (C), \(t\)=time (s)


Resistance
\(R = \frac{V}{I}\)
\(R\)=resistance (Ω), \(V\)=p.d. (V), \(I\)=current (A)


Electrical power
\(P = IV = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}\)
\(P\)=power (W)


Electrical energy
\(E = IVt = Pt\)
\(E\)=energy (J)


e.m.f. / p.d.
\(E \text{ or } V = \frac{W}{Q}\)

title: 24  Electromagnetic Effects
text:
24.2 Electromagnetic Induction

24.2.1 What Is Electromagnetic Induction?
In 1831, Michael Faraday discovered that a changing magnetic field can produce an electric current. This phenomenon is known as electromagnetic induction.

Electromagnetic induction is the process through which an induced e.m.f. is produced in a conductor due to a changing magnetic field.

If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, the induced e.m.f. will drive an induced current.


24.2.2 Demonstrating Electromagnetic Induction
Apparatus:

Solenoid (coil of insulated wire)
Strong bar magnet
Centre-zero galvanometer (sensitive ammeter)
Connecting wires

Procedure and Observations:

Move the N pole of the magnet into the solenoid.

Observation: Galvanometer needle deflects momentarily to one side.
Conclusion: An e.m.f. is induced, causing a current to flow.

Hold the magnet stationary inside the solenoid.

Observation: Galvanometer needle returns to zero and stays there.
Conclusion: No e.m.f. is induced when there is no relative motion or change in magnetic flux.

Withdraw the magnet out of the solenoid.

Observation: Galvanometer needle deflects momentarily to the opposite side.
Conclusion: The direction of the induced e.m.f. reverses when the direction of motion reverses.

Repeat with the S pole, or reverse the magnet’s poles.

Observation: Deflection directions reverse accordingly.




24.2.3 Factors Affecting the Magnitude of Induced E.m.f.
The size of the induced e.m.f. depends on the rate of change of magnetic flux through the coil. It can be increased by:

Increasing the speed of relative motion between the magnet and the coil.
Increasing the strength of the magnetic field (using a stronger magnet).
Increasing the number of turns on the solenoid.
Increasing the cross-sectional area of the coil.



24.2.4 Lenz’s Law and Fleming’s Right-Hand Rule (Extended)
Lenz’s Law:
The direction of the induced e.m.f. (and hence induced current) is always such that it opposes the change causing it.

When a N pole moves into a coil, the induced current creates a N pole at that end to repel the incoming magnet.
When a N pole moves out of a coil, the induced current creates a S pole at that end to attract the departing magnet.
This ensures conservation of energy: mechanical work must be done to overcome the magnetic opposition, which is converted into electrical energy.

Fleming’s Right-Hand Rule (for generators):
Used to determine the direction of induced current when a conductor moves in a magnetic field.

Thumb: Direction of motion (force applied)
Forefinger: Direction of magnetic field (N to S)
Second finger: Direction of induced current

title: 24  Electromagnetic Effects
text:
24.3 The A.C. Generator

24.3.1 How Does an A.C. Generator Work?
An a.c. generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction.
Key Components:

Armature coil: Rectangular coil of wire mounted on an axle.
Magnets: Provide a uniform magnetic field.
Slip rings: Two continuous metal rings attached to the coil ends, rotating with it.
Carbon brushes: Stationary contacts pressing against the slip rings to transfer current to the external circuit without twisting wires.

Operation:

As the coil rotates, it cuts through magnetic field lines.
This changes the magnetic flux linking the coil, inducing an alternating e.m.f.
The direction of induced current reverses every half-turn, producing alternating current (a.c.).



24.3.2 E.m.F. Against Time Graph
The induced e.m.f. varies sinusoidally with time:

Maximum e.m.f. (peaks/troughs): Occur when the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field. The sides of the coil cut field lines at the maximum rate.
Zero e.m.f.: Occurs when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field. The sides move parallel to field lines and cut none.

Factors increasing maximum induced e.m.f.:

Increasing the number of turns in the coil.
Using stronger magnets.
Increasing the frequency of rotation.
Winding the coil around a soft iron core to concentrate flux.

title: 24  Electromagnetic Effects
text:
24.4 Magnetic Effect of a Current

24.4.1 Magnetic Field Patterns
When an electric current flows through a conductor, it produces a magnetic field around it.
1. Straight Current-Carrying Wire:

Pattern: Concentric circles centred on the wire.
Direction: Determined by the right-hand grip rule (thumb = current direction, curled fingers = field direction).
Strength: Strongest near the wire; decreases with distance. Increases with current magnitude.

2. Solenoid (Coil of Wire):

Pattern: Resembles a bar magnet; field lines emerge from one end (N) and enter the other (S).
Inside: Field lines are straight, parallel, and equally spaced → uniform magnetic field.
Direction: Right-hand grip rule (fingers curl in current direction, thumb points to N pole).
Strength increased by: Increasing current, increasing turns per unit length, inserting a soft iron core.



24.4.2 Applications
Relays:

An electromagnetic switch that uses a small current in one circuit to control a large current in another.
When the control circuit is closed, the electromagnet attracts an iron armature, closing the high-power circuit contacts.
Provides safe isolation between low-voltage control circuits and high-voltage power circuits.

Loudspeakers:

An alternating current passes through a coil attached to a paper cone, placed in a radial magnetic field.
The motor effect produces an alternating force on the coil, causing the cone to vibrate.
Cone vibrations produce sound waves matching the electrical signal frequency.

title: 24  Electromagnetic Effects
text:
24.5 Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor

24.5.1 The Motor Effect
When a current-carrying conductor is placed in an external magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is the motor effect.
Conditions:

The conductor must not be parallel to the magnetic field.
Maximum force occurs when the conductor is perpendicular to the field.

Reversing the Force:

Reversing the current direction reverses the force.
Reversing the magnetic field direction reverses the force.



24.5.2 Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule (Extended)
Used to determine the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field:

Thumb: Direction of Force (Motion)
Forefinger: Direction of Magnetic Field (N to S)
Second finger: Direction of Current (conventional, + to –)

Force on Charged Particle Beams:

A beam of moving charges is equivalent to a current.
Positive particles: Deflect according to conventional current direction.
Negative particles (electrons): Deflect in the opposite direction to the second finger, as electron flow is opposite to conventional current.
Particles move in circular paths while inside a uniform magnetic field.

title: 24  Electromagnetic Effects
text:
24.6 The D.C. Motor

24.6.1 How a D.C. Motor Works
A d.c. motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.
Structure:

Rectangular coil mounted on an axle between magnetic poles.
Connected to a split-ring commutator and carbon brushes.

Operation Cycle:

Current flows through the coil.
Forces on opposite sides of the coil are in opposite directions (Fleming’s left-hand rule), creating a turning effect (torque).
The coil rotates.
When the coil reaches the vertical position, the split-ring commutator gaps align with the brushes, cutting off current momentarily.
Momentum carries the coil past the vertical.
The commutator reverses contact, reversing current direction in the coil.
Forces reverse, ensuring continuous rotation in the same direction.



24.6.2 Increasing the Turning Effect

Increasing the current through the coil.
Increasing the number of turns on the coil.
Using stronger permanent magnets.
Winding the coil on a soft iron core to concentrate the magnetic field.

title: 24  Electromagnetic Effects
text:
24.7 The Transformer

24.7.1 Construction and Principle
A transformer changes the voltage of an alternating current supply.
Construction:

Primary coil: Connected to a.c. supply.
Secondary coil: Connected to the load.
Laminated soft iron core: Links the two coils magnetically. Lamination reduces eddy current heating.

Principle of Operation:

Alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field.
The soft iron core channels this changing flux to the secondary coil.
The changing flux induces an alternating e.m.f. in the secondary coil (mutual induction).
Does not work with d.c. because d.c. produces a constant magnetic field → no change in flux → no induced e.m.f.



24.7.2 Transformer Equations
Voltage and Turns Ratio:
\[\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}\]

Step-up transformer: \(N_s > N_p\) → \(V_s > V_p\) (used at power stations).
Step-down transformer: \(N_s < N_p\) → \(V_s < V_p\) (used in homes, chargers).

Power and Efficiency (Ideal Transformer):
Assuming 100% efficiency (power in = power out):
\[I_p V_p = I_s V_s\]
Where:

\(V_p, V_s\) = primary and secondary voltages
\(I_p, I_s\) = primary and secondary currents
\(N_p, N_s\) = number of turns in primary and secondary coils



24.7.3 High-Voltage Power Transmission
Problem: Power cables have resistance \(R\). Power loss due to heating is given by:
\[P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R\]
Solution:

Use step-up transformers to increase voltage at the power station.
Since \(P = VI\), for constant power \(P\), increasing \(V\) drastically decreases current \(I\).
Lower current means \(I^2R\) losses are minimised.
Step-down transformers reduce voltage to safe levels (e.g., 230 V or 240 V) for domestic use.

title: 24  Electromagnetic Effects
text:
24.8 Key Concepts Summary

24.8.1 Core Concepts

Electromagnetic induction: Changing magnetic flux induces e.m.f.; requires relative motion or changing current.
Factors affecting induction: Speed, magnetic field strength, number of turns, coil area.
A.C. generator: Rotating coil in magnetic field produces a.c.; slip rings and brushes transfer current.
Magnetic effect of current: Straight wires produce circular fields; solenoids produce bar-magnet-like fields.
Applications: Relays (electromagnetic switches), loudspeakers (motor effect converts electricity to sound).
Motor effect: Force on current-carrying conductor in magnetic field; maximum when perpendicular.
D.C. motor: Split-ring commutator reverses current every half-turn for continuous rotation.
Transformer: Changes a.c. voltage via mutual induction; \(V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s\).
Power transmission: High voltage reduces current, minimising \(I^2R\) heating losses in cables.



24.8.2 Extended Concepts

Lenz’s Law: Induced e.m.f. direction opposes the change causing it (conservation of energy).
Fleming’s rules: Left-hand rule for motors/force; Right-hand rule for generators/induction.
Charged particle deflection: Direction depends on charge sign; negative charges deflect opposite to conventional current.
Ideal transformer equation: \(I_pV_p = I_sV_s\); step-up increases voltage but decreases current proportionally.
Power loss explanation: \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2R\); doubling voltage quarters the current, reducing loss by factor of 16.

title: 24  Electromagnetic Effects
text:
24.9 Common Misconceptions

24.9.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “A transformer works with both a.c. and d.c.”
Incorrect: “Transformers can step up or step down direct current.”
Correct:

Transformers rely on a changing magnetic flux to induce e.m.f.
D.c. produces a constant magnetic field → no change in flux → zero induced e.m.f. in secondary.
Transformers only work with alternating current.




24.9.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Induced current flows in the same direction as the motion causing it”
Incorrect: “Moving a N pole into a coil makes that end a S pole to help it enter.”
Correct:

Lenz’s Law states the induced current opposes the change.
Moving N pole in → induced N pole to repel it.
Mechanical work is required to overcome this repulsion, conserving energy.




24.9.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Slip rings and split-ring commutators are the same”
Incorrect: “Both are used interchangeably in generators and motors.”
Correct:

Slip rings: Continuous rings; maintain same electrical contact; used in a.c. generators to output alternating current.
Split-ring commutator: Split into two halves; reverses contact every half-turn; used in d.c. motors to maintain unidirectional rotation.




24.9.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Fleming’s left-hand and right-hand rules can be used interchangeably”
Incorrect: “Either hand rule works for both motors and generators.”
Correct:

Left-hand rule: For motors (current + magnetic field → force/motion).
Right-hand rule: For generators/induction (motion + magnetic field → induced current).
Mixing them gives incorrect directions.




24.9.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “High voltage transmission causes high power loss”
Incorrect: “Stepping up voltage increases energy waste in cables.”
Correct:

Power loss depends on current, not voltage: \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2R\).
High voltage transmission reduces current for the same power (\(P = VI\)).
Lower current drastically reduces \(I^2R\) heating losses.




24.9.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “The magnetic field inside a solenoid is zero”
Incorrect: “Coils only produce magnetic fields outside themselves.”
Correct:

Inside a solenoid, field lines are straight, parallel, and closely spaced.
This indicates a strong, uniform magnetic field inside the coil.
Outside, the field resembles a bar magnet and is weaker.




24.9.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “Electron beams deflect in the same direction as conventional current”
Incorrect: “A beam of electrons deflects according to Fleming’s left-hand rule second finger.”
Correct:

Electrons are negatively charged.
Their motion is opposite to conventional current direction.
When applying Fleming’s left-hand rule, the second finger must point opposite to electron motion to find the correct force direction.

title: 24  Electromagnetic Effects
text:
24.10 Worked Examples

24.10.1 Example 1: Transformer Calculations
Question:
A step-down transformer has 2400 turns on the primary coil and 120 turns on the secondary coil. The primary voltage is 240 V.

Calculate the secondary voltage.
If the secondary current is 4.0 A, calculate the primary current (assume 100% efficiency).
State one advantage of using this transformer in a phone charger.

Solution:
(a) Secondary voltage:
\[\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s} \Rightarrow V_s = V_p \times \frac{N_s}{N_p} = 240 \times \frac{120}{2400} = \boxed{12 \text{ V}}\]
(b) Primary current:
\[I_p V_p = I_s V_s \Rightarrow I_p = \frac{I_s V_s}{V_p} = \frac{4.0 \times 12}{240} = \boxed{0.20 \text{ A}}\]
(c) Advantage:

Steps down high mains voltage to a safe, low voltage suitable for charging delicate electronic devices without damage.




24.10.2 Example 2: Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule Application
Question:
A straight wire carries a current flowing vertically upwards. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field directed horizontally from left to right. Determine the direction of the force on the wire.
Solution:
Step 1: Align left hand.
Step 2: Forefinger points right (magnetic field direction).
Step 3: Second finger points up (current direction).
Step 4: Thumb points into the page (away from observer).
Answer: The force acts perpendicularly into the plane of the page.



24.10.3 Example 3: A.C. Generator Graph Interpretation
Question:
The graph shows the e.m.f. output of an a.c. generator against time. At \(t = 0\), the coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field.

At what times is the e.m.f. zero? Explain why.
At what times is the e.m.f. maximum? Explain why.

Solution:
(a) Zero e.m.f. times:

Occurs at \(t = 0\), \(T/2\), \(T\), etc.
Explanation: Coil plane is perpendicular to magnetic field. Sides of coil move parallel to field lines and cut no flux. Rate of change of flux is zero.

(b) Maximum e.m.f. times:

Occurs at \(t = T/4\), \(3T/4\), etc.
Explanation: Coil plane is parallel to magnetic field. Sides cut field lines at maximum rate. Rate of change of flux is maximum.




24.10.4 Example 4: Power Transmission Loss Calculation
Question:
A power station transmits 500 kW of power to a town.

Calculate the current in the transmission cables if the voltage is 10 kV.
Calculate the power loss if the total cable resistance is 5.0 Ω.
If the voltage is stepped up to 100 kV, calculate the new power loss and explain the benefit.

Solution:
(a) Current at 10 kV:
\[I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{500\,000}{10\,000} = 50 \text{ A}\]
(b) Power loss at 10 kV:
\[P_{\text{loss}} = I^2R = 50^2 \times 5.0 = \boxed{12\,500 \text{ W} = 12.5 \text{ kW}}\]
(c) Current at 100 kV:
\[I = \frac{500\,000}{100\,000} = 5.0 \text{ A}\]
\[P_{\text{loss}} = 5.0^2 \times 5.0 = \boxed{125 \text{ W} = 0.125 \text{ kW}}\]
Benefit: Increasing voltage by 10× reduces current by 10×, reducing power loss by a factor of 100 (\(I^2R\) dependence). This greatly improves transmission efficiency.



24.10.5 Example 5: Electromagnetic Induction Factors
Question:
A student moves a bar magnet into a solenoid connected to a galvanometer. State what happens to the galvanometer deflection if:

The magnet is moved faster.
The magnet is held stationary inside the coil.
The magnet is withdrawn with the same speed as insertion.

Solution:
(a) Moved faster:

Deflection angle increases.
Reason: Higher rate of change of magnetic flux → larger induced e.m.f. → larger current.

(b) Held stationary:

Deflection returns to zero.
Reason: No change in magnetic flux → no induced e.m.f.

(c) Withdrawn:

Deflection is in the opposite direction.
Reason: Change in flux is reversed → induced e.m.f. polarity reverses (Lenz’s Law).

24.12 Laboratory Investigation

24.12.1 Experiment 21.1: Investigating Transformer Turns Ratio
Objective:
To investigate the relationship between the number of turns on the primary and secondary coils of a transformer and the output voltage.
Apparatus:

Laminated soft iron core (C-cores or E-cores)
Primary coil (known turns, e.g., 100 turns)
Secondary coils (varying turns, e.g., 50, 150, 200, 300 turns)
Low-voltage a.c. power supply (e.g., 2 V or 6 V a.c.)
A.C. voltmeter (dual range or two meters)
Connecting wires

Variables:

Independent: Number of turns on secondary coil (\(N_s\))
Dependent: Secondary voltage (\(V_s\))
Controlled: Primary voltage (\(V_p\)), primary turns (\(N_p\)), core material, coil tightness

Procedure:

Assemble the transformer by clamping the C-cores together with the primary and secondary coils.
Connect the primary coil to the a.c. power supply set to a fixed voltage (e.g., 6.0 V).
Measure and record the actual primary voltage \(V_p\) using an a.c. voltmeter.
Connect the secondary coil with \(N_s = 50\) turns to a second a.c. voltmeter.
Measure and record the secondary voltage \(V_s\).
Repeat steps 4–5 for secondary coils with 100, 150, 200, and 300 turns.
Record all results in a table.

Data Table:











\(N_p\) (turns)
\(V_p\) (V)
\(N_s\) (turns)
\(V_s\) (V)
Calculated ratio \(V_s/V_p\)
Expected ratio \(N_s/N_p\)




100

50





100

100





100

150





100

200





100

300






Analysis:

Calculate the ratio \(V_s/V_p\) and \(N_s/N_p\) for each trial.
Plot a graph of \(V_s\) (y-axis) against \(N_s\) (x-axis).
Determine the gradient of the graph. The gradient should equal \(V_p/N_p\).
Comment on whether the results support the equation \(V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p\).

Precautions:

✓ Ensure the iron cores are tightly clamped to minimise magnetic flux leakage.
✓ Use a.c. supply only; d.c. will not induce voltage and may overheat the coil.
✓ Allow the power supply and coils to cool between readings if they become warm.
✓ Check voltmeter zero error and select appropriate ranges.

Expected Results:

The graph of \(V_s\) against \(N_s\) will be a straight line through the origin.
The ratio \(V_s/V_p\) will approximately equal \(N_s/N_p\).
Slight deviations may occur due to energy losses (eddy currents, hysteresis, resistance).

Conclusion Template:
“The experiment verified the transformer equation \(V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p\). The secondary voltage was directly proportional to the number of turns on the secondary coil. The gradient of the \(V_s\) vs \(N_s\) graph agreed with \(V_p/N_p\) within experimental limits, confirming ideal transformer behaviour.”
Extension (Supplement):

Investigate efficiency by measuring primary and secondary currents simultaneously.
Compare results with and without the soft iron core to demonstrate its role in flux linkage.
Research sources of energy loss in real transformers and suggest engineering solutions.

title: 24  Electromagnetic Effects
text:
24.14 Chapter Summary

24.14.1 Key Points to Remember
✓ Electromagnetic induction: Changing magnetic flux induces e.m.f.; requires relative motion or changing current
✓ Induction factors: Speed, magnetic field strength, number of turns, coil area
✓ A.C. generator: Rotating coil produces a.c.; slip rings maintain continuous contact; output is sinusoidal
✓ Magnetic effect of current: Straight wire → concentric circles; solenoid → uniform inside, bar-magnet-like outside
✓ Applications: Relays (electromagnetic switches), loudspeakers (motor effect on coil)
✓ Motor effect: Force on current-carrying conductor in magnetic field; max when perpendicular
✓ D.C. motor: Split-ring commutator reverses current every half-turn for continuous rotation
✓ Transformer: Changes a.c. voltage via mutual induction; \(V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s\)
✓ High-voltage transmission: Reduces current, minimising \(I^2R\) heating losses in cables
✓ Lenz’s Law (Extended): Induced e.m.f. opposes the change causing it (conservation of energy)
✓ Fleming’s rules (Extended): Left-hand = motor/force; Right-hand = generator/induction
✓ Ideal transformer (Extended): \(I_pV_p = I_sV_s\); power loss \(P_{\text{loss}} = I^2R\)

title: 24  Electromagnetic Effects
text:
24.16 Glossary







Term
Definition




A.C. generator
Device that converts mechanical energy to alternating electrical energy using electromagnetic induction


D.C. motor
Device that converts electrical energy to mechanical rotation using the motor effect and split-ring commutator


Electromagnetic induction
Production of an e.m.f. in a conductor due to a changing magnetic field


Fleming’s left-hand rule
Rule to determine direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field


Fleming’s right-hand rule
Rule to determine direction of induced current when a conductor moves in a magnetic field


Lenz’s Law
The direction of induced e.m.f. opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it


Motor effect
The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in an external magnetic field


Relay
An electromagnetic switch used to control a high-current circuit with a low-current signal


Slip rings
Continuous metal rings in an a.c. generator that transfer alternating current to the external circuit


Split-ring commutator
A split metal ring in a d.c. motor that reverses current direction in the coil every half-turn


Step-down transformer
Transformer where secondary voltage is lower than primary voltage (\(N_s < N_p\))


Step-up transformer
Transformer where secondary voltage is higher than primary voltage (\(N_s > N_p\))


Transformer
Device that changes the voltage of an alternating current supply using mutual induction


Mutual induction
Induction of an e.m.f. in one coil due to a changing current in a nearby coil

title: 25  Nuclear Physics
section: 25.2 The Nuclear Model of the Atom
text:
25.2 The Nuclear Model of the Atom

25.2.1 What Is an Atom?
An atom is the smallest unit of a chemical element that retains the chemical properties of that element. However, atoms are not indivisible — they consist of even smaller particles.
Structure of an atom:

Nucleus: A small, dense, positively charged centre containing protons and neutrons
Electrons: Negatively charged particles that orbit the nucleus at relatively large distances

                    Electron orbit
                    ↗
    ┌─────────────────────────┐
    │                         │
    │    ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ●     │  ← Electrons in orbit
    │                         │
    │         [Nucleus]       │  ← Protons (+) and neutrons (0)
    │                         │
    └─────────────────────────┘






Note



Key Concept: The nucleus contains almost all the mass of the atom but occupies a tiny fraction of its volume. If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a marble at the centre!




25.2.2 Relative Charges and Masses of Subatomic Particles









Particle
Relative Charge
Relative Mass (atomic mass units)
Location




Proton

Nucleus

Nucleus

Orbiting nucleus









Warning



Important: The relative mass of an electron is so small that it is often considered negligible when calculating the mass of an atom. The mass of an atom is essentially the mass of its nucleus.




25.2.3 Proton Number and Nucleon Number
Proton number (atomic number) Z:

The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom
Determines the identity of the element (e.g., all carbon atoms have Z = 6)
In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the proton number

Nucleon number (mass number) A:

The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
A = number of protons + number of neutrons

Calculating the number of neutrons:
\[\text{Number of neutrons} = A - Z\]


25.2.4 Nuclide Notation
Atoms are represented using nuclide notation:
\[^A_ZX\]
Where: - \(X\) = chemical symbol of the element - \(A\) = nucleon number (mass number) - \(Z\) = proton number (atomic number)
Example: Carbon-12 is written as \(^{12}_6\text{C}\)

6 protons in the nucleus
12 – 6 = 6 neutrons in the nucleus
6 electrons orbiting the nucleus (in a neutral atom)



25.2.5 Isotopes
Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have:

The same proton number (same number of protons)
Different nucleon numbers (different numbers of neutrons)

Example: Isotopes of carbon



Isotope

Note



Key Insight: Isotopes of the same element have identical chemical properties (because they have the same number of electrons) but may have different physical properties (e.g., mass, stability).




25.2.6 Formation of Ions
Atoms can gain or lose electrons to form ions:
Positive ions (cations):

Formed when an atom loses electrons
Has more protons than electrons → net positive charge
Example: Sodium atom (Na) loses 1 electron → sodium ion (Na\(^+\))

Negative ions (anions):

Formed when an atom gains electrons
Has more electrons than protons → net negative charge
Example: Chlorine atom (Cl) gains 1 electron → chloride ion (Cl\(^-\))







Warning



Important: Only electrons are transferred when atoms form ions. Protons remain fixed in the nucleus and do not participate in ion formation.




25.2.7 Evidence for the Nuclear Model: Rutherford’s Scattering Experiment
In 1911, Ernest Rutherford, with his assistants Geiger and Marsden, conducted an experiment that provided crucial evidence for the nuclear model of the atom.
The experiment:

A beam of alpha (α) particles was directed at a very thin sheet of gold foil
A fluorescent screen surrounding the foil detected where the α-particles landed
The scattering pattern was observed and recorded

Observations:

Most α-particles passed straight through the foil with little or no deflection
Some α-particles were deflected at small angles
A very few α-particles (about 1 in 8000) were deflected at angles greater than 90° — some even bounced straight back!

Conclusions:







Observation
Conclusion




Most α-particles passed through
The atom is mostly empty space


Some α-particles deflected at small angles
The nucleus is positively charged (like charges repel)


Very few α-particles deflected at large angles
The nucleus is very small and contains most of the mass









Note



Key Concept: Rutherford’s experiment overturned the earlier “plum pudding” model and established that atoms have a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space where electrons orbit.

title: 25  Nuclear Physics
text:
25.3 Radioactivity

25.3.1 What Is Radioactivity?
Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation from the nucleus of an unstable atom.
Key characteristics:

Spontaneous: Cannot be influenced by external factors (temperature, pressure, chemical state)
Random: Impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when it will decay
Ionising: The emitted radiation has enough energy to knock electrons from atoms, forming ions



25.3.2 Background Radiation
Background radiation is ionising nuclear radiation that is present in the environment from natural and artificial sources, even when no radioactive source is deliberately introduced.
Sources of background radiation:








Source
Contribution
Description




Radon gas (in air)
~50%
Radioactive gas from decay of uranium in rocks; can accumulate in buildings


Rocks and buildings
~15%
Natural radioactive materials (uranium, thorium) in soil and construction materials


Food and drink
~10%
Naturally occurring radioactive isotopes (e.g., potassium-40 in bananas)


Cosmic rays
~10%
High-energy particles from space; intensity increases with altitude


Medical procedures
~10%
X-rays, nuclear medicine scans, radiotherapy


Other artificial sources
~5%
Nuclear power, fallout from weapons testing, consumer products









Warning



Important: Background radiation levels vary by location. Areas with granite rock or high altitude have higher background radiation. However, typical levels are well below those that cause harm.




25.3.3 Measuring Radioactivity
Geiger-Müller (GM) tube and counter:

Detects ionising radiation by measuring the electrical pulses produced when radiation ionises gas in the tube
Displays count rate in counts per second (counts/s) or counts per minute (counts/min)

Corrected count rate:
\[\text{Corrected count rate} = \text{Measured count rate} - \text{Background count rate}\]






Note



Key Concept: Always measure background radiation first and subtract it from measurements with a radioactive source to obtain the true count rate from the source alone.

25.4.2 Relative Ionising Effects
Ionising effect: The ability of radiation to knock electrons from atoms, creating ions.

Warning



Important: Alpha particles are the most dangerous if ingested or inhaled because they cause intense ionisation in a small volume of tissue. Outside the body, alpha particles are stopped by skin and pose little risk.




25.4.4 Deflection in Electric and Magnetic Fields
In an electric field:

Alpha particles (+2 charge): Deflected towards the negative plate; small deflection due to large mass
Beta particles (–1 charge): Deflected towards the positive plate; large deflection due to small mass
Gamma rays (no charge): Not deflected; travel in a straight line

In a magnetic field:

Alpha particles: Deflected according to Fleming’s left-hand rule; circular path with large radius (due to large mass)
Beta particles: Deflected in the opposite direction to alpha; circular path with small radius (due to small mass)
Gamma rays: Not deflected; travel in a straight line







Note



Key Insight: The direction and amount of deflection can be used to identify the type of radiation and distinguish between α, β, and γ emissions.

title: 25  Nuclear Physics
text:
25.5 Radioactive Decay

25.5.1 What Is Radioactive Decay?
Radioactive decay is a spontaneous change in an unstable nucleus that results in the emission of α-particles, β-particles, and/or γ-radiation.
Key points:

Decay is spontaneous: Cannot be sped up, slowed down, or stopped by external conditions
Decay is random: Impossible to predict which specific nucleus will decay next
Decay increases stability: The nucleus moves towards a more stable configuration



25.5.2 Alpha Decay
Process:

Nucleus emits an alpha particle (\(^4_2\alpha\))
Nucleon number decreases by 4; proton number decreases by 2
Element changes to one two places earlier in the periodic table

Nuclide equation:
\[^A_ZX \rightarrow ^{A-4}_{Z-2}Y + ^4_2\alpha\]
Example: Radon-222 decays to polonium-218:
\[^{222}_{86}\text{Rn} \rightarrow ^{218}_{84}\text{Po} + ^4_2\alpha\]


25.5.3 Beta Decay
Process:

A neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron: \(n \rightarrow p + e^-\)
The proton remains in the nucleus; the electron is emitted as a beta particle
Nucleon number remains unchanged; proton number increases by 1
Element changes to one place later in the periodic table

Nuclide equation:
\[^A_ZX \rightarrow ^A_{Z+1}Y + ^0_{-1}\beta\]
Example: Carbon-14 decays to nitrogen-14:
\[^{14}_6\text{C} \rightarrow ^{14}_7\text{N} + ^0_{-1}\beta\]


25.5.4 Gamma Emission
Process:

Nucleus releases excess energy after α- or β-decay
No change in nucleon number or proton number
Element does not change

Nuclide equation:
\[^A_ZX^* \rightarrow ^A_ZX + \gamma\]
Where \(X^*\) indicates an excited (high-energy) nucleus.






Note



Key Concept: Gamma emission often accompanies α- or β-decay. The nucleus first decays by emitting α or β, then releases excess energy as γ-rays to reach a more stable state.




25.5.5 Why Are Some Isotopes Radioactive?
Isotopes may be radioactive due to:

Excess neutrons: Nucleus has too many neutrons relative to protons → unstable → β– decay reduces neutron excess
Too massive: Very heavy nuclei (e.g., uranium, radium) are unstable → α decay reduces mass and increases stability
High energy state: Nucleus has excess energy after another decay → γ emission releases energy







Warning



Important: Radioactive decay is a natural process that moves nuclei towards greater stability. It cannot be controlled or influenced by chemical or physical conditions.

title: 25  Nuclear Physics
text:
25.6 Half-life

25.6.1 What Is Half-life?
Half-life (\(t_{1/2}\)) of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for:

Half the nuclei of that isotope in any sample to decay, or
The count rate (or activity) of the isotope to fall to half its initial value

Key properties:

Half-life is constant for a given isotope (cannot be changed)
Half-life is independent of the amount of substance, temperature, pressure, or chemical state
Different isotopes have vastly different half-lives (from fractions of a second to billions of years)



25.6.2 Calculations Using Half-life
Method 1: Using the definition directly
After each half-life, the number of undecayed nuclei (or count rate) is halved:

Fraction remaining
Percentage remaining

\(n\)

\(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n \times 100\%\)



Method 2: Using decay curves
A decay curve plots count rate (or number of nuclei) against time. The half-life can be determined by:

Finding the initial count rate
Finding the time when count rate has fallen to half this value
This time interval is the half-life







Note



Key Concept: The decay curve is exponential — the count rate never reaches zero but approaches it asymptotically. Background radiation must be subtracted before analysing decay curves.

title: 25  Nuclear Physics
text:
25.8 Nuclear Fission and Fusion (Extended)

25.8.1 Nuclear Fission
Definition: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei, accompanied by the release of energy and (usually) neutrons.
Example: Uranium-235 fission
\[^{235}_{92}\text{U} + ^1_0\text{n} \rightarrow ^{144}_{56}\text{Ba} + ^{90}_{36}\text{Kr} + 2^1_0\text{n} + \text{energy}\]
Key points:

Triggered by neutron absorption
Releases additional neutrons → can sustain a chain reaction
Mass of products < mass of reactants → mass converted to energy (\(E = mc^2\))
Used in nuclear power stations and nuclear weapons



25.8.2 Nuclear Fusion
Definition: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, accompanied by the release of energy.
Example: Deuterium-tritium fusion
\[^2_1\text{H} + ^3_1\text{H} \rightarrow ^4_2\text{He} + ^1_0\text{n} + \text{energy}\]
Key points:

Occurs naturally in stars (including the Sun) at extremely high temperatures and pressures
Releases more energy per unit mass than fission
Produces less long-lived radioactive waste than fission
Not yet achieved for sustained power generation on Earth (research ongoing, e.g., ITER project)



25.8.3 Mass–Energy Conversion
In both fission and fusion:

Total mass of products < total mass of reactants
The “missing” mass is converted to energy according to Einstein’s equation:

\[E = mc^2\]
Where:

\(E\) = energy released (J)
\(m\) = mass defect (kg)
\(c\) = speed of light in vacuum (\(3.0 \times 10^8\) m/s)







Note



Key Insight: Because \(c^2\) is an enormous number (\(9 \times 10^{16}\) m²/s²), even a tiny mass defect produces a huge amount of energy. This explains why nuclear reactions release vastly more energy than chemical reactions.

title: 25  Nuclear Physics
text:
25.9 Safety Precautions

25.9.1 Effects of Ionising Radiation on Living Things
Ionising radiation can damage living cells by:

Direct damage: Breaking chemical bonds in DNA or other critical molecules
Indirect damage: Ionising water molecules to produce reactive free radicals that damage cells

Consequences of exposure:







Exposure Level
Effect




Low dose
Possible cell mutation; increased long-term cancer risk


Moderate dose
Cell death; tissue damage; radiation sickness (nausea, fatigue, hair loss)


High dose
Severe radiation sickness; organ failure; death





25.9.2 Principles of Radiation Protection
Three key principles to minimise exposure:

Time: Reduce the time spent near radioactive sources
Distance: Increase distance from sources (intensity decreases with square of distance)
Shielding: Use appropriate materials to absorb radiation:

α: Paper, skin, a few cm of air
β: Aluminium, plastic, a few mm of metal
γ: Lead, thick concrete, several cm of dense material




25.9.3 Safe Handling of Radioactive Materials
Storage:

Keep sources in labelled, shielded containers (e.g., lead-lined boxes for γ-emitters)
Store in secure, access-controlled areas

Use:

Use tongs or remote-handling tools to increase distance
Wear protective clothing (lab coat, gloves, safety glasses)
Work behind shielding (e.g., lead glass screens for γ-sources)
Monitor exposure with personal dosimeters

Disposal:

Follow institutional and regulatory procedures
Store waste in appropriate shielded containers until decay or disposal







Warning



Important: Never eat, drink, or apply cosmetics in areas where radioactive materials are used. Always wash hands after handling sources. Report spills or accidents immediately.

title: 25  Nuclear Physics
text:
25.10 Key Concepts Summary

25.10.1 Core Concepts

Atomic structure: Atom = small, dense, positively charged nucleus (protons + neutrons) + orbiting electrons
Proton number (Z): Number of protons; defines the element; equals electrons in neutral atom
Nucleon number (A): Total protons + neutrons; number of neutrons = \(A - Z\)
Nuclide notation: \(^A_ZX\) represents an atom of element X with mass number A and atomic number Z
Isotopes: Atoms of same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A)
Ions: Formed by loss (positive ion) or gain (negative ion) of electrons; protons unchanged
Background radiation: Natural and artificial ionising radiation present in environment; sources include radon, rocks, food, cosmic rays
Detection: GM tube + counter measures count rate (counts/s or counts/min); subtract background for corrected count rate
Three emissions:

α: Helium nucleus, +2 charge, high ionising, low penetrating
β: Fast electron, –1 charge, medium ionising, medium penetrating
γ: EM wave, 0 charge, low ionising, high penetrating

Radioactive decay: Spontaneous, random change in unstable nucleus; α- or β-decay changes element; γ emission releases excess energy
Half-life: Time for half the nuclei in a sample to decay (or count rate to halve); constant for a given isotope
Applications: Smoke alarms (α), sterilisation (γ), medical tracers (γ, short \(t_{1/2}\)), thickness control (β/γ), cancer treatment (γ/β)
Safety: Effects include cell death, mutation, cancer; protect by reducing time, increasing distance, using shielding



25.10.2 Extended Concepts

Rutherford scattering: α-particle experiment provided evidence for small, massive, positively charged nucleus surrounded by empty space
Deflection in fields: α (+2) and β (–1) deflected in opposite directions in electric/magnetic fields; γ (0) not deflected
Ionising effect explanation: Depends on charge (electric force) and kinetic energy; α has highest due to +2 charge and high KE
Decay equations: Use nuclide notation to show α, β, γ emissions; conserve nucleon number and charge
Why isotopes are radioactive: Excess neutrons → β– decay; too massive → α decay; excited state → γ emission
Half-life with background: Subtract background count rate before determining half-life from decay data or curves
Choosing isotopes: Match radiation type (penetration/ionisation) and half-life to application requirements
Nuclear fission: Heavy nucleus splits into lighter nuclei + neutrons + energy; used in power stations
Nuclear fusion: Light nuclei join to form heavier nucleus + energy; powers stars; research ongoing for power generation
Mass–energy conversion: \(E = mc^2\); small mass defect → large energy release in nuclear reactions

title: 25  Nuclear Physics
text:
25.11 Common Misconceptions

25.11.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Atoms are solid spheres with electrons embedded in them”
Incorrect: “The atom is like a plum pudding — electrons stuck in a positive sphere”
Correct:

Rutherford’s scattering experiment showed atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons
Electrons orbit at relatively large distances; the atom is mostly empty space
The plum pudding model was disproved in 1911




25.11.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “Isotopes have different chemical properties”
Incorrect: “Carbon-12 and carbon-14 behave differently in chemical reactions”
Correct:

Isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons → identical electron configuration
Chemical properties depend on electron arrangement → isotopes have identical chemical properties
Physical properties (e.g., mass, nuclear stability) may differ




25.11.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “Radioactive decay can be sped up or slowed down”
Incorrect: “Heating a radioactive sample makes it decay faster”
Correct:

Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random; cannot be influenced by temperature, pressure, or chemical state
Half-life is a fixed property of each isotope
Only the probability of decay per nucleus is fixed; we cannot control when individual nuclei decay




25.11.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Alpha particles are the most dangerous type of radiation”
Incorrect: “Alpha radiation is always the most harmful”
Correct:

Danger depends on exposure pathway:

Outside body: α stopped by skin → low risk; γ most penetrating → highest external risk
Inside body: α causes intense ionisation in small volume → highest internal risk if ingested/inhaled

Risk assessment must consider radiation type, energy, exposure route, and dose




25.11.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Gamma rays are particles like alpha and beta”
Incorrect: “Gamma rays are heavy particles emitted from the nucleus”
Correct:

Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves (like light or X-rays), not particles
They have no mass and no charge → not deflected by electric/magnetic fields
Emitted when an excited nucleus releases excess energy after α- or β-decay




25.11.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “After two half-lives, all the radioactive material has decayed”
Incorrect: “If half-life is 10 years, after 20 years the sample is no longer radioactive”
Correct:

After 1 half-life: 50% remains
After 2 half-lives: 25% remains
After \(n\) half-lives: \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\) remains
Radioactive material never completely disappears; it approaches zero asymptotically




25.11.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “Nuclear fusion is the same as nuclear fission”
Incorrect: “Fusion and fission are just different names for splitting atoms”
Correct:

Fission: Heavy nucleus splits into lighter nuclei (e.g., uranium → barium + krypton)
Fusion: Light nuclei join to form heavier nucleus (e.g., hydrogen → helium in the Sun)
Both release energy via \(E = mc^2\), but mechanisms, conditions, and applications differ greatly

title: 25  Nuclear Physics
text:
25.12 Worked Examples

25.12.1 Example 1: Nuclide Notation and Neutron Calculation
Question: An atom of uranium has a nucleon number of 238 and a proton number of 92. (a) Write the nuclide notation for this atom. (b) Calculate the number of neutrons in its nucleus. (c) How many electrons does a neutral atom of this isotope have?
Solution:
(a) Nuclide notation: \[^{238}_{92}\text{U}\]
(b) Number of neutrons: \[\text{Neutrons} = A - Z = 238 - 92 = \boxed{146}\]
(c) Electrons in neutral atom: In a neutral atom, number of electrons = number of protons = \(\boxed{92}\)



25.12.2 Example 2: Identifying Decay Type from Nuclide Equation
Question: Complete the following decay equation and identify the type of decay: \[^{210}_{84}\text{Po} \rightarrow ^{206}_{82}\text{Pb} + \text{?}\]
Solution:
Step 1: Check conservation of nucleon number (A): \[210 = 206 + A_{\text{?}} \Rightarrow A_{\text{?}} = 4\]
Step 2: Check conservation of charge/proton number (Z): \[84 = 82 + Z_{\text{?}} \Rightarrow Z_{\text{?}} = 2\]
Step 3: Identify particle with \(A = 4\), \(Z = 2\): This is an alpha particle: \(^4_2\alpha\)
Answer: \[^{210}_{84}\text{Po} \rightarrow ^{206}_{82}\text{Pb} + \boxed{^4_2\alpha}\] Type of decay: Alpha decay



25.12.3 Example 3: Half-life Calculation
Question: A radioactive source has an initial count rate of 800 counts/min. The background count rate is 50 counts/min. The half-life of the isotope is 15 minutes. (a) Calculate the corrected initial count rate. (b) Calculate the corrected count rate after 45 minutes. (c) Calculate the measured count rate after 45 minutes (including background).
Solution:
(a) Corrected initial count rate: \[\text{Corrected} = 800 - 50 = \boxed{750 \text{ counts/min}}\]
(b) Corrected count rate after 45 minutes: Number of half-lives: \(n = \frac{45}{15} = 3\) \[\text{Corrected after 45 min} = 750 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = 750 \times \frac{1}{8} = \boxed{93.75 \text{ counts/min}}\]
(c) Measured count rate (including background): \[\text{Measured} = 93.75 + 50 = \boxed{143.75 \text{ counts/min} \approx 144 \text{ counts/min}}\]



25.12.4 Example 4: Choosing an Isotope for an Application (Extended)
Question: A company wants to use a radioactive source to monitor the thickness of aluminium foil during production. Suggest whether an alpha, beta, or gamma source would be most suitable and explain your choice.
Solution:
Analysis: - Aluminium foil is relatively thin but denser than paper/plastic - Need radiation that is partially absorbed so count rate changes with thickness - Radiation must penetrate the foil to reach the detector
Evaluation of options:








Radiation
Suitability for aluminium foil
Reason




Alpha
❌ Unsuitable
Stopped by paper; cannot penetrate aluminium foil at all


Beta
✅ Suitable
Partially absorbed by thin metal; count rate varies with thickness; aluminium is within β penetration range


Gamma
❌ Less suitable
Too penetrating; most γ-rays pass through thin foil with little absorption → small change in count rate



Conclusion: A beta source (e.g., strontium-90) is most suitable because beta particles are partially absorbed by aluminium foil, allowing the count rate to vary measurably with thickness changes.



25.12.5 Example 5: Nuclear Fission Equation (Extended)
Question: In a nuclear reactor, uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission to produce barium-141, krypton-92, and three neutrons. Write the balanced nuclide equation for this reaction.
Solution:
Step 1: Write reactants: \[^{235}_{92}\text{U} + ^1_0\text{n} \rightarrow \text{?}\]
Step 2: Write known products: \[\rightarrow ^{141}_{56}\text{Ba} + ^{92}_{36}\text{Kr} + 3^1_0\text{n}\]
Step 3: Verify conservation: - Nucleon number: \(235 + 1 = 236\); \(141 + 92 + 3(1) = 236\) ✓ - Proton number: \(92 + 0 = 92\); \(56 + 36 + 3(0) = 92\) ✓
Answer: \[\boxed{^{235}_{92}\text{U} + ^1_0\text{n} \rightarrow ^{141}_{56}\text{Ba} + ^{92}_{36}\text{Kr} + 3^1_0\text{n} + \text{energy}}\]
