title: 25  Nuclear Physics
text:
25.14 Laboratory Investigation

25.14.1 Experiment 22.1: Investigating Radioactive Decay and Half-life
Objective: To determine the half-life of a radioactive isotope using count rate measurements and to understand the random nature of radioactive decay.
Apparatus:

Geiger-Müller tube and counter (or radiation sensor with data logger)
Radioactive source with suitable half-life (e.g., protactinium-234 generator, or simulated data)
Retort stand and clamp
Stopwatch
Lead shielding (for safety)
Distance measuring tool

Variables:

Independent: Time
Dependent: Count rate (counts/min)
Controlled: Distance from source to detector, background radiation level, detector settings

Safety Precautions:

✓ Handle radioactive sources with tongs; never touch with bare hands
✓ Keep source in shielded container when not in use
✓ Maintain maximum practical distance from source
✓ Limit exposure time; plan measurements in advance
✓ Wear personal dosimeter if available
✓ Follow institutional radiation safety protocols

Procedure:

Measure background radiation:

Remove all radioactive sources from the area
Record count rate for 5 minutes; calculate average background count rate in counts/min

Set up the experiment:

Clamp the GM tube at a fixed height
Position the radioactive source at a fixed distance (e.g., 10 cm) from the detector
Ensure the setup is stable and will not be disturbed during measurements

Collect decay data:

Start the counter and stopwatch simultaneously
Record the total counts for successive 1-minute intervals (or use data logger for continuous recording)
Continue for at least 5–6 half-lives of the isotope (or until count rate approaches background)

Data processing:

Convert total counts per interval to count rate (counts/min)
Subtract background count rate to obtain corrected count rate
Tabulate time vs. corrected count rate


Data Table:









Time (min)
Total counts in interval
Count rate (counts/min)
Corrected count rate (counts/min)




0–1





1–2





2–3





3–4





4–5





…






Analysis:

Plot a graph of corrected count rate (y-axis) against time (x-axis)
Determine the half-life by:

Finding the initial corrected count rate (\(R_0\))
Finding the time when count rate falls to \(\frac{1}{2}R_0\) → this is one half-life
Repeat for \(\frac{1}{4}R_0\), \(\frac{1}{8}R_0\) to check consistency

Alternatively, plot ln(corrected count rate) against time; the gradient = \(-\lambda\) (decay constant), and \(t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}\)
Comment on the random variation in count rates and how averaging over longer intervals reduces this effect

Precautions:

✓ Ensure detector is properly calibrated and zeroed
✓ Keep geometry (distance, orientation) constant throughout
✓ Account for dead time of GM tube if count rates are high
✓ Repeat measurements to assess random uncertainty

Expected Results:

Graph shows exponential decay: count rate decreases by half every half-life
Random fluctuations around the smooth decay curve demonstrate the random nature of decay
Calculated half-life should agree with accepted value within experimental uncertainty

Conclusion Template: “The experiment demonstrated the exponential nature of radioactive decay. The corrected count rate decreased by approximately half every ______ minutes, giving a half-life of ______ min for the isotope. Random variations in count rate confirmed the spontaneous and random nature of nuclear decay. The measured half-life agreed with the accepted value of ______ min within experimental error.”
Extension (Supplement): - Investigate how background subtraction affects half-life determination - Compare decay curves for isotopes with different half-lives - Research how half-life data is used in radiometric dating (e.g., carbon-14 dating)

title: 25  Nuclear Physics
text:
25.16 Chapter Summary

25.16.1 Key Points to Remember
✓ Atomic structure: Nucleus (protons + neutrons) at centre; electrons orbit at distance; atom mostly empty space
✓ Proton number (Z): Number of protons; defines element; = electrons in neutral atom
✓ Nucleon number (A): Protons + neutrons; neutrons = \(A - Z\)
✓ Nuclide notation: \(^A_ZX\)
✓ Isotopes: Same Z, different A; same chemical properties, different nuclear properties
✓ Ions: Formed by electron loss/gain; protons unchanged
✓ Background radiation: Natural/artificial ionising radiation; measure and subtract for accurate source measurement
✓ Three emissions: α (He nucleus, +2, high ionising, low penetrating), β (electron, –1, medium), γ (EM wave, 0, low ionising, high penetrating)
✓ Radioactive decay: Spontaneous, random; α/β change element; γ releases excess energy
✓ Half-life: Time for half nuclei to decay (or count rate to halve); constant for given isotope
✓ Applications: Match radiation type and half-life to use (smoke alarms, sterilisation, medical tracers, thickness control, radiotherapy)
✓ Safety: Radiation can cause cell damage, mutation, cancer; protect by time, distance, shielding
✓ Rutherford scattering: Evidence for small, massive, positive nucleus in empty space (Extended)
✓ Deflection in fields: α and β deflected oppositely; γ not deflected (Extended)
✓ Decay equations: Conserve A and Z; use nuclide notation (Extended)
✓ Fission/fusion: Splitting/joining nuclei; \(E = mc^2\) explains energy release (Extended)


25.16.2 Formulae Sheet








Quantity
Formula
Variables




Number of neutrons
\(N = A - Z\)
\(A\)=nucleon number, \(Z\)=proton number


Corrected count rate
\(R_{\text{corr}} = R_{\text{meas}} - R_{\text{bg}}\)
\(R_{\text{meas}}\)=measured rate, \(R_{\text{bg}}\)=background rate


Fraction remaining after \(n\) half-lives
\(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\)
\(n\)=number of half-lives


Decay constant and half-life (Extended)
\(t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}\)
\(\lambda\)=decay constant


Mass–energy equivalence (Extended)
\(E = mc^2\)
\(E\)=energy (J), \(m\)=mass defect (kg), \(c\)=speed of light

title: 25  Nuclear Physics
text:
25.18 Glossary







Term
Definition




Alpha particle (α)
A helium nucleus (\(^4_2\text{He}\)) emitted during alpha decay; +2 charge, high ionising, low penetrating


Background radiation
Ionising radiation present in the environment from natural and artificial sources


Beta particle (β)
A high-speed electron (\(^0_{-1}\text{e}\)) emitted during beta decay; –1 charge, medium ionising and penetrating


Count rate
Number of radiation detections per unit time (counts/s or counts/min) measured by a detector


Electron
Negatively charged subatomic particle orbiting the nucleus; relative charge –1, relative mass ≈ \(\frac{1}{2000}\)


Gamma ray (γ)
High-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted by excited nuclei; no charge or mass, low ionising, high penetrating


Geiger-Müller tube
A detector that measures ionising radiation by counting electrical pulses from ionisation events


Half-life (\(t_{1/2}\))
Time taken for half the nuclei in a radioactive sample to decay, or for count rate to halve


Ion
An atom or molecule with a net electric charge due to loss or gain of electrons


Ionising radiation
Radiation with sufficient energy to remove electrons from atoms, creating ions


Isotope
Atoms of the same element (same proton number) with different numbers of neutrons (different nucleon number)


Neutron
Neutral subatomic particle in the nucleus; relative charge 0, relative mass 1


Nuclear fission
Splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons


Nuclear fusion
Joining of light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy


Nucleon
A proton or neutron; constituent of atomic nuclei


Nucleon number (A)
Total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus (mass number)


Nucleus
Small, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons


Nuclide notation
Symbolic representation of an atom: \(^A_ZX\), where A = nucleon number, Z = proton number, X = element symbol


Proton
Positively charged subatomic particle in the nucleus; relative charge +1, relative mass 1


Proton number (Z)
Number of protons in a nucleus (atomic number); defines the element


Radioactive decay
Spontaneous, random change in an unstable nucleus with emission of α, β, and/or γ radiation


Radioactivity
The property of unstable nuclei to spontaneously emit ionising radiation

title: 26  Space Physics
section: 26.2 23.1 The Earth, Moon and Solar Motions
text:
26.2 23.1 The Earth, Moon and Solar Motions

26.2.1 Earth’s Rotation: Day and Night
The Earth rotates on its axis once every approximately 24 hours.

The side facing the Sun experiences daytime.
The side facing away experiences nighttime.
Because the Earth rotates from west to east, the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.







Note



Key Concept: The apparent motion of the Sun across the sky is caused by the Earth’s actual rotation. We do not feel this rotation because it is smooth, constant, and we move with the Earth.




26.2.2 Earth’s Revolution and Tilt: The Seasons
The Earth orbits the Sun once every approximately 365.25 days (one year).
Why do seasons occur?

The Earth’s axis is tilted at an angle of approximately 23.5° relative to its orbital plane.
As the Earth orbits, this tilt causes different hemispheres to receive different amounts of direct sunlight at different times of the year.
Summer: Hemisphere tilted towards the Sun → longer days, higher Sun angle, more concentrated solar energy.
Winter: Hemisphere tilted away from the Sun → shorter days, lower Sun angle, more spread out solar energy.
Spring/Autumn: Axis tilted neither towards nor away → roughly equal day and night lengths.







Warning



Important: Seasons are not caused by the Earth’s changing distance from the Sun. The Earth is actually closest to the Sun (perihelion) in early January (Northern Hemisphere winter).




26.2.3 The Moon: Phases and Orbit
The Moon orbits the Earth once every approximately 27.3 days (roughly one month).

The Moon does not produce its own light. It reflects sunlight.
As the Moon orbits, the portion of its sunlit side visible from Earth changes, creating phases.
New Moon: Moon between Earth and Sun → dark side faces Earth.
Full Moon: Earth between Moon and Sun → fully lit side faces Earth.
Waxing: Illuminated portion increases.
Waning: Illuminated portion decreases.

title: 26  Space Physics
section: 26.3 23.2 The Solar System and Its Formation
text:
26.3 23.2 The Solar System and Its Formation

26.3.1 Structure of the Solar System







Component
Description




The Sun
Central star, contains ~99% of Solar System’s mass


Inner Planets
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars (rocky, small, dense, few/no moons)


Outer Planets
Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (gaseous/icy, large, low density, many moons, rings)


Asteroids
Rocky remnants, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter


Comets
Icy/dusty bodies with highly elliptical orbits, develop tails near Sun


Dwarf Planets
Spherical but not dominant in their orbit (e.g., Pluto in Kuiper Belt)





26.3.2 Formation: The Nebular Hypothesis

Giant Molecular Cloud: A vast cloud of gas (mostly hydrogen) and dust begins to collapse under its own gravity.
Protostar & Accretion Disc: The cloud spins faster as it collapses. The centre heats up to form a protostar. Surrounding material flattens into a spinning accretion disc.
Nuclear Fusion Ignites: The protostar becomes hot/dense enough for hydrogen fusion → becomes a star (the Sun).
Planet Formation:


Inner Region: Close to the hot Sun, only heavy elements (rock, metal) can condense → rocky planets.
Outer Region: Cooler temperatures allow lighter gases (hydrogen, helium) and ices to condense → gas/ice giants.







Note



Key Concept: The accretion model explains the compositional difference between inner and outer planets. Gravity sorted materials by mass and boiling point during formation.

title: 26  Space Physics
text:
26.4 23.3 Orbital Mechanics and Gravitation

26.4.1 Average Orbital Speed
For a roughly circular orbit, the average speed \(v\) is given by:
\[v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}\]
Where: - \(v\) = average orbital speed (m/s)

\(r\) = average orbital radius (m)
\(T\) = orbital period (s)



26.4.2 Gravitational Field and Orbits

The gravitational field strength \(g\) at a planet’s surface depends on its mass and radius.
\(g\) decreases as distance from the planet increases (\(g \propto \frac{1}{r^2}\)).
The Sun’s gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps planets in orbit.
Planets do not fly off into space because gravity constantly pulls them inward, changing their direction.



26.4.3 Elliptical Orbits and Conservation of Energy (Extended)

Planetary orbits are elliptical, with the Sun at one focus (not the centre).
Perihelion: Closest point to Sun → highest gravitational potential energy (GPE) converted to kinetic energy (KE) → fastest speed.
Aphelion: Furthest point from Sun → highest KE converted to GPE → slowest speed.
Total mechanical energy (KE + GPE) remains constant (conservation of energy).

title: 26  Space Physics
text:
26.5 23.4 Stars and Stellar Evolution

26.5.1 The Sun as a Star

Medium-sized, yellow star.
Composition: ~73% hydrogen, ~25% helium, ~2% heavier elements.
Radiates energy across the spectrum: mostly infrared, visible light, and ultraviolet.
Power Source: Nuclear fusion in the core. Hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, releasing vast energy (\(E=mc^2\)).



26.5.2 Life Cycle of Stars
The path a star takes depends on its initial mass.








Stage
Low/Medium Mass Star (like the Sun)
High Mass Star (>8 solar masses)




1. Birth
Nebula → Protostar
Nebula → Protostar


2. Stable Phase
Main Sequence (H → He fusion). Outward radiation pressure balances inward gravity.
Main Sequence (H → He fusion). Burns hotter, faster, shorter life.


3. Fuel Depletion
Hydrogen runs out → core contracts, outer layers expand → Red Giant
Hydrogen runs out → core contracts, outer layers expand → Red Supergiant


4. Late Stage
Outer layers shed → Planetary Nebula. Core remains → White Dwarf (cools slowly)
Core collapses → violent explosion (Supernova). Creates elements heavier than iron.


5. Remnant
White Dwarf cools to black dwarf (theoretical)
Core becomes Neutron Star or, if massive enough, a Black Hole









Warning



Important: A black hole’s gravity is not “stronger” than the original star’s at a distance. If the Sun became a black hole, Earth’s orbit would remain unchanged. The extreme gravity only exists very close to the event horizon.




26.5.3 Astronomical Distances: The Light-Year
Distances in space are too vast for metres or kilometres.

Light-year (ly): The distance light travels in one year in a vacuum.
\(c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\)
\(1 \text{ year} \approx 3.15 \times 10^7 \text{ s}\)
\(1 \text{ ly} = c \times t = (3.0 \times 10^8) \times (3.15 \times 10^7) \approx \boxed{9.5 \times 10^{15} \text{ m}}\)

title: 26  Space Physics
text:
26.6 23.5 The Expanding Universe

26.6.1 Galaxies and the Milky Way

A galaxy is a massive system of billions of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter bound by gravity.
The Milky Way is our galaxy, ~100,000 light-years in diameter, containing 100–400 billion stars.
The Universe contains billions of galaxies.



26.6.2 Redshift and the Big Bang Theory
Redshift: When a light source moves away from an observer, the observed wavelength increases (shifts towards the red end of the spectrum).

Distant galaxies show redshifted spectra.
The further away the galaxy, the greater the redshift → the faster it is moving away.
Conclusion: The Universe is expanding.
Rewinding time: All matter was concentrated at a single, extremely hot, dense point → Big Bang.



26.6.3 Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR)

Evidence 2 for Big Bang: The early Universe was filled with high-energy gamma radiation.
As space expanded, the wavelength of this radiation stretched into the microwave region.
CMBR is uniform in all directions, confirming the Universe was once hot and dense everywhere.



26.6.4 Hubble’s Law and the Age of the Universe
Edwin Hubble discovered a linear relationship between galaxy distance and recessional velocity:
\[v \propto d \quad \text{or} \quad H_0 = \frac{v}{d}\]
Where: - \(v\) = recessional velocity (m/s)

\(d\) = distance from Earth (m)
\(H_0\) = Hubble constant \(\approx 2.2 \times 10^{-18} \text{ s}^{-1}\)

Estimating the Age of the Universe:
If expansion has been roughly constant: \[\text{Time} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Speed}} = \frac{d}{v} = \frac{1}{H_0}\]
\[\text{Age} \approx \frac{1}{2.2 \times 10^{-18}} \approx 4.5 \times 10^{17} \text{ s} \approx \boxed{14 \text{ billion years}}\]






Note



Key Concept: The Big Bang was not an explosion in space. It was the rapid expansion of space itself. Galaxies are not flying through space; the space between them is stretching.

title: 26  Space Physics
text:
26.7 Key Concepts Summary

26.7.1 Core Concepts

Earth’s motions: Rotation (~24h) → day/night; Revolution (~365d) + 23.5° tilt → seasons
Moon phases: Caused by changing viewing angle of sunlit side during ~28-day orbit
Solar System structure: Sun (99% mass), 8 planets, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets, moons
Accretion model: Gravity collapses nebula → disc forms → inner rocky, outer gaseous planets
Gravity & orbits: Sun’s gravity provides centripetal force; \(g\) depends on mass, decreases with distance
Light travel time: \(t = \frac{d}{c}\); used to measure Solar System distances
Stars: Powered by nuclear fusion (H → He); Sun radiates IR, visible, UV
Light-year: Distance light travels in 1 year (\(9.5 \times 10^{15}\) m)
Galaxies: Billions of stars; Milky Way ~100,000 ly across
Redshift: Wavelength increases as source recedes → evidence of expanding Universe → Big Bang



26.7.2 Extended Concepts

Orbital speed: \(v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}\); calculate using consistent SI units
Elliptical orbits: Sun at focus; conservation of energy explains speed variation (faster at perihelion)
Stellar evolution: Mass determines fate (White Dwarf vs Supernova/Black Hole)
CMBR: Stretched relic radiation from early Universe; uniform microwave background
Hubble’s Law: \(H_0 = v/d\); current estimate \(2.2 \times 10^{-18} \text{ s}^{-1}\)
Universe age: \(\approx \frac{1}{H_0} \approx 14\) billion years

title: 26  Space Physics
text:
26.8 Common Misconceptions

26.8.1 ⚠️ Misconception 1: “Seasons are caused by Earth’s changing distance from the Sun”
Incorrect: “Earth is closer to the Sun in summer”
Correct:

Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth’s axis, not distance
Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January (Northern Hemisphere winter)
Tilt changes the angle and duration of sunlight, not proximity




26.8.2 ⚠️ Misconception 2: “The Moon produces its own light”
Incorrect: “The Moon glows like the Sun”
Correct:

The Moon reflects sunlight
Phases occur because we see different portions of the illuminated half as it orbits
No light source of its own; only visible when reflecting sunlight




26.8.3 ⚠️ Misconception 3: “The Solar System formed because the Sun exploded”
Incorrect: “The Sun was first, then exploded to create planets”
Correct:

Sun and planets formed simultaneously from the same collapsing nebula
Accretion disc spun around the protostar → planets condensed from disc material
No explosion involved in formation; gravity drove the process




26.8.4 ⚠️ Misconception 4: “Orbits are perfect circles with the Sun at the exact centre”
Incorrect: “Planets move in circular paths around the centre”
Correct:

Orbits are elliptical (oval-shaped)
The Sun is at one focus, not the geometric centre
This causes varying distances (perihelion/aphelion) and varying orbital speeds




26.8.5 ⚠️ Misconception 5: “Black holes suck everything in like cosmic vacuums”
Incorrect: “Black holes pull matter from far away”
Correct:

Black hole gravity behaves normally at a distance
Only extreme within the event horizon
If the Sun became a black hole, Earth’s orbit would not change (same mass, same distance)




26.8.6 ⚠️ Misconception 6: “Redshift means galaxies are moving away from Earth specifically”
Incorrect: “Earth is the centre of the expansion”
Correct:

Space itself is expanding uniformly
From any galaxy, all others appear to be receding
Redshift is observed from all directions → no centre to the Universe




26.8.7 ⚠️ Misconception 7: “The Big Bang was an explosion in space”
Incorrect: “A bomb went off and debris flew outwards”
Correct:

The Big Bang was the rapid expansion of space itself
There was no pre-existing space or centre
Matter and energy expanded together as the Universe stretched

title: 26  Space Physics
text:
26.9 Worked Examples

26.9.1 Example 1: Orbital Speed Calculation
Question: A satellite orbits Earth at an average radius of \(7.0 \times 10^6\) m. It completes one orbit in 5800 s. Calculate its average orbital speed.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify values

\(r = 7.0 \times 10^6 \text{ m}\)
\(T = 5800 \text{ s}\)

Step 2: Apply formula \[v = \frac{2\pi r}{T} = \frac{2 \times \pi \times 7.0 \times 10^6}{5800}\]
Step 3: Calculate \[v = \frac{4.398 \times 10^7}{5800} \approx \boxed{7580 \text{ m/s}}\]



26.9.2 Example 2: Light Travel Time
Question: Mars is approximately \(2.25 \times 10^{11}\) m from Earth at closest approach. Calculate the time it takes for a radio signal (travelling at light speed) to reach Mars.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify values

\(d = 2.25 \times 10^{11} \text{ m}\)
\(c = 3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\)

Step 2: Apply formula \[t = \frac{d}{c} = \frac{2.25 \times 10^{11}}{3.0 \times 10^8}\]
Step 3: Calculate \[t = \boxed{750 \text{ s}} \text{ or } \boxed{12.5 \text{ minutes}}\]



26.9.3 Example 3: Conservation of Energy in Orbit (Extended)
Question: Explain why a comet moves fastest when it is closest to the Sun, using the principle of conservation of energy.
Solution:
Step 1: Identify energy forms

Total mechanical energy = Kinetic Energy (KE) + Gravitational Potential Energy (GPE)
In space (neglecting drag), total energy is conserved (constant).

Step 2: Analyse position change

At closest approach (perihelion), GPE is at its minimum (most negative).
To keep total energy constant, KE must be at its maximum.

Step 3: Relate to speed

\(KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\) → maximum KE means maximum speed.
Therefore, the comet moves fastest when closest to the Sun.




26.9.4 Example 4: Hubble’s Law and Universe Age (Extended)
Question: A distant galaxy is observed to be receding at \(4.4 \times 10^6\) m/s. Its distance is estimated at \(2.0 \times 10^{23}\) m.

Calculate the Hubble constant \(H_0\) from this data.
Estimate the age of the Universe using your answer.

Solution:
(a) Hubble constant: \[H_0 = \frac{v}{d} = \frac{4.4 \times 10^6}{2.0 \times 10^{23}} = \boxed{2.2 \times 10^{-18} \text{ s}^{-1}}\]
(b) Age of Universe: \[\text{Age} \approx \frac{1}{H_0} = \frac{1}{2.2 \times 10^{-18}} = 4.545 \times 10^{17} \text{ s}\] Convert to years: \(\frac{4.545 \times 10^{17}}{3.15 \times 10^7} \approx \boxed{14.4 \text{ billion years}}\)

title: 26  Space Physics
text:
26.11 Laboratory Investigation

26.11.1 Experiment 23.1: Modelling Orbital Mechanics and Redshift
Objective: To qualitatively demonstrate the relationship between orbital radius, speed, and gravitational pull, and to model redshift using sound.
Apparatus:

String (1 m)
Small rubber stopper or cork
Plastic tube (pen casing)
Masses (slotted weights)
Smartphone with sound generator app
Assistant or recording device

Part A: Orbital Speed vs Radius

Thread string through tube. Attach stopper to one end, masses to the other.
Swing stopper in horizontal circle above head.
Vary the orbital radius by pulling/lifting tube.
Observe how speed must change to maintain circular motion as radius decreases.

Part B: Doppler Shift (Redshift) Modelling

Play a constant tone on smartphone speaker.
Have assistant swing phone horizontally in a circle above head.
Listen to pitch change as phone moves towards/away from you.

Observations:

Smaller radius → faster rotation needed to maintain tension (simulating stronger gravity closer to Sun).
Pitch increases as source approaches (blueshift), decreases as it recedes (redshift).

Analysis:

Relate string tension to gravitational force.
Explain why planets closer to Sun orbit faster.
Connect pitch change to wavelength shift in light from receding galaxies.

Conclusion Template: “The investigation demonstrated that objects in tighter orbits must move faster to maintain balance, mirroring planetary motion. The Doppler effect on sound models how receding galaxies stretch light wavelengths, providing observable evidence of cosmic expansion.”

B. \(v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}\)
C. \(H_0 = \frac{v}{d}\)

26.12.2 Paper 3 Style (Structured)
6. (a) Describe how the tilt of the Earth’s axis causes winter in the Northern Hemisphere. [3]

Explain why the Moon appears to change shape over a period of approximately one month. [2]

7. (a) Describe the formation of the Solar System using the nebular hypothesis. Include reference to gravity and the accretion disc. [3]

Explain why the four inner planets are rocky and dense, while the four outer planets are gaseous and less dense. [2]
Calculate the time it takes for light to travel from Jupiter to Earth when they are \(6.3 \times 10^{11}\) m apart. [2]

8. (a) State the process that powers the Sun and explain how it releases energy. [2]

Describe the life cycle of a star much more massive than the Sun, from nebula to final remnant. [3]
Explain why a white dwarf is stable and does not collapse immediately. [2]

9. (Extended) (a) Define redshift and explain how it is observed in the spectra of distant galaxies. [2]

State two pieces of evidence that support the Big Bang Theory. [2]
A galaxy is measured to be \(1.5 \times 10^{23}\) m away and receding at \(3.3 \times 10^6\) m/s. Calculate \(H_0\) from this data. [2]
Using your answer, estimate the age of the Universe in seconds and years. [3]

title: 26  Space Physics
text:
26.13 Chapter Summary

26.13.1 Key Points to Remember
✓ Earth’s rotation (24h) → day/night; tilt (23.5°) + revolution (365d) → seasons
✓ Moon phases → changing view of sunlit side during ~28-day orbit
✓ Solar System → Sun (99% mass), 8 planets, asteroids, comets, moons, dwarf planets
✓ Accretion model → gravity collapses nebula → disc forms → inner rocky, outer gaseous planets
✓ Gravity provides centripetal force for orbits; \(g\) depends on mass, decreases with distance
✓ Elliptical orbits → Sun at focus; conservation of energy explains speed variation
✓ Orbital speed → \(v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}\)
✓ Stars → powered by nuclear fusion (H → He); Sun emits IR, visible, UV
✓ Light-year → distance light travels in 1 year ≈ \(9.5 \times 10^{15}\) m
✓ Stellar evolution → mass determines path: low/medium → white dwarf; high → supernova → neutron star/black hole
✓ Redshift → wavelength increases as source recedes → evidence of expanding Universe
✓ Big Bang → Universe began hot, dense, and has been expanding since
✓ CMBR → stretched relic radiation from early Universe
✓ Hubble’s Law → \(H_0 = v/d \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-18} \text{ s}^{-1}\); age \(\approx 1/H_0 \approx 14\) billion years


26.13.2 Formulae Sheet








Quantity
Formula
Variables




Average orbital speed
\(v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}\)
\(v\)=speed (m/s), \(r\)=radius (m), \(T\)=period (s)

\(t = \frac{d}{c}\)
\(d\)=distance (m), \(c\)=speed of light (\(3.0 \times 10^8\) m/s)


Hubble constant
\(H_0 = \frac{v}{d}\)
\(v\)=recessional velocity (m/s), \(d\)=distance (m)


Universe age estimate
\(t \approx \frac{1}{H_0}\)
\(H_0\)=Hubble constant (\(2.2 \times 10^{-18} \text{ s}^{-1}\))

\(1 \text{ ly} = 9.5 \times 10^{15} \text{ m}\)

title: 26  Space Physics
text:
26.15 Glossary







Term
Definition




Accretion disc
Rotating disc of gas and dust around a young star where planets form


Big Bang Theory
Theory that the Universe began as a hot, dense point and has been expanding ever since


Black hole
Remnant of a massive star with gravity so strong that not even light can escape


Comet
Icy/dusty Solar System body with highly elliptical orbit; develops tail near Sun


Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation (CMBR)
Uniform microwave radiation remnant from the early Universe, stretched by expansion


Dwarf planet
Spherical body orbiting Sun but not cleared its orbital neighbourhood (e.g., Pluto)


Elliptical orbit
Oval-shaped orbit with the Sun at one focus; speed varies with distance


Galaxy
Massive system of billions of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter bound by gravity


Hubble constant (\(H_0\))
Ratio of galaxy recessional velocity to distance; \(\approx 2.2 \times 10^{-18} \text{ s}^{-1}\)


Light-year (ly)
Distance light travels in one year in vacuum \(\approx 9.5 \times 10^{15}\) m


Nebula
Cloud of gas and dust in space; birthplace of stars


Nuclear fusion
Process where light nuclei combine to form heavier nuclei, releasing energy (powers stars)


Redshift
Increase in observed wavelength of light from receding objects; evidence of expansion


Red giant
Late stage of low/medium mass star; expanded outer layers, cooled surface


Supernova
Violent explosion of a massive star; creates elements heavier than iron


White dwarf
Hot, dense remnant core of a low/medium mass star; slowly cools over time

title: 27  Practical Skills
text:
27.2 Making Measurements

27.2.1 Avoiding Errors
Parallax Error - Position your eye perpendicular to the scale - Look straight at the measurement mark - Use a mirror behind the pointer if available
Zero Error - Check that instruments read zero when they should - For vernier calipers: close jaws completely and check reading - For ammeters/voltmeters: check with no current/voltage applied - Subtract zero error from measurements
Random Errors - Take multiple readings and calculate average - Repeat measurements to check consistency - Ignore anomalous results (after checking for mistakes)

title: 27  Practical Skills
text:
27.3 Common Instruments

27.3.1 Length Measurements



Instrument
Precision
Range




Metre rule
1 mm
Up to 1 m


Vernier calipers
0.1 mm
0–15 cm


Measuring tape
1 mm
Several metres



Using a metre rule: - Align the object with the zero mark (or another mark if zero is damaged) - View at right angles to avoid parallax error - Record to the nearest mm
Using vernier calipers: - Check for zero error before use - Close jaws gently on the object - Read main scale to left of vernier zero - Find vernier division that aligns with main scale - Add vernier reading to main scale reading



27.3.2 Time Measurements



Instrument
Precision




Stopwatch
0.01 s (display to 0.1 s)


Digital timer
0.01 s or better



Timing oscillations: - Ignore first few oscillations - Start timing when motion is steady - Time multiple oscillations (e.g., 20) - Calculate average: \(T = \frac{t}{n}\) - Human reaction time: ~0.3–0.5 s



27.3.3 Mass and Volume
Electronic balance: - Zero before use - Do not place wet objects directly on pan - Use container of known mass for powders/liquids
Measuring cylinder: - Place on level surface - Read at eye level with bottom of meniscus - Remove air bubbles before reading
Displacement method (irregular objects): - Record initial volume \(V_1\) - Immerse object completely - Record final volume \(V_2\) - Volume of object: \(V = V_2 - V_1\)



27.3.4 Temperature
Liquid-in-glass thermometer: - Do not use as a stirrer - Read to nearest half division - Avoid parallax error - Ensure bulb is fully immersed - Stir liquid for uniform temperature



27.3.5 Electrical Measurements
Ammeter: - Connect in series - Check zero error - Select appropriate range - Avoid parallax error - Break circuit after readings to minimize heating
Voltmeter: - Connect in parallel - Check zero error - Select appropriate range - Avoid parallax error

title: 27  Practical Skills
text:
27.5 Graphs

27.5.1 Drawing Graphs
Axes: - Label with quantity and unit (e.g., “Time/s”) - Use sensible scales (1, 2, 5, or multiples) - Avoid awkward scales (3, 6, 7, etc.) - Use more than half the graph paper in both directions - Origin not necessarily at (0,0)
Plotting points: - Mark clearly with × or ⊕ - Accuracy: ±½ small square - Use sharp pencil
Best-fit line: - Draw thin, smooth line - Equal number of points on each side - Ignore anomalous points (circle them) - Does not need to pass through all points - Use transparent ruler for straight lines



27.5.2 Analyzing Graphs
Gradient: - Draw large triangle (hypotenuse > ½ line length) - Show triangle on graph - \(\text{Gradient} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}\) - Calculate to 2–3 significant figures - Include units
Intercept: - Read where line crosses axis - Extrapolate if necessary - Include units

title: 27  Practical Skills
text:
27.7 Safety in the Laboratory

27.7.1 General Rules

Before starting:

Read all instructions carefully
Clear work area of unnecessary items
Identify potential hazards

During experiment:

Wear eye protection when required
Follow instructions precisely
Do not perform unauthorized experiments
Keep work area tidy
Never leave heating apparatus unattended

After experiment:

Turn off all equipment
Clean work area
Dispose of materials properly
Wash hands thoroughly





27.7.2 Specific Hazards
Electrical: - Check insulation is not damaged - Do not overload circuits - Use appropriate voltage - Turn off when not in use - Keep away from water
Heating: - Use heat-resistant mat - Handle hot apparatus with tongs - Allow time to cool - Point test tubes away from people
Radioactive sources: - Minimize exposure time - Maximize distance from source - Use shielding (lead containers) - Use tongs to handle sources - Store in locked cabinet
Glass: - Handle with care - Report breakages immediately - Do not use cracked glassware - Clean up broken glass safely

title: 27  Practical Skills
text:
27.8 Evaluating Experiments

27.8.1 Identifying Errors
Systematic errors: - Consistent bias in measurements - Examples: zero error, calibration error, parallax error - Cannot be reduced by repeating
Random errors: - Unpredictable variations - Examples: reaction time, reading fluctuations - Reduced by taking averages
Anomalous results: - Clearly different from pattern - Check for mistakes - Repeat if possible - Exclude from analysis if justified



27.8.2 Improving Experiments
Suggestions for improvement: - Use more precise instruments - Increase number of readings - Extend range of values - Control variables more carefully - Reduce heat loss/energy loss - Minimize friction - Use data loggers for accuracy - Repeat readings for reliability

title: 27  Practical Skills
text:
27.9 Data Analysis

27.9.1 Calculations
Significant figures: - Give answers to same sf as least precise data - Usually 2–3 sf for IGCSE - Do not round intermediate calculations
Uncertainty: - Assume ±10% at IGCSE level - Compare with expected values - Comment on accuracy


27.9.2 Conclusions
Writing conclusions: - State relationship found - Refer to graph/evidence - Compare with expected results - Comment on accuracy - Suggest improvements

title: 29  Common Question Types
text:
29.1 Practical Papers (5 & 6)
Descriptive questions: - Use bullet points for clarity - One mark = one point - Use correct scientific terminology - Be concise but complete - Include relevant details
Graph questions: - Use a ruler for straight lines - Label axes with quantities and units - Choose appropriate scales - Plot points accurately (±½ small square) - Draw smooth best-fit line - Calculate gradient using large triangle
Definitions: - Learn key definitions precisely - Include units where relevant - Examples: speed, acceleration, pressure, power
Laws and principles: - State exactly as learned - Examples: Newton’s laws, conservation of energy, Ohm’s law
Explanations: - Use the structure: “Because… therefore…” - Link cause and effect - Use particle model where appropriate - Refer to relevant physics principles
Comparisons: - Address both items being compared - Use comparative language: “greater than,” “less than,” “similar to” - Give specific differences/similarities

title: 29  Common Question Types
text:
29.1.1 Paper 5: Practical Test
What to expect: - Hands-on experiments in laboratory - Usually 3–4 experiments - 1 hour 15 minutes - 40 marks
Skills tested: - Setting up apparatus correctly - Taking accurate measurements - Recording data in tables - Plotting and analyzing graphs - Drawing conclusions - Evaluating methods
Tips: 1. Read all instructions before starting 2. Set up apparatus carefully 3. Take readings to appropriate precision 4. Record units in table headings 5. Plot graphs neatly and accurately 6. Show all working for calculations 7. Comment on sources of error 8. Suggest realistic improvements



29.1.2 Paper 6: Alternative to Practical
What to expect: - Written questions about practical work - No laboratory work required - 1 hour - 40 marks
Question types: - Drawing and labeling apparatus - Completing data tables - Plotting graphs from given data - Analyzing results - Identifying errors - Suggesting improvements
Preparation: - Know common experimental setups - Understand how to use standard apparatus - Practice drawing circuit diagrams - Learn how to plot and interpret graphs - Understand sources of error - Know how to improve experiments

title: 29  Common Question Types
text:
29.2 Revision Strategies

29.2.1 Before the Exam
Content review: - Create summary notes for each topic - Make formula sheets - Practice past papers - Review practical work - Identify weak areas and focus on them
Formula learning: - Understand what each symbol means - Know the units - Practice rearranging equations - Learn which formulas are provided
Practical skills: - Review all required practicals - Know the methods - Understand sources of error - Practice data analysis



29.2.2 During Revision
Active learning: - Do not just read—practice - Solve problems without looking at solutions - Explain concepts to others - Create mind maps - Use flashcards for definitions
Past papers: - Do under timed conditions - Mark using mark scheme - Identify common question types - Learn from mistakes - Track progress

Checking work: - Verify calculations make sense - Check units are correct - Ensure answers are reasonable - Review multiple choice answers - Check all questions answered
Common mistakes to avoid: - Forgetting units - Wrong number of significant figures - Misreading scales on graphs - Confusing mass and weight - Mixing up series and parallel circuits - Forgetting to convert units (cm to m, etc.) - Not showing working for calculations

title: 29  Common Question Types
text:
29.5 Mark Scheme Insights

29.5.1 How marks are awarded
Method marks (M): - Awarded for correct method - Even if final answer is wrong - Show all working
Accuracy marks (A): - Awarded for correct answer - Dependent on method mark - Must have correct units
Independent marks (B): - Awarded independently - Often for definitions or statements - Do not depend on other marks
Error carried forward (ECF): - If you make an early error - You can still get marks for correct method - Using your incorrect value correctly



29.5.2 Maximizing marks
Show working: - Even if answer is wrong - Method marks available - Helps if you make calculation error - Essential for full credit
Use correct terminology: - Use physics terms precisely - Avoid vague language - Be specific
Answer the question: - Read carefully what is asked - Do not provide irrelevant information - Match answer to command word
Check your answer: - Does it make physical sense? - Are units correct? - Is magnitude reasonable? - Have you answered all parts?

title: 30  Formula Sheet
text: 30.1 Mechanics

title: 30  Formula Sheet
text:
30.1.1 Motion

Average speed: \(v = \frac{s}{t}\)
Acceleration: \(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\)
\(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\)
\(s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2\)



30.1.2 Forces

Weight: \(W = mg\)
Force: \(F = ma\)
Momentum: \(p = mv\)
Impulse: \(F\Delta t = \Delta p\)
Resultant force: \(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\)



30.1.3 Energy and Power

Kinetic energy: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\)
Gravitational potential energy: \(\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h\)
Work done: \(W = Fd\)
Power: \(P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{\Delta E}{t}\)
Efficiency: \(\text{Efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}} \times 100\%\)



30.1.4 Pressure

Pressure: \(p = \frac{F}{A}\)
Pressure in liquids: \(\Delta p = \rho g \Delta h\)



30.1.5 Circular Motion

Centripetal force: \(F = \frac{mv^2}{r}\)

title: 30  Formula Sheet
text:
30.2 Thermal Physics

30.2.1 Temperature

\(T(\text{K}) = \theta(°\text{C}) + 273\)



30.2.2 Thermal Properties

Specific heat capacity: \(c = \frac{\Delta E}{m\Delta\theta}\)
Thermal energy: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)



30.2.3 Gas Laws

\(pV = \text{constant}\) (at constant temperature)

title: 30  Formula Sheet
text:
30.3 Waves

30.3.1 Wave Properties

Wave speed: \(v = f\lambda\)
Frequency: \(f = \frac{1}{T}\)
Refractive index: \(n = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r}\)
Critical angle: \(n = \frac{1}{\sin c}\)

title: 30  Formula Sheet
text:
30.4 Electricity and Magnetism

30.4.1 Electrical Quantities

Charge: \(Q = It\)
Potential difference: \(V = \frac{W}{Q}\)
E.m.f.: \(E = \frac{W}{Q}\)
Resistance: \(R = \frac{V}{I}\)
Electrical power: \(P = IV = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}\)
Electrical energy: \(E = IVt\)



30.4.2 Transformers

\(\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}\)
For 100% efficiency: \(I_pV_p = I_sV_s\)



30.4.3 Magnetic Effects

Force on current-carrying conductor: \(F = BIl\) (Extended)

title: 30  Formula Sheet
text:
30.5 Nuclear Physics

30.5.1 Radioactivity

Half-life calculations: \(N = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\)
where \(n\) = number of half-lives

title: 30  Formula Sheet
text:
30.6 Space Physics

30.6.1 Orbital Motion

Average orbital speed: \(v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}\)
Hubble’s Law: \(H_0 = \frac{v}{d}\)
Age of Universe: \(t \approx \frac{1}{H_0}\)

1 light-year: \(1 \text{ ly} = 9.5 \times 10^{15} \text{ m}\)
